title: Determinants of Cervical Cancer Knowledge Among Parents/Guardians of Girls Aged 9–14 Years In Irepodun, Osun State, Nigeria.
abstract: Background: Cervical cancer accounted for an estimated 13,676 new cases and 7,093 deaths in Nigeria in 2023, despite being largely preventable through human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and screening. Parents and guardians play an important role in informed HPV vaccination decisions. This study assessed the level and predictors of cervical cancer knowledge among parents and guardians of girls aged 9–14 years in Irepodun Local Government Area, Osun State, Nigeria. Methods: A community-based descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 305 parents and guardians selected using multistage sampling. Data were collected using a pretested interviewer-administered questionnaire. Cervical cancer knowledge was assessed using a five-item scale and categorized as poor (0–2) or good (3–5). Data were analyzed using SPSS version 23. Associations were examined using Chi-square tests, followed by multivariable logistic regression. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: Although 55.7% had heard of cervical cancer, only 34.4% demonstrated good knowledge. Educational attainment, occupation, prior awareness, and information source were significantly associated with knowledge at bivariate analysis. After adjustment, respondents with primary (AOR = 8.3; 95% CI: 1.6–42.2), secondary (AOR = 6.0; 95% CI: 1.2–29.3), and tertiary education (AOR = 21.6; 95% CI: 4.0–117.3) had higher odds of good knowledge than those without formal education. Self-employed respondents had lower odds (AOR = 0.4; 95% CI: 0.2–1.0), while those previously aware of cervical cancer had higher odds (AOR = 14.2; 95% CI: 7.0–29.3). Conclusion: Cervical cancer knowledge was low despite moderate awareness. Education and prior awareness were strong predictors of knowledge. Targeted community-based health education should strengthen accurate cervical cancer information, particularly among less-educated and rural populations, to support informed HPV vaccination decisions. Keywords: Cervical cancer; Knowledge; Parents; Determinants; Girls; Nigeria

title: Inflammatory and Nutritional Indices Associated with Histopathological Severity of Cervical Lesions in HPV-Positive Women
abstract: Abstract Objective This study aimed to evaluate the association of inflammatory and nutritional indices, including HALP (Hemoglobin × Albumin × Lymphocyte / Platelet), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade and invasive disease in HPV positive women. Materials and Methods This retrospective observational study included 122 patients who underwent cervical biopsy between January 2020 and December 2025. Patients were classified according to the highest histopathological diagnosis as CIN1 ( n = 39), CIN2 ( n = 30), CIN3 ( n = 35), and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) ( n = 18). Inflammatory indices (HALP, NLR, and SII) were calculated using routine hematological and biochemical parameters. Comparisons among histopathological groups were performed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc tests. Multinomial logistic regression analysis was conducted to identify independent predictors of histopathological severity. Additional analyses were performed according to HPV oncogenic risk groups, including high risk HPV negative (HR (-)), HR HPV positive (+), HR HPV and ultra HR HPV positive (HR + UHR(+)). Results Age, NLR, SII and HALP scores significantly differed across histopathological groups, with SCC patients showing higher age, NLR, SII and lower HALP scores ( p < 0.001, p = 0.008, p = 0.02, p = 0.04 ; respectively). Serum albumin emerged as the strongest independent predictor separating CIN from SCC ( p < 0.001). HPV genotype influenced inflammatory profiles, with HR (+) associated with lower HALP and higher SII values ( p = 0.002 and p = 0.03). In multivariate analysis, NLR remained independently associated only with the CIN3–SCC comparison, whereas HALP and SII failed to reach statistical significance. Conclusion Serum albumin may represent a potential biomarker associated with invasive cervical disease, although its clinical relevance requires confirmation in larger prospective cohorts. Inflammatory indices such as HALP, NLR, and SII appear to reflect disease severity, but their predictive performance may be influenced by HPV oncogenic risk. These findings suggest a potential interaction between systemic inflammatory status and viral oncogenic burden in the progression of cervical neoplasia.

title: Diagnosis and Management of Oral Leukoplakia
abstract: Oral leukoplakia (OLK) is a potentially malignant lesion found in the oral cavity, currently defined by the WHO Collaborating Centre as a predominantly white plaque of questionable risk once other known disorders have been excluded. Its global pooled prevalence is approximately 3.4%, with higher rates in men, in people over 60 years, and in tobacco and alcohol users. This chapter reviews the historical evolution of the definition and terminology from 1861 to the 2020 WHO consensus, the clinical classification into homogeneous and non-homogeneous forms, and the recognised etiological factors: tobacco and areca nut, alcohol and human papillomavirus, Candida infection, chronic local trauma, and the emerging role of the oral microbiome. Histopathology remains the diagnostic gold standard, with dysplasia grade the single strongest prognostic determinant for malignant transformation.Molecular adjuncts such as loss of heterozygosity at 3p/9p/17p, aneuploidy and p53 overexpression, and the cancer-hallmark biomarkers Ki-67, podoplanin and PD-L1. One aggressive form of OLK is proliferative verrucous leukoplakia, which has a higher risk of malignant transformation. A structured clinical workflow, the diagnostic accuracy of adjunctive optical and cytological aids, and risk-stratified management — excision versus active surveillance with risk-factor cessation — are presented, underlining that long-term surveillance remains the cornerstone of care.

title: Social Media and HPV Vaccine Hesitancy: How Misinformation Affects Latino Parents
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine coverage in the United States remains suboptimal, with Latino communities facing disproportionately lower rates and a higher burden of HPV-associated cancers. Health misinformation and disinformation (M&D) on social media represents a barrier to HPV vaccine uptake, yet little empirical evidence exists on how such content shapes vaccine decision-making. We conducted a cross-sectional study of 98 Latino parents drawn from two randomized, community-based prospective trials conducted across four U.S. Eligible participants confirmed their HPV vaccine-eligible child remained unvaccinated and reported active social media use. A structured survey assessed platform use, access frequency, health information-seeking behaviors, and exposure to HPV vaccine-specific social media content. All 98 parents reported regular social media use. Facebook (68%), Instagram (61%), WhatsApp (61%), and YouTube (48%) were the most used platforms. Three-quarters of parents (77%, n = 75) reported vaccine-related social media exposure in the prior year, with 99% (n = 74) characterizing it as negative. Over half (52%, n = 51) recalled HPV vaccine-specific content, all of whom described it as negative. 41% of all parents (n = 40) reported that perceived negative social media content directly influenced their decision to delay or refuse HPV vaccination; this proportion rose to 78% among those with HPV-specific negative exposure. Social media M&D is a self-reported, substantial driver of HPV vaccine hesitancy among Latino parents. Passive exposure and negativity of vaccine content encountered underscore an urgent need for culturally tailored counter-messaging strategies that operate within social media platforms.

abstract_zh: 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 疫苗 在美国的覆盖率仍然不理想,拉丁裔社区面临着 HPV 相关癌症的不成比例的较低发病率和较高负担。社交媒体上的健康错误信息和虚假信息 (M&D) 是 HPV 疫苗 吸收的障碍,但很少有经验证据表明此类内容如何影响 疫苗 决策。我们对 98 名拉丁裔父母进行了一项横断面研究,这些父母来自两项随机、基于社区的前瞻性试验,这些试验在四名符合条件的美国参与者中进行,证实他们符合 HPV 疫苗 条件的孩子仍未接种疫苗,并报告了活跃的社交媒体使用情况。一项结构化调查评估了平台使用情况、访问频率、健康信息寻求行为以及 HPV 疫苗 特定社交媒体内容的暴露情况。所有 98 名家长均表示经常使用社交媒体。Facebook (68%)、Instagram (61%)、WhatsApp (61%) 和 YouTube (48%) 是最常用的平台。四分之三的家长 (77%,n = 75) 报告称,去年曾在社交媒体上曝光过与 疫苗 相关的内容,其中 99% (n = 74) 将其描述为负面。超过一半 (52%,n = 51) 的人回忆起 HPV 疫苗 的特定内容,所有这些人都将其描述为阴性。41% 的家长 (n = 40) 表示,感知到的负面社交媒体内容直接影响了他们推迟或拒绝 HPV 疫苗接种 的决定;在 HPV 特异性阴性暴露人群中,这一比例上升至 78%。据自我报告,社交媒体 M&D 是拉丁裔父母对 HPV 疫苗 犹豫不决的重要驱动因素。所遇到的 疫苗 内容的被动曝光和负面性凸显了迫切需要在社交媒体平台上运作的、根据文化量身定制的反信息策略。

title: HPV DNA Positivity, Genotype Distribution, and Their Relationship With Cytological Findings in Cervical Samples: 2025 Data From a University Hospital
abstract: Giriş: İnsan papilloma virüsü (HPV), serviks kanserinin başlıca etiyolojik etkenidir.HPV prevalansı ve genotip dağılımı coğrafi bölgeye, yaşa ve incelenen popülasyona göre değişiklik gösterebilmektedir.Bu çalışmada, bir üniversite hastanesinde 2025 yılında değerlendirilen servikal örneklerde HPV DNA pozitifliği, genotip dağılımı ve sitolojik bulgular arasındaki ilişkinin araştırılması amaçlanmıştır.Materyal ve Metod: Çalışmaya, 2025 yılında tıbbi mikrobiyoloji laboratuvarında incelenen ve eş zamanlı servikal sitoloji sonucu bulunan, 18 yaş ve üzerindeki hastalara ait servikal sürüntü örnekleri dahil edildi.Birden fazla test sonucu bulunan hastalarda yalnızca ilk başvuruya ait veriler değerlendirildi.Ayrıca HPV DNA genotiplendirmesi gerçek zamanlı polimeraz zincir reaksiyonu yöntemiyle yapıldı.Sitoloji sonuçları Bethesda sınıflamasına göre değerlendirildi ve istatistiksel analizlerde normal veya anormal sitoloji olarak gruplandırıldı.Verilerin analizinde Mann-Whitney U testi, Pearson ki-kare testi ve lojistik regresyon analizi kullanıldı.Bulgular: Çalışmaya toplam 1671 hasta dahil edildi.Örneklerin 364 (%22)'ünde HPV DNA pozitifliği saptandı.Çalışmada HPV pozitif hastaların 252 (%69)'sinde tek genotip, 112 (%31)'sinde ise çoklu genotip pozitifliği saptandı.En sık HPV16, ikinci sıklıkta ise HPV52 genotipi saptandı.İnsan papilloma virüsü pozitif hastaların 60 (%16)'ında, HPV negatif hastaların ise dördünde (%0.3) anormal sitoloji saptandı.Çoklu genotip pozitif örneklerde anormal sitoloji oranı, tek genotip pozitif örneklere göre anlamlı olarak daha yüksekti.İnsan papilloma virüsü pozitif hastaların ortanca yaşı HPV negatif hastalardan, çoklu genotip pozitif hastaların ortanca yaşı ise tek genotip pozitif hastalardan anlamlı olarak düşüktü.Lojistik regresyon analizinde, çoklu HPV infeksiyonunun anormal sitolojiyle bağımsız olarak ilişkili olduğu gösterildi.Sonuç: Çalışmamızda servikal örneklerde HPV pozitiflik oranı %22 olarak saptandı; en sık saptanan genotip ise HPV16 idi.Çoklu HPV infeksiyonu, anormal sitolojiyle bağımsız olarak ilişkili bulundu.Bulgularımız, HPV prevalansı ve genotip dağılımının bölgesel olarak değerlendirilmesinin tarama ve aşılama stratejilerinin planlanmasında yararlı olabileceğini düşündürmektedir.

title: HPV-Associated Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Arab Populations: Histological Heterogeneity, Regional Evidence, and the Syrian Knowledge Gap
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) is biologically and clinically distinct from HPV-independent disease. Classically, HPV-associated OPSCC is nonkeratinizing in morphology, less desmoplastic in stroma, and more lymphoid-rich in background; however, it is increasingly recognized as histologically heterogeneous. Keratinizing, maturing, basaloid, papillary, lymphoepithelial, glandular, and other components can be encountered in an HPV-associated tumor, and recent evidence suggests that such micromorphological diversity may be prognostically significant after HPV association has been demonstrated through established assays. In contrast, research from Arab populations has focused largely on HPV prevalence, p16 expression, genotype, and clinical outcome rather than on detailed histology or tumor organization. This critical review synthesizes evidence from Arab countries (focused on Syria) into the contemporary international literature and suggests a regional framework for understanding HPV-associated OPSCC pathology. Studies from Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have demonstrated HPV-related or p16-positive OPSCC, with widely varying estimates due to differing anatomical selection and testing strategies. Syrian studies identify high-risk HPV in head-and-neck squamous carcinomas but have not yet estimated the HPV-attributable fraction or histology of anatomically verified Syrian OPSCC. We speculate that future regional research should shift from dichotomous HPV categorization to quantitative characterization of squamous maturation, tumor architecture, stromal response, tumor-associated lymphocytes, front of invasion morphology, and spatial tumor heterogeneity. Digital pathology and interpretable artificial intelligence offer exciting opportunities to engage with these questions. A principal unresolved regional question is the extent and biological significance of HPV involvement in oropharyngeal SCCs, while an important research challenge is to understand how HPV-associated carcinogenesis is expressed through regional variations in tissue architecture.
journal: International Journal of Clinical Case Reports and Reviews

source_records.title: HPV-Associated Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Arab Populations: Histological Heterogeneity, Regional Evidence, and the Syrian Knowledge Gap
source_records.abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) is biologically and clinically distinct from HPV-independent disease. Classically, HPV-associated OPSCC is nonkeratinizing in morphology, less desmoplastic in stroma, and more lymphoid-rich in background; however, it is increasingly recognized as histologically heterogeneous. Keratinizing, maturing, basaloid, papillary, lymphoepithelial, glandular, and other components can be encountered in an HPV-associated tumor, and recent evidence suggests that such micromorphological diversity may be prognostically significant after HPV association has been demonstrated through established assays. In contrast, research from Arab populations has focused largely on HPV prevalence, p16 expression, genotype, and clinical outcome rather than on detailed histology or tumor organization. This critical review synthesizes evidence from Arab countries (focused on Syria) into the contemporary international literature and suggests a regional framework for understanding HPV-associated OPSCC pathology. Studies from Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have demonstrated HPV-related or p16-positive OPSCC, with widely varying estimates due to differing anatomical selection and testing strategies. Syrian studies identify high-risk HPV in head-and-neck squamous carcinomas but have not yet estimated the HPV-attributable fraction or histology of anatomically verified Syrian OPSCC. We speculate that future regional research should shift from dichotomous HPV categorization to quantitative characterization of squamous maturation, tumor architecture, stromal response, tumor-associated lymphocytes, front of invasion morphology, and spatial tumor heterogeneity. Digital pathology and interpretable artificial intelligence offer exciting opportunities to engage with these questions. A principal unresolved regional question is the extent and biological significance of HPV involvement in oropharyngeal SCCs, while an important research challenge is to understand how HPV-associated carcinogenesis is expressed through regional variations in tissue architecture.

title: Single-Particle ICP−MS Enabled Multiplex Digital Detection of Nucleic Acids via Feedback Recombinase Polymerase Amplification
abstract: Abstract Digital droplet assays, with their single-molecule sensitivity, hold great promise for early disease diagnosis by enabling precise biomarker quantification and the generation of patient-specific molecular profiles. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP−MS) has shown its great potential in the quantification of biomolecules with elemental labeling strategies. However, the development of ICP−MS-based digital assays has been limited, primarily due to the challenge of efficiently anchoring elemental labels within droplets. To address this, we developed a feedback recombinase polymerase amplification (F-RPA)-based digital analyzer via a facile droplet generator and combined it with single particle (sp)-ICP−MS for the quantitative analysis of human papillomavirus (HPV) genetic markers. In this system, HPV DNA molecules are randomly partitioned across tens of thousands of agarose droplets, following a Poisson distribution. Individual encapsulated target DNA molecules initiate on-demand F-RPA amplification and anchoring of elemental tags for subsequent signal transduction. Leveraging the discrete event counting characteristics and multi-element analytical capabilities of sp-ICP−MS, the digital F-RPA assay achieved highly sensitive and multiplexed analysis, with detection limits as low as 20 copies/μL for HPV16 and 9 copies/μL for HPV18 DNA. The method was validated by quantifying the HPV DNA load in cervical cancer cell lines and further applied to clinical cervical swab samples, where it identified 26 HPV16-positive and 20 HPV18-positive cases with 100% precision. This digital F-RPA sp-ICP−MS system emerges as a robust diagnostic platform for trace biomarker analysis, significantly advancing the role of sp-ICP−MS in digital droplet detection and clinical diagnosis.

title: Introduction
abstract: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide, and India accounts for about 13% of the global burden. On 28 February 2026, India launched its first national human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme, eight years after its National Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (NTAGI) first recommended the vaccine’s inclusion in the Universal Immunisation Programme, and a decade after the 2009-10 Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat demonstration-project controversy that shaped India’s relationship with this vaccine afterward. This narrative review synthesises the evidence a national immunisation decision rests on, across six domains: HPV virology and vaccine pharmacology; global efficacy and immunogenicity trials from the first licensed vaccines through single-dose regimens; the safety evidence base, including the Scandinavian pharmacovigilance cohorts and India’s 2009-10 controversy; the introduction experience of eight national programmes (Australia, England, Sweden, Rwanda, Bhutan, Kenya, Japan, India); the cost-effectiveness evidence for HPV vaccination; and India’s vaccine-development and policy trajectory through the 2026 launch and the licensure of the indigenous Cervavac vaccine. We searched PubMed and Scopus and supplemented peer-reviewed evidence with independently verified grey literature; the full search strategies are in Supplementary File S1. Three independent single-dose datasets, an Indian cohort followed for 12–15 years, a Kenyan trial (KEN SHE), and a Costa Rican trial (ESCUDDO), together show high, concordant single-dose protection over the follow-up each has actually completed, and two Scandinavian pharmacovigilance cohorts with a combined study population exceeding four million, of whom just over half a million were vaccinated, found no safety signal warranting a policy change. Register data show observed cervical cancer reductions of 87% in England (girls offered the vaccine at age 12–13) and 88% in Sweden (women vaccinated before age 17); modelled projections suggest further reductions with sustained coverage. In our assessment, this evidence supports India’s 2026 programme on the vaccination decision itself. The evidence for the rollout’s specific design is more limited: the single-age cohort, the choice of an imported vaccine over the newly trialled indigenous Cervavac, and the eight-year gap between recommendation and launch are less directly supported by published evidence. We conclude that two priorities remain open: closing the screening gap (about 2% in NFHS-5, 2019-21, against a 70% WHO target; later programme data use a different indicator and denominator) and a funded, time-bound plan to move from GAVI-donated supply to domestic manufacture. HPV vaccination prevents cervical cancer through a well-characterised mechanism (VLP-induced neutralising antibody against the L1 capsid antigen), and three vaccine generations now carry two decades of converging efficacy data. Single-dose HPV vaccination is supported by three independent, prospectively followed cohorts (India, Kenya, Costa Rica) and is no longer an emerging idea. WHO recommended it in 2022, and later Indian, Kenyan and Costa Rican reports add to that evidence. It is the basis of India’s 2026 programme design. Large-cohort pharmacovigilance data (> 4 million women followed, ~ 550,000 vaccinated, two countries) show no safety signal warranting a change in policy; the adverse events that actually occur commonly are injection-site reactions and vasovagal syncope, not the rare serious outcomes public concern usually centres on. Observed, register-based cervical cancer reductions of 87–88% are now documented in early-vaccinated cohorts in England and Sweden, evidence that a national programme’s age-of-vaccination choice materially determines its eventual impact. India’s 2026 programme is well justified on the vaccination decision itself. In our assessment, its narrower age-cohort design and its eight-year delay from recommendation to launch reflect resource and institutional constraints rather than scientific uncertainty, and should be evaluated on that separate basis. In our view, screening remains a major gap in India’s cervical cancer control effort. The last survey estimate was about 2% (NFHS-5, 2019-21) against a 70% WHO target. Programme data use a different indicator and denominator. Screening protects the women currently at highest risk.

title: The Unique Sexual and Reproductive Health Needs of Community College Students: Evidence from a National Sample
abstract: Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) are crucial issues for young adults, and college campuses often provide education and services to support students in this area. However, most research does not delineate the needs of community college students, and the literature focusing solely on community college students has limitations. This study aims to address those shortcomings by investigating potential differences between community and four-year college students’ SRH. Using data from the 2022–23 American College Health Association-National College Health Assessment III, SRH behaviors and conditions were examined among 127,345 students at community colleges and four-year institutions. Initial bivariate differences based on student status at a community college or four-year institution were assessed by chi-square tests. Binomial logistic regressions with institution type and demographics as co-variates were used to identify significant predictors for SRH behaviors and conditions. Chi-square results indicated community college students had lower rates of condom and contraceptive use, were more likely to have ever been tested for HIV and experience a pregnancy in the prior year, and to have ever been diagnosed with endometriosis, Hepatitis B or C, HPV/genital warts, and polycystic ovary syndrome compared to students at four-year institutions. For the regressions, enrollment type remained a significant predictor only for contraception use and being tested for HIV, indicating differences in student demographics contribute more to SRH differences than institution type. This study provides a critically needed examination of college students’ SRH to better understand the unique experiences of community college students and to inform future community college SRH initiatives.

full_text: Abstract Objectives This study aimed to investigate the genetic variability of the E6 and E7 genes of HR HPV isolates obtained from women diagnosed with cervical carcinoma in North Karnataka, India. Methods 102 cervical tissue samples from women with histopathologically confirmed cervical carcinoma were analyzed. HPV DNA was detected using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The E6 and E7 gene regions of 34 randomly selected sub samples based on geno type were amplified and subjected to sanger sequencing. Sequence alignments were performed against reference strains K02718 (HPV16), X05015(HPV18) and X74479 (HPV45) to identify nucleotide and amino acid variations. Results HPV DNA was detected in 102 cervical carcinoma samples. HPV 16 and 18 were the predominant genotypes, followed by HPV 45. Multiple nucleotide substitutions were identified in both E6 and E7 genes of HPV 16, 18 and 45. A total of 26 mutations were identified within E6 and E7 regions of HPV16, 18 and 45. Of which 14 were novel mutations and 12 were already reported. Among fourteen novel mutations, 6 were synonymous mutations and 8 were missense mutations. Conclusion The presence of genetic variability in the E6 and E7 oncogenes of HRHPV among cervical carcinoma patients from North Karnataka highlights regional viral diversity. These variations may have biological relevance in HPV-associated carcinogenesis and underscore the importance of continuous molecular surveillance. title_original: Molecular Profiling of High-Risk HPV E6 and E7 Oncogenes in Cervical Carcinoma: Evidence from a Regional Indian Cohort

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the genetic variability of the E6 and E7 genes of high-risk HPV isolates obtained from women diagnosed with cervical carcinoma in North Karnataka, India. The scientific problem is the need to understand regional viral diversity in HPV-associated cervical cancer.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using 102 cervical tissue samples from women with histopathologically confirmed cervical carcinoma. The study focused on high-risk HPV types, specifically HPV16, HPV18, and HPV45, collected from North Karnataka, India.
analysis.methods: HPV DNA was detected using polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and the E6 and E7 gene regions of 34 randomly selected sub samples based on genotype were amplified and subjected to Sanger sequencing. Sequence alignments were performed against reference strains K02718 (HPV16), X05015 (HPV18) and X74479 (HPV45) to identify nucleotide and amino acid variations.
analysis.main_results: HPV DNA was detected in 102 cervical carcinoma samples. Multiple nucleotide substitutions were identified in both E6 and E7 genes of HPV16, HPV18 and HPV45. Of these, 14 were novel mutations and 12 were already reported.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The presence of genetic variability in the E6 and E7 oncogenes of high-risk HPV among cervical carcinoma patients from North Karnataka highlights regional viral diversity. Among the fourteen novel mutations, 6 were synonymous mutations and 8 were missense mutations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These variations may have biological relevance in HPV-associated carcinogenesis and underscore the importance of continuous molecular surveillance for effective prevention and treatment strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and analysis of a single regional cohort, which may affect generalisability. The evidence is moderate as it is based on sequence analysis of a limited number of samples.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the genetic variability of the E6 and E7 oncogenes of high-risk HPV isolates from cervical carcinoma patients in North Karnataka, India. Using PCR and Sanger sequencing, the researchers analyzed 102 cervical tissue samples and identified multiple nucleotide substitutions in HPV16, HPV18, and HPV45. Of these, 14 were novel mutations, with 6 being synonymous and 8 missense. The findings highlight regional viral diversity in HPV-associated cervical cancer, suggesting potential biological relevance in carcinogenesis. The study's significance lies in its implications for molecular surveillance, as it underscores the need for ongoing monitoring of HPV genetic variations. However, the study's retrospective design and limited regional scope may affect its generalisability, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

full_text: AbstractObjectiveTo conduct a three-year cervical cancer screen in Zhejiang, Sichuan, Beijing, and Inner Mongolia and analyse clinical and population data to identify possible improvements to the screening protocol.MethodsA standard protocol including human papillomavirus (HPV) detection, cytology test, colposcopy, and histopathology inspection was adapted for the screening. Additional HPV genotyping was performed for participants in Sichuan, Beijing, and Inner Mongolia.Results12,086 women were included in this study, and 178 cases of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) were identified. Detailed analyses on features of age, region, ethnicity, and origin showed a notable correlation between age strata and high-grade CIN rates. Moreover, apart from HPV16/18, other HPV types such as HPV33, HPV52, and HPV58 were found to be enriched in high-grade CIN cases, as was repeat positivity.ConclusionsOur results suggest that age, HPV16, and ThinPrep cytologic test (TCT) are prominent exploratory predictors for CIN2+ detection, and HPV33, 52, and 58 may pose higher risks than other non-HPV16/18 types. Future studies incorporating prospective effectiveness and health-economic evaluation are required to validate the clinical utility of these predictors.Keywords: age, cervical cancer screening, genotyping, HPV, repeat positivity 2.Methodology2.1.Study population and screening protocolThis research was conducted in 4 provinces (including a municipality): Sichuan, Zhejiang, Inner Mongolia and Beijing. Women between 20 and 65 years of age with a history of sexual activity were recruited for screening. The exclusion criteria were: (a) a previous diagnosis of cervical cancer; (b) current chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or both; (c) being pregnant or within 8 weeks postpartum; (d) a history of pelvic radiotherapy or chemotherapy, cervical resection within 12 months before the study, or total hysterectomy; and (e) a history of HPV vaccination. A 3-year screening and follow-up protocol, illustrated in Figure 1, was implemented. In brief, participants underwent routine testing (pooled detection of 18 high-risk HPV (hrHPV) types with separate identification of HPV16/18) and TCTs at the beginning of screening and were assigned to colposcopy assessment, next-year follow-up, or third-year follow-up according to the results. At the next-year follow-up, TCTs were performed, and participants with abnormal cytology were referred to colposcopy, while those with a TCT result negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM) were scheduled for another follow-up before the third year. At the third-year follow-up, HPV genotyping and TCTs were performed, and participants with a positive HPV result or abnormal cytology were referred to colposcopy. Participants who underwent colposcopy had histological samples taken for pathological diagnosis. Those diagnosed with CIN2 or worse (CIN2+) left the study and were treated accordingly, while the others continued to the next follow-up until the end of the study. Extended genotyping was available for all Sichuan participants, for participants enrolled during the last three screening rounds in Beijing and Inner Mongolia, and for none in Zhejiang. This was an operational, site- and round-dependent implementation rather than a random sample of the full cohort. Repeat positivity was defined as positive results at two consecutive available HPV tests. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractObjectiveTo conduct a three-year cervical cancer screen in Zhejiang, Sichuan, Beijing, and Inner Mongolia and analyse clinical and population data to identify possible improvements to the screening protocol.MethodsA standard protocol including human papillomavirus (HPV) detection, cytology test, colposcopy, and histopathology inspection was adapted for the screening. Additional HPV genotyping was performed for participants in Sichuan, Beijing, and Inner Mongolia.Results12,086 women were included in this study, and 178 cases of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) were identified. Detailed analyses on features of age, region, ethnicity, and origin showed a notable correlation between age strata and high-grade CIN rates. Moreover, apart from HPV16/18, other HPV types such as HPV33, HPV52, and HPV58 were found to be enriched in high-grade CIN cases, as was repeat positivity.ConclusionsOur results suggest that age, HPV16, and ThinPrep cytologic test (TCT) are prominent exploratory predictors for CIN2+ detection, and HPV33, 52, and 58 may pose higher risks than other non-HPV16/18 types. Future studies incorporating prospective effectiveness and health-economic evaluation are required to validate the clinical utility of these predictors.Keywords: age, cervical cancer screening, genotyping, HPV, repeat positivity

full_text_sections.discussion: 4.Discussion4.1.Model-assisted feature importance analysisRF models were implemented to identify crucial features from the screening data and produced results that were verified by analyses of subgroups with sufficient sample sizes. As the full baseline dataset was used for model fitting without an independent test set, these results are exploratory associations rather than causal effects. The importance of feature selection has been recognised in machine learning (Parikh and Zitnick, 2010) and data mining (Visalakshi and Radha, 2014), making it a standalone research topic (Kaur et al., 2021) in machine learning. However, the application of these techniques has only recently extended to medical practice alongside artificial intelligence and has mostly involved visual recognition (Abdualgalil and Abraham, 2020). We found these techniques are particularly useful in analysing complex data with multiple categorical variables with different numbers of categories, together with age as a numerical variable, which makes them powerful tools for analysing big data, such as population data and epidemiologic data, for assisting decision making or protocol adjusting.SHAP values and permutation importance were both adopted in this study to provide perspectives with and without feature interactions. While SHAP values are obtained by considering influences between features (Lundberg and Lee, 2017), permutation importance is calculated by shuffling values of the target feature regardless of its relation to other features. Applying both methods may outline dependent and independent importance of the features, and when differences in importance are reported by the different methods, relationships between the relevant features can be analysed further. Besides, compared with permutation importance, SHAP values may provide further information on feature influence for individual samples, improving model transparency.4.2.Potential application of the age factor in cancer screeningIn this study, cervical cancer risk was associated with population features, such as region, ethnicity, urbanisation level at birth, and age, along with HPV infections and TCT results. Among these population features, some, such as region and ethnicity, displayed notable but not quantifiable associations with histopathology results, while age showed similar associations repeatedly across regions and ethnicities in this study. Furthermore, CIN2+ cases identified in participants not followed annually showed a clear bias toward older participants. However, this pattern may reflect surveillance bias and lower TCT sensitivity in older women, rather than a purely biological age effect. The biological effect of age and the surveillance-bias effect are confounded and cannot be separated in the present design. HPV prevalence has been reported for a number of regions across China by age stratum (Yan et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023), but age has rarely been analysed separately from other features or in depth. CIN2+ rates and HPV infection rates for certain populations were reported here by age stratum and showed similar intergroup profiles, but the relevant case numbers were small, limiting the reliability of these results. In addition, other researchers have reported similar HPV infection profiles but different CIN2+ profiles in other populations (Castellsagué et al., 2016; Song et al., 2020). Meanwhile, conflicting results suggesting that the importance of age is unclear have also been reported (Carozzi et al., 2014). A lack of attention to older women was noted by some researchers, but the relevant characteristics were not compared with those of other age groups to establish age-specific screening protocols (Chen et al., 2025). The main cause of the inconsistency between these profiles has not been fully identified, so further investigation is required.4.3.Test frequency and HPV infection historyAccording to local guidelines (Branch of Cancer Prevention and Control CPMA et al., 2023), persistent HPV infection was defined as testing positive for high-risk HPV in two consecutive tests at an interval of 6 to 12 months. This required a corresponding testing or screening frequency, consistent with the guideline requirements for those infected with HPV. The results of this study demonstrated a notable association between high-grade lesions and a history of high-risk HPV infection, highlighting the importance of considering repeat hrHPV positivity in screening. On the other hand, CIN2+ cases identified during the Year 3 follow-up accounted for 39.41% of the total 178 CIN2+ cases. Specifically, 20 cases (38.46% of Year 3 cases, including one cancer) were identified in women not included in annual follow-up. These 20 protocol-delayed cases, concentrated at ages 50–59, are likely attributable to surveillance bias and lower TCT sensitivity rather than age biology alone. These observations identify a surveillance limitation in the current protocol. However, earlier studies indicated that screening every 3–5 years in the general population was more economically efficient, as the benefits of shortening the screening interval to 1 year were lower than the associated increase in costs (Miller, 2003; Lees et al., 2016). Since this study did not randomise screening intervals, compare clinical strategies, or collect cost data, it cannot establish that shorter population-wide intervals are effective or cost-effective. Recommendations for screening optimisation require prospective effectiveness and health-economic evaluation. Besides, our results demonstrated insufficient willingness to undergo annual screening tests, indicating that more education and promotion regarding cervical cancer and HPV infection were required (Wang et al., 2023).4.4.HPV genotyping for additional high-risk HPV typesOur results suggested that HPV genotype was another important factor in cervical cancer risk estimation. Different cancer risks associated with HPV types other than HPV16/18 have been reported in many studies (Carozzi et al., 2014; Li et al., 2024), but guidelines for these specific HPV types have not yet been published in China. This study suggests that HPV33, 52, and 58 may be associated with a higher cervical cancer risk than other non-HPV16/18 high-risk types, and similar results have been reported by other researchers (Yan et al., 2021; Song et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). Due to limited HPV genotyping data, only the most common high-risk types were mentioned in the results presented here, but other less common types should not be overlooked. For example, Chen et al. described the pathogenicity of HPV82 and its association with viral load (Chen et al., 2025), while the pathogenicity of HPV45 has been reported in studies conducted in other countries (Chen et al., 2014; Koestler et al., 2025). In this study, although HPV45 and HPV82 were detected in only a small number of cases, HPV82 was detected more frequently in CIN2+ cases and CIN2+ cases with repeat positivity, which agrees with the findings mentioned above. Moreover, an understanding of local HPV type distribution may enable in-depth studies of infections with multiple HPV types (Salazar et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2021) and more efficient vaccination (Jiang et al., 2019). Routine implementation of extended genotyping requires confirmation in uniformly tested populations to fully validate its clinical utility and cost-effectiveness.4.5.Limitations and future requirementsThis study has several limitations. Second, routine HPV retesting was not conducted in Years 1 and 2 of the screening protocol, limiting the ability to assess type-specific persistence of HPV infections. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn this research, rates of high-grade CIN and high-risk HPV infection were analysed across different regions, ethnicities, and age strata. Based on exploratory RF/SHAP modelling, our results suggested an association between age and the CIN2+ rate, and age, HPV16, and TCT were prominent exploratory predictors. Directly standardised comparisons did not support greater susceptibility by region, birthplace, or ethnicity, and genotype findings arose from incomplete site-dependent testing. However, given the limitations outlined above—including non-uniform extended genotyping, absence of confounder data, and sparse CIN2+ outcomes—these findings are hypothesis-generating and should be interpreted with caution. Moreover, our preliminary observations from the subset with extended genotyping suggest that HPV33, 52, and 58 may pose higher risks than other non-HPV16/18 types. But these findings require confirmation in future studies with uniform extended genotyping across all participants to fully validate their significance. Finally, while HPV genotyping and repeat positivity show potential for cancer risk estimation, independent validation, uniform genotyping, prespecified multivariable analysis, and health-economic evaluation are required before screening-interval or policy changes can be recommended.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionCervical cancer is the fourth most common malignant tumour in women (Li et al., 2025), causing around 250,000 deaths annually in China (Cao et al., 2021). Fortunately, it is highly preventable as most cervical cancers are induced by human papillomavirus (HPV) infections (Crosbie et al., 2013). The common cervical cancer prevention approach implemented by China is screening with cytology inspection, HPV testing, and colposcopy-guided biopsy (Molina et al., 2024). However, due to complicated conditions across the country, screening protocols and coverage vary in different regions, and a more effective and adaptable protocol is required (Jinghe and Qiang, 2022).Efforts were made to collect data worldwide to optimise resources and strategies for regional cervical cancer screening. Castellsagué et al. summarised HPV genotypes detected in cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) cases and reported differences in vaccination contribution between continents (Castellsagué et al., 2016), suggesting that screening strategies should align with local vaccination coverage. Some researchers focused on the burden of HPV-related diseases and emphasised that a higher burden is likely associated with limited screening resources in developing countries (Kombe Kombe et al., 2021). Perkins et al. pointed out that HPV detection can be used to replace cytology tests, especially in regions lacking screening resources (Perkins et al., 2023). Meanwhile, Wheeler et al. suggested that HPV genotyping may reduce unnecessary colposcopy examinations in cervical cancer screening (Wheeler et al., 2014). In China, although ThinPrep cytologic tests (TCTs) and HPV tests are the main screening methods for cervical cancer screening, similar but differing protocols were introduced by the national cervical cancer screening guidelines (Li et al., 2023) for adaptation according to local healthcare resources and requirements. In a more recent guideline for cervical cancer screening in China (Li et al., 2025), HPV testing was suggested for use as a primary test with TCTs rather than as a secondary test after TCT, and younger women, such as those aged 25 to 30, were advised to be included as part of the main target population.In this study, HPV testing and TCTs were used as the primary tests for cervical cancer screening conducted in Zhejiang, Sichuan, Beijing, and Inner Mongolia. All high-risk HPV types were included in the detection assay, but only HPV16 and HPV18 were genotyped. Additional HPV genotyping was conducted for participants in Sichuan, Beijing, and Inner Mongolia, providing insights into regional HPV type distributions. Population features were combined with testing results to explore possible improvements to the current national protocol or potential adjustments for the regions involved. 2.1.Study population and screening protocolThis research was conducted in 4 provinces (including a municipality): Sichuan, Zhejiang, Inner Mongolia and Beijing. Women between 20 and 65 years of age with a history of sexual activity were recruited for screening. The exclusion criteria were: (a) a previous diagnosis of cervical cancer; (b) current chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or both; (c) being pregnant or within 8 weeks postpartum; (d) a history of pelvic radiotherapy or chemotherapy, cervical resection within 12 months before the study, or total hysterectomy; and (e) a history of HPV vaccination. A 3-year screening and follow-up protocol, illustrated in Figure 1, was implemented. In brief, participants underwent routine testing (pooled detection of 18 high-risk HPV (hrHPV) types with separate identification of HPV16/18) and TCTs at the beginning of screening and were assigned to colposcopy assessment, next-year follow-up, or third-year follow-up according to the results. At the next-year follow-up, TCTs were performed, and participants with abnormal cytology were referred to colposcopy, while those with a TCT result negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM) were scheduled for another follow-up before the third year. At the third-year follow-up, HPV genotyping and TCTs were performed, and participants with a positive HPV result or abnormal cytology were referred to colposcopy. Participants who underwent colposcopy had histological samples taken for pathological diagnosis. Those diagnosed with CIN2 or worse (CIN2+) left the study and were treated accordingly, while the others continued to the next follow-up until the end of the study. Extended genotyping was available for all Sichuan participants, for participants enrolled during the last three screening rounds in Beijing and Inner Mongolia, and for none in Zhejiang. This was an operational, site- and round-dependent implementation rather than a random sample of the full cohort. Repeat positivity was defined as positive results at two consecutive available HPV tests. Because routine HPV testing was not performed in Years 1 and 2, and extended genotyping was not uniformly conducted at baseline, same-genotype continuity was not consistently demonstrable. Therefore, clearance, reinfection, new infection, and true persistence cannot be distinguished, and this measure must not be interpreted as guideline-defined persistent infection.Figure 1Process of cervical cancer screening.Flowchart of the three-year cervical screening pathway. Cervical exfoliated cells undergo HPV genotyping and ThinPrep cytology testing (TCT). Depending on baseline results, participants proceed to first-year TCT, return for HPV and TCT testing in year three, or undergo colposcopy and histopathology. Abnormal cytology during annual follow-up prompts colposcopy; HPV positivity or abnormal cytology in year three also prompts colposcopy. Histopathology showing CIN2 or worse leads to “Trial end.” Participants with normal final cytology or histopathology no worse than CIN1 reach “Follow-up end.” Arrows connect the test results to subsequent assessments and endpoints. 2.2.Sample collectionCervical exfoliated cells were collected by gynaecologists using collectors (Hologic Inc., Marlborough, MA, USA) and preserved in PreservCyt Solution (Hologic Inc., Marlborough, MA, USA) for TCT and HPV genotyping within 48 h. 2.3.HPV detectionDNA was extracted using DNA extraction kits (Yaneng BIOscience (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, Guangdong, China), and HPV DNA was routinely tested using HPV DNA detection and HPV16/18 genotyping kits (PCR-fluorescence probing; Yaneng BIOscience (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, Guangdong, China), which can detect 18 hrHPV types in a pooled assay (16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 53, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68, 73, and 82) and separately genotype HPV16 and HPV18. For all extended type-specific genotyping, HPV DNA detection and genotyping kits (PCR-reverse dot hybridisation; Yaneng BIOscience (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, Guangdong, China) were used. The detection experiments were conducted strictly according to the manufacturer’s instructions. 2.4.Liquid-based cytologyExfoliated cell cytology was examined by experienced pathologists according to the 2014 Bethesda System and characterised as follows: (a) negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM); (b) atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US); (c) atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) (ASC-H); (d) atypical glandular cells (AGC); (e) low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL); and (f) high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL). 2.5.Colposcopy and histopathologyColposcopies were performed by gynaecologists, and biopsies were performed when visible lesions were found. The histopathological examinations were then performed to establish final diagnoses of <CIN1, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grades 1 to 3, and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). 2.6.Statistical analysis and modellingStatistical analyses were performed using Python 3.6 with the NumPy module. title_original: A multi-centre study on cervical cancer screening reveals population-related impact on cervical intraepithelial neoplasia rate

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the impact of cervical cancer screening on the population-related rates of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 2 or worse (CIN2+), addressing the need to understand how screening programs affect disease prevalence across different demographic and geographic groups.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a multi-centre, operational study conducted in four provinces (Sichuan, Zhejiang, Inner Mongolia, and Beijing) involving 12,086 women aged 20 to 65 with a history of sexual activity. Participants were recruited for cervical cancer screening, with specific exclusion criteria including prior cervical cancer diagnosis, current chemotherapy or radiotherapy, pregnancy, and HPV vaccination history.
analysis.methods: Cervical exfoliated cells were collected and preserved for TCT and HPV genotyping. HPV DNA was detected using PCR-fluorescence probing, and extended genotyping was performed for participants in Sichuan, Beijing, and Inner Mongolia. A 10-fold cross-validation was used to assess the model's ability to capture relations between features and CIN2+ results, and feature importance was evaluated using permutation-induced changes in prediction accuracy and SHAP values.
analysis.main_results: At first enrolment, the HPV detection rate was 14.81%, and the abnormal TCT rate was 7.84%. A total of 93 patients were diagnosed with CIN2+ and referred for further treatment. The overall cumulative three-year CIN2+ rate was 1.47% (178/12,086), while the baseline rate was 0.77% (93/12,086). Crude CIN2+ rates varied between regions, with the lowest in Zhejiang (0.43%) and the highest in Inner Mongolia (0.93%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that while some numerical variations in crude CIN2+ rates were observed across subgroups, these differences did not reach statistical significance in the cohort. This study provides novel insights into the population-related impact of cervical cancer screening on CIN2+ rates, highlighting the importance of demographic and geographic factors.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform cervical cancer screening programs by highlighting the need to consider demographic and geographic variations in CIN2+ rates, potentially guiding targeted interventions and resource allocation in high-risk regions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was an operational, site- and round-dependent implementation rather than a random sample, and the number of positive cases at the first screen was insufficient for robust statistical analyses on certain features. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This multi-centre study investigated the impact of cervical cancer screening on cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) rates across different demographic and geographic groups. The study included 12,086 women aged 20 to 65 with a history of sexual activity, recruited from four provinces in China. HPV detection and TCT were performed, with extended genotyping available in some regions. The overall cumulative three-year CIN2+ rate was 1.47%, while the baseline rate was 0.77%. Crude CIN2+ rates varied between regions, with the lowest in Zhejiang and the highest in Inner Mongolia. However, statistical tests showed no significant differences across subgroups. The study's findings suggest that while demographic and geographic factors may influence CIN2+ rates, further research is needed to validate these observations. The evidence is moderate due to the study's operational design and limited sample size for certain analyses.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在调查 宫颈癌 筛查对宫颈上皮内瘤变 (CIN) 2 级或更严重 (CIN2+) 的人群相关率的影响,解决了解筛查计划如何影响不同人口和地理群体的疾病 患病率 的需要。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一项在四个省(四川、浙江、内蒙古和北京)开展的多中心、操作性研究,涉及 12,086 名年龄在 20 岁至 65 岁之间有性活动史的女性。招募参与者进行 宫颈癌 筛查,具体排除标准包括既往 宫颈癌、诊断、当前化疗或放疗、妊娠和 HPV 疫苗接种 病史。
elements_zh.methods: 收集并保存宫颈脱落细胞用于 TCT 和 HPV 基因分型。使用 PCR 荧光探针检测 HPV DNA,并对四川、北京和内蒙古的参与者进行了扩展基因分型。使用 10 倍交叉验证来评估模型捕获特征和 CIN2+ 结果之间关系的能力,并使用排列引起的预测精度和 SHAP 值的变化来评估特征重要性。
elements_zh.main_results: 首次入组时HPV检出率为14.81%,TCT异常率为7.84%。共有 93 名患者被诊断为 CIN2+,并转诊进一步接受 治疗。总体累计三年 CIN2+ 率为 1.47% (178/12,086),而基线率为 0.77% (93/12,086)。粗CIN2+比率因地区而异,浙江最低(0.43%),内蒙古最高(0.93%)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,虽然在各个亚组中观察到粗 CIN2+ 率存在一些数值差异,但这些差异在 队列研究 中并未达到统计显着性。这项研究为 宫颈癌 筛查对 CIN2+ 率与人群相关的影响提供了新颖的见解,强调了人口和地理因素的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可以为 宫颈癌 筛查计划提供信息,强调需要考虑 CIN2+ 发生率的人口和地理差异,并有可能指导高风险地区的针对性干预措施和资源分配。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究是一项可操作的、与地点和回合相关的实施,而不是随机样本,并且第一次筛选的阳性病例数量不足以对某些特征进行稳健的统计分析。由于这些限制,证据是中等的。

analysis_zh.main_results: 首次入组时HPV检出率为14.81%,TCT异常率为7.84%。共有 93 名患者被诊断为 CIN2+,并转诊进一步接受 治疗。总体累计三年 CIN2+ 率为 1.47% (178/12,086),而基线率为 0.77% (93/12,086)。粗CIN2+比率因地区而异,浙江最低(0.43%),内蒙古最高(0.93%)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,虽然在各个亚组中观察到粗 CIN2+ 率存在一些数值差异,但这些差异在 队列研究 中并未达到统计显着性。这项研究为 宫颈癌 筛查对 CIN2+ 率与人群相关的影响提供了新颖的见解,强调了人口和地理因素的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可以为 宫颈癌 筛查计划提供信息,强调需要考虑 CIN2+ 发生率的人口和地理差异,并有可能指导高风险地区的针对性干预措施和资源分配。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究是一项可操作的、与地点和回合相关的实施,而不是随机样本,并且第一次筛选的阳性病例数量不足以对某些特征进行稳健的统计分析。由于这些限制,证据是中等的。

title: Penile lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma: a rare variant of human papillomavirus-associated penile cancer.
abstract: Penile lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma (LELC) is an extremely rare variant of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), with only five previously reported cases. We describe a man in his late 70s with an incidental 3 cm penile lesion. Initial biopsy revealed high-grade penile intraepithelial neoplasia and subsequent partial glansectomy demonstrated poorly differentiated human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated SCC with features of LELC, with positive p16 and p40 immunohistochemical stain. He then underwent completion glansectomy, partial penectomy and bilateral sentinel lymph node biopsy, which showed localised moderately differentiated SCC without features of LELC. At 24 months post-surgery, he remains recurrence-free. While classified as HPV-associated, one-third of reported cases are p16-negative, raising uncertainty about its pathogenesis. In the limited number of described cases, penile LELC appears to have a similar prognosis to other penile SCC subtypes and management should follow current existing guidelines.

full_text: Abstract Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women globally, with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection as the primary etiological factor. Cervical precancerous lesions, including high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions and adenocarcinoma in situ, represent the critical window for intervention prior to invasive cancer development. However, additional factors such as immunosuppression, smoking, and microbiome composition also play crucial roles in the development of cervical precancerous lesions. While HPV vaccination, screening, and treatment have reduced cancer incidence, these must be complemented by personalized approaches that target the molecular mechanisms driving carcinogenesis. Key dysregulated tumor suppressors (e.g., p16) and signaling pathways (PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin) highlight the need for advanced therapeutic strategies. The immune microenvironment also plays a critical role in cancer progression, suggesting potential for immunotherapy. Promising biomarkers like p16, Ki67, and microRNAs require integration with technologies such as single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics for deeper insights into tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment dynamics. Additionally, while deep learning models hold promise in improving diagnostic accuracy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), challenges such as data variability and interpretability need addressing. In conclusion, incorporating genomics, transcriptomics, immunotherapy, and artificial intelligence will enable more personalized and effective interventions, ultimately reducing the global burden of cervical cancer. analysis.research_question_and_background: This study investigates the molecular mechanisms linking HPV infection to cervical precancer, emphasizing the role of immunosuppression, smoking, and microbiome composition in lesion development.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a comprehensive review of existing literature and data on HPV infection, cervical precancerous lesions, and related molecular and immunological factors, with a focus on human papillomavirus and its association with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.
analysis.methods: The study integrates genomic, transcriptomic, and immunological data, utilizing single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics to explore tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment dynamics, while also discussing the application of deep learning models in improving diagnostic accuracy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.
analysis.main_results: The study reports that key dysregulated tumor suppressors, such as p16, and signaling pathways like PI3K/AKT/mTOR and Wnt/β-catenin are critical in carcinogenesis, and that the immune microenvironment significantly influences cancer progression.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these findings as highlighting the necessity for advanced therapeutic strategies targeting molecular mechanisms and the immune microenvironment, and they emphasize the novelty of integrating emerging technologies like single-cell RNA sequencing and artificial intelligence into cervical cancer research.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform the development of more personalized interventions for cervical cancer prevention and treatment, particularly through targeted therapies and improved diagnostic tools that incorporate genomics and immunological insights.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a review of existing literature and does not present original experimental data, which may affect the strength of its conclusions. However, the integration of multiple technologies and pathways provides a robust framework for future research.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the molecular mechanisms connecting HPV infection to cervical precancer, highlighting the role of immunosuppression, smoking, and microbiome composition in lesion development. It reviews the importance of dysregulated tumor suppressors and signaling pathways in carcinogenesis and discusses the potential of immunotherapy and emerging technologies like single-cell RNA sequencing and artificial intelligence in improving cervical cancer interventions. The findings suggest that personalized approaches targeting these mechanisms could reduce the global burden of cervical cancer. However, the study is limited to a literature review and does not present original experimental data, which may affect the strength of its conclusions.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究探讨了 HPV 感染与宫颈癌前病变之间的分子机制,强调了免疫抑制、吸烟和微生物组组成在病变发展中的作用。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究综合回顾了有关HPV感染、宫颈癌前病变以及相关分子和免疫因素的现有文献和数据,重点关注人乳头瘤病毒及其与宫颈上皮内瘤变的关系。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究整合基因组学、转录组学和免疫学数据,利用单细胞RNA测序和空间转录组学来探索肿瘤异质性和微环境动态,同时还讨论了深度学习模型在提高宫颈上皮内瘤变诊断准确性中的应用。
elements_zh.main_results: 该研究报告称,关键失调的肿瘤抑制因子(例如 p16)以及信号通路(例如 PI3K/AKT/mTOR 和 Wnt/β-连环蛋白)在癌症发生中至关重要,并且免疫微环境显着影响癌症进展。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为强调针对分子机制和免疫微环境的先进治疗策略的必要性,并强调将单细胞 RNA 测序和人工智能等新兴技术整合到 宫颈癌 研究中的新颖性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为 宫颈癌 预防和 治疗 开发更个性化的干预措施提供信息,特别是通过结合基因组学和免疫学见解的靶向治疗和改进的诊断工具。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于对现有文献的回顾,并未提供原始实验数据,这可能会影响其结论的力度。然而,多种技术和途径的整合为未来的研究提供了一个强大的框架。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究探讨了 HPV 感染与宫颈癌前病变之间的分子机制,强调了免疫抑制、吸烟和微生物组组成在病变发展中的作用。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究综合回顾了有关HPV感染、宫颈癌前病变以及相关分子和免疫因素的现有文献和数据,重点关注人乳头瘤病毒及其与宫颈上皮内瘤变的关系。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究整合基因组学、转录组学和免疫学数据,利用单细胞RNA测序和空间转录组学来探索肿瘤异质性和微环境动态,同时还讨论了深度学习模型在提高宫颈上皮内瘤变诊断准确性中的应用。
analysis_zh.main_results: 该研究报告称,关键失调的肿瘤抑制因子(例如 p16)以及信号通路(例如 PI3K/AKT/mTOR 和 Wnt/β-连环蛋白)在癌症发生中至关重要,并且免疫微环境显着影响癌症进展。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为强调针对分子机制和免疫微环境的先进治疗策略的必要性,并强调将单细胞 RNA 测序和人工智能等新兴技术整合到 宫颈癌 研究中的新颖性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为 宫颈癌 预防和 治疗 开发更个性化的干预措施提供信息,特别是通过结合基因组学和免疫学见解的靶向治疗和改进的诊断工具。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于对现有文献的回顾,并未提供原始实验数据,这可能会影响其结论的力度。然而,多种技术和途径的整合为未来的研究提供了一个强大的框架。

full_text: Abstract Persistent infection with high-risk Human Papillomavirus (hr-HPV) is a majorrisk factor in the development of cervical cancer, and the distribution of viral genotypes and the occurrence of multiple HPV infections are reported worldwide. Therefore, region-specific data on HPV genotype distribution are essential for strengthening viral surveillance and guiding cervical cancer prevention strategies. In this cross-sectional study, HPV infection status and genotype distribution were investigated among 152 histologically confirmed cervical cancer patients and 132 cancer-free women as control group. Cervical swab samples were subjected to real-time PCR-based HPV genotyping capable of detecting 14 high-risk and 2 low-risk HPV types. HPV DNA was identified in 90.1% of cervical cancer cases, compared with 9.1% of control group, demonstrating a statistically significant difference between the two groups (p < 0.0001). The likelihood of HPV infection was substantially higher among cancer patients (OR = 91.3; 95% CI: 41.1–202.8). HPV16 emerged as the most frequently detected genotype, followed by HPV18. A high proportion of cervical cancer patients (48.0%) harboured multiple HPV genotype infections, whereas multiple infections were less common among control group (2.3%). HPV-associated cervical cancer burden peaked in women aged 40–60 years. The data indicate a high prevalence of various hr-HPV types and co-infections in cervical cancer patients, which underscores the need for comprehensive hr-HPV typing studies to monitor the virus and also supports the need for prevention strategies in areas with high prevalence. full_text: AbstractBackgroundPrimary endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the cervix (PEAC) is a rare subtype of HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma. Due to overlapping clinical, histological, and immunophenotypic features, distinguishing PEAC from endometrioid adenocarcinoma of endometrial origin with cervical involvement remains challenging.Case presentationWe present two cases illustrating the diagnostic pitfalls in determining the primary site of endometrioid adenocarcinoma involving the cervix. The first case was ultimately diagnosed as PEAC based on comprehensive evaluation of the hysterectomy specimen, with no identifiable endometrial primary lesion. Molecular testing revealed microsatellite instability-high status and a pathogenic PMS2 germline variant associated with Lynch syndrome. The second case represented lower uterine segment endometrioid adenocarcinoma with secondary cervical involvement, which closely mimicked a cervical primary tumor. Careful assessment of tumor distribution and the relationship between uterine and cervical lesions supported an endometrial origin.ConclusionThe primary site of endometrioid adenocarcinoma involving the cervix cannot be reliably determined by morphology or immunohistochemistry alone. Accurate diagnosis requires integrated evaluation of clinical, radiological, pathological, and molecular findings, with comprehensive examination of the hysterectomy specimen—particularly assessment of the tumor epicenter, lesion distribution, and the presence of precursor lesions—remaining crucial for definitive site assignment in operable cases. The suggestive framework presented here is intended to provide a systematic, teaching-oriented approach to this challenging differential diagnosis.Keywords: cervical involvement, endometrial carcinoma, immunohistochemistry, lynch syndrome, primary endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the cervix 3.DiscussionPEAC is a rare subtype of HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma. Due to its considerable overlap with lower uterine segment endometrioid carcinoma in clinical presentation, morphology, and immunophenotype, accurate preoperative diagnosis remains challenging. As no universally accepted diagnostic criteria have been established, the diagnosis relies on a comprehensive assessment of clinical findings, imaging features, and pathological evaluation.The two cases presented herein represent two clinically important diagnostic scenarios. Case 1 was ultimately confirmed as primary endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the cervix, although an endometrial origin could not be excluded preoperatively. In contrast, Case 2 represented lower uterine segment endometrioid carcinoma with secondary cervical involvement, which closely mimicked a primary cervical tumor in clinical and pathological features. These two cases demonstrate that the primary site of endometrioid adenocarcinoma involving the cervix cannot be reliably determined based solely on morphology or immunophenotype.Gross examination may provide initial clues regarding the primary site of the tumor. Cervical primary tumors typically demonstrate a cervical-centered distribution, whereas endometrioid carcinomas of the uterine corpus are usually centered within the endometrial cavity. However, tumor location and size alone cannot reliably determine the site of origin, as secondary cervical involvement may occasionally be more extensive than the primary lesion (7). In our two cases, preoperative biopsy specimens, including cervical biopsy and endometrial sampling, showed similar morphological and immunophenotypic features, making it difficult to distinguish the tumor origin. The final diagnosis relied on comprehensive evaluation of the radical hysterectomy specimens, particularly the overall tumor distribution and the relationship between cervical and endometrial lesions. These findings further emphasize that determination of the primary site should not be based solely on limited biopsy specimens.Immunohistochemical markers, including ER, PR, p16, and p53, often show overlapping expression patterns in these two types of adenocarcinomas and therefore cannot be used alone to determine the primary site (6, 8, 9). In both cases presented in this study, the tumors demonstrated ER and PR positivity, patchy p16 expression, and a wild-type p53 staining pattern, indicating that immunophenotypic findings should be considered supportive rather than definitive evidence for determining tumor origin. In diagnostically challenging cases, particularly those with poorly differentiated morphology, HPV testing and molecular classification may provide additional supportive information in selected diagnostically challenging cases.Table 1 summarizes a suggestive, teaching-oriented diagnostic framework integrating clinical, radiological, pathological, immunohistochemical, and molecular findings. This framework is derived from the present cases and available literature and is intended to systematize diagnostic reasoning rather than to serve as a validated clinical decision rule or a new diagnostic standard. Based on the findings of the present study and previous reports, a practical diagnostic approach can be proposed for cases of endometrioid adenocarcinoma involving the cervix (1–4, 10, 11). First, clinical presentation and imaging findings should be carefully evaluated to identify the tumor epicenter and determine whether the lesion is primarily cervical or endometrial in origin. Second, cervical biopsy and endometrial sampling should be performed to assess the extent and distribution of the lesions at both sites. Third, immunohistochemical analysis can be used to exclude HPV-associated cervical adenocarcinoma and other specific histological subtypes. Finally, comprehensive evaluation of the entire surgical specimen remains essential, with particular attention to tumor distribution, the relationship between cervical and endometrial lesions, surrounding tissue changes, and the presence of in situ or precursor lesions. The primary site should ultimately be determined through integrated clinicopathological correlation and, whenever feasible, multidisciplinary discussion. not prospectively validatedThis framework has important limitations. It is based on two illustrative cases and a narrative synthesis of the available literature, and it has not undergone prospective or external validation. Therefore, it should not be regarded as a formal diagnostic rule. Its application may be constrained by sampling error in cervical biopsy or endometrial curettage specimens, overlapping morphological and immunophenotypic features, and limited access to high-quality imaging, HPV testing, or molecular assays in different practice settings. In cases with discordant clinical, radiological, and pathological findings, multidisciplinary review and additional targeted sampling, when feasible, may be helpful. However, in operable cases, definitive assignment of the primary site may still depend on comprehensive examination of the hysterectomy specimen. Thus, the framework is intended primarily as a practical teaching tool to guide systematic diagnostic thinking.It is important to emphasize that when preoperative pathological findings are discordant with clinical or radiological features, diagnosis should not be based solely on limited biopsy specimens. Misinterpretation of the primary site may result in inaccurate staging and inappropriate initial treatment planning. For example, when cervical biopsy demonstrates endometrioid adenocarcinoma but imaging suggests involvement of the endometrial cavity, an endometrial origin should be carefully considered and further evaluated. Accurate determination of the primary site is therefore critical, as cervical and endometrial carcinomas differ substantially in FIGO staging, surgical management, lymph node assessment, and indications for adjuvant therapy.The therapeutic consequences of an incorrect assignment of the primary site should also be considered. Although treatment strategies may overlap in selected patients with advanced disease, cervical and endometrial carcinomas are managed according to distinct treatment paradigms. For a cervical primary, treatment is generally determined by cervical cancer stage and may include radical surgery for selected early-stage tumors or definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy with brachytherapy for locally advanced disease. In contrast, endometrial carcinoma is typically managed by total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and surgical staging, followed by risk-adapted adjuvant therapy based on factors such as histologic subtype, grade, myometrial invasion, lymphovascular space invasion, nodal status, and molecular classification. Consequently, misclassification may lead to an inappropriate treatment sequence or surgical procedure, inadequate or excessive lymph node assessment, inappropriate radiotherapy field design, omission or inappropriate use of brachytherapy, and inaccurate prognostic counseling and surveillance planning.
