full_text: Primary vaginal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a rare clinical entity, with few prospective studies regarding its treatment available in the literature. We report a case of a 64-year-old female patient with a two-year history of vulvar itching, burning, and intermittent vulvar bleeding. She was diagnosed with stage III (T2, N1, M0) vaginal SCC. The patient subsequently received chemotherapy with cisplatin, external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), as well as high-dose-rate (HDR) cylinder brachytherapy. She achieved a complete clinical and radiographic response, with no evidence of disease on examination or post-treatment PET at six-month follow-up. This case highlights a multimodal treatment approach for advanced vaginal SCC and contributes to the limited body of literature guiding management of this rare malignancy. DiscussionPrimary vaginal cancer is rare, accounting for only 1-2% of all gynecologic cancers [1,2]. Table 1 summarizes incidence rates for all gynecologic malignancies [3]. Of the primary vaginal cancers, squamous cell carcinoma is the most common histology, representing between 80% and 90% of these malignancies. Adenocarcinoma represents between 5% and 10% of malignancies, with other histologies such as neuroendocrine carcinoma and melanoma making up the remainder of diagnoses [6].Table 1Incidence rates of gynecological malignancies in the United States, 2018-2022.Cancer siteRate per 100,000 woman-yearsPercentage of gynecological malignanciesCervix uteri7.715.5Corpus and uterus28.357.1Ovary10.320.8Vagina0.71.4Vulva2.65.2Risk factors for vaginal SCC include high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, with HPV16 being the most predominant form [7,8]. One retrospective study of 593 patients with vaginal SCC showed that 66.7% of patients had a high-risk strain of HPV [9]. It is more common in older, post-menopausal women, reflecting the accumulation of risk factors over time. Like many malignancies, tobacco smoking and immunosuppression are strongly associated with the risk of developing vaginal cancer [10].The most common symptom of vaginal cancer is painless vaginal bleeding and discharge [10]. In more advanced disease, it can impact nearby organs, leading to urinary tract symptoms such as dysuria, urinary retention, and hematuria [10]. Tumors invading the posterior vaginal wall may produce gastrointestinal symptoms such as constipation or hematochezia [10].The preferred imaging modality for pretreatment assessment and recurrent vaginal cancer is MRI. PET/CT is used for detecting nodal and distant metastases, as well as recurrent disease [6]. While imaging findings are widely used to assess tumor size and guide therapy, the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) guidelines note that they should not be used to change the initial clinical stage [1].Staging is generally performed by combining the following two systems: the FIGO guidelines and the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) system [6]. According to FIGO criteria, a tumor involving the cervix must be classified as a cervical primary and one involving the vulva as a vulvar primary; primary vaginal carcinoma is in this respect a diagnosis of exclusion [1]. This distinction is particularly relevant in patients such as ours, with a prior history of HPV-related cervical and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, in whom multifocal or metachronous lower genital tract disease must be considered. Notably, p16 positivity and HPV association are shared across HPV-driven neoplasia of the cervix, vagina, and vulva, and therefore cannot by themselves localize the site of origin; the distinction rests on anatomic and clinical distribution. In this case, prior hysterectomy precluded a cervical primary, no invasive vulvar lesion was identified on examination, and the tumor was centered within the vagina without vulvar involvement. Our patient was therefore classified as having stage III (T2, N1, M0) primary vaginal SCC, with invasion of nearby structures and nodal metastasis near the vaginal cuff.Tumor stage at the time of diagnosis is the strongest prognostic factor for vaginal SCC [11,12]. In one study of 124 patients, the five-year disease-specific survival (DSS) rates for vaginal cancer (including SCC and adenocarcinoma) were 84.3%, 73.7%, 78.6%, and 26.5% for stage I, II, III, and IV, respectively [13]. In another study of 91 patients with primary vaginal SCC, the two-year overall survival rates were 96.2%, 92.3%, 66.6%, and 25.0% for stages I, II, III, and IV, respectively [14]. Measures of tumor spread, including advanced stage (III/IV) disease, lymph node metastasis, and tumors larger than 4 cm, are all negative prognostic factors [15]. Tumors located outside the upper one-third of the vagina also carry poor prognostic value, potentially owing to greater proximity to organs such as the bladder and rectum [15]. Favorable prognostic factors for vaginal SCC include presence of high-risk HPV DNA, p16 positivity (used as a surrogate marker for HPV infection), and low Molecular Immunology Borstel-1 (MIB-1) index [7,15].Tumor grade and degree of differentiation have also been studied as potential prognostic indicators. In a Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER)-based analysis of primary vaginal cancer, five-year cause-specific survival differed significantly by grade on univariate analysis (61.7%, 61.0%, 55.1%, and 36.2% for grade I through IV, respectively; grade IV vs. grade I, HR: 1.82, p=0.013), but grade did not retain independent significance once tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) stage, tumor size, and treatment modality were included in multivariate modeling [16]. This suggests that grade may correlate with disease behavior but is not established as an independent predictor of outcome apart from stage, underscoring that the absence of grading data in the present case, while a limitation, is less likely to materially affect interpretation of her outcome than would, for example, missing stage or HPV status.According to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Clinical Practice Guidelines, the treatment options for stage I vaginal SCC include radiation therapy or surgical resection [17]. Radiation therapy is preferred as a primary treatment due to the decreased risk of incidental organ damage and consists of intracavitary brachytherapy (preferred for cases with lesions <2 cm and thickness <5 mm) or EBRT with intracavitary brachytherapy [17]. Because of anatomical considerations, such as proximity to the bladder, surgical resection is considered only if complete resection with clear margins is possible and the likelihood of needing future adjuvant radiotherapy is low [14,17].The NCCN guidelines recommend platinum-based chemoradiation with brachytherapy or EBRT with brachytherapy as the first-line treatment for stage II-IVA cancers [17]. Within this treatment paradigm, brachytherapy serves a distinct role as a boost to the primary tumor following EBRT, rather than as a stand-alone modality, in locally advanced disease. Analogous to its function in cervical cancer, a brachytherapy boost permits dose escalation to the vaginal tumor bed beyond what can be safely delivered by EBRT alone, while limiting dose to the adjacent bladder and rectum through the rapid dose fall-off characteristic of intracavitary and interstitial techniques [5]. Image-guided adaptive brachytherapy, using target concepts developed specifically for primary vaginal cancer, has been associated with improved local control when delivered without unnecessary treatment delay [5].In 2024, a prospective study on vaginal cancer was performed on 21 patients with varying stages of disease using a standardized trimodal approach. Combining EBRT, cisplatin-based chemotherapy, and brachytherapy, the two-year actuarial local control, metastasis-free survival, and overall survival rates were 79.4%, 90.5%, and 79.4%, respectively [18].LimitationsThe most fundamental limitation is that this is a single case report. Findings from a single patient cannot be generalized to the broader population of patients with vaginal SCC, and no causal inferences can be drawn regarding treatment efficacy. The favorable outcome observed may reflect patient-specific factors, most notably her HPV-positive/p16-positive status, a known favorable prognostic marker, rather than the treatment approach itself. Without a comparator arm or a larger cohort, it is impossible to disentangle the relative contribution of tumor biology, patient factors, and treatment technique to the observed response [7,15].Further pathologic characterization, including tumor grade and degree of differentiation, was sought but could not be obtained. The limited specimen supported a cytologic diagnosis but was insufficient for full histopathologic grading. Repeat biopsy was recommended to obtain adequate tissue; however, the patient, who had a severe alcohol-use disorder characterized by daily consumption, episodes of blackout, and multiple traumatic falls, declined to pursue further diagnostic evaluation. Consequently, tumor grade and degree of differentiation could not be determined, and the pathologic data available for this case remain limited to histologic subtype.The follow-up period extends only to six months post-treatment. Given that vaginal SCC recurrences can occur years after initial treatment, the current follow-up is insufficient to draw conclusions about durable local control, disease-free survival, or overall survival. Longer-term surveillance, including the planned three- and six-month visits extending to annual follow-up, will be necessary to meaningfully assess durability of response and to capture late toxicity.Related to this, the assessment of late treatment-related morbidity is similarly limited by the short observation window. Radiation-associated toxicities, including vaginal stenosis, mucosal ulceration, and genitourinary or gastrointestinal complications, are known to manifest or worsen over months to years following completion of therapy [5]. As such, this report cannot speak to the patient's long-term functional or quality-of-life outcomes, both of which are critical considerations in a malignancy located so close to the bladder, urethra, and rectum.Additionally, because vaginal SCC is rare and disease-specific phase III data are lacking, this patient's treatment plan was extrapolated largely from cervical cancer protocols. While this is standard practice in the field given the paucity of vaginal-cancer-specific evidence, it introduces uncertainty as to whether the dosing, fractionation, and chemotherapy regimen used represent the optimal approach for vaginal primary disease specifically, as opposed to an adapted cervical cancer protocol.Finally, as a single-institution case managed by a single multidisciplinary team, the treatment planning, imaging interpretation, and follow-up protocols reflect institution-specific practices and resources that may not be uniformly available or reproducible elsewhere, thereby limiting the external applicability of this approach. ConclusionsWe presented a case of stage III (T2, N1, M0) primary vaginal SCC in a patient with a prior history of HPV-related lower genital tract neoplasia, treated with a trimodal approach of concurrent cisplatin-based chemotherapy, EBRT with volumetric modulated arc therapy/intensity-modulated radiation therapy/image-guided radiation therapy/simultaneous integrated boost (VMAT/IMRT/IGRT/SIB) planning, and HDR cylinder brachytherapy. She achieved a clinically and radiographically disease-free status at six-month follow-up, an outcome that may reflect favorable biologic features, HPV positivity, and p16 overexpression, as much as the treatment delivered.Given the limited follow-up, this case should be viewed as a single illustrative data point rather than a demonstration of treatment efficacy. Continued longitudinal follow-up of this patient, alongside additional cases and pooled retrospective analyses, will be necessary to characterize durable outcomes, late toxicity, and optimal treatment sequencing, and to move the field beyond reliance on cervical cancer-derived protocols toward vaginal-cancer-specific standards of care. Despite treatment with spiramycin, later changed to pyrimethamine-based therapy, and ursodeoxycholic acid, liver injury progressed (ALT/AST 1,363/466 U/L). Amniocentesis at 25 weeks showed negative T. gondii PCR. At 27 weeks, liver injury peaked (ALT/AST 1,734/728 U/L); anti-SS-A/Ro52 antibodies were detected, and bile acids subsequently increased to 82.4 μmol/L. Extensive investigations excluded viral hepatitis and did not support autoimmune hepatitis, while serial fetal assessment and amniotic fluid PCR showed no evidence of congenital toxoplasmosis. The clinical picture was considered most consistent with multifactorial liver injury involving possible drug-induced hepatotoxicity and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy in the setting of suspected toxoplasmosis. Labor was induced at 38 weeks. A healthy male infant (3,140 g, Apgar scores 10/10) was delivered vaginally. Three days postpartum, ALT/AST decreased to 90/57 U/L.ConclusionSevere transaminitis during pregnancy may have a multifactorial etiology, particularly when infectious, pregnancy-specific, medication-related, and immunological findings coexist. This case highlights the importance of careful differential diagnosis and multidisciplinary management when severe hepatocellular injury develops during pregnancy. DiscussionToxoplasmosis and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy are well-recognized conditions that may complicate pregnancy. However, the coexistence of severe and persistent liver injury in this setting presents a considerable diagnostic challenge. This case highlights the complexity of evaluating severe hepatocellular injury in the setting of suspected maternal toxoplasmosis and subsequent intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, while also raising the possibility of drug-induced liver injury associated with antiparasitic therapy. We believe this report serves as an important reminder that marked transaminitis during pregnancy may have a multifactorial etiology and should not be attributed solely to more common pregnancy-specific liver disorders such as preeclampsia, HELLP syndrome, or acute fatty liver of pregnancy.Toxoplasmosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the obligate intracellular protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. It is one of the most common chronic parasitic infections worldwide, affecting approximately one-third of the global population. The prevalence of toxoplasmosis varies considerably across geographic regions and is influenced by climatic conditions, dietary habits, and environmental exposures. Among women of reproductive age in industrialized countries, seroprevalence rates range from 10% to 50%. Higher rates, reaching up to 80%, have been reported in certain tropical regions where exposure to contaminated soil, undercooked meat, or untreated water is common (9, 10). Primary maternal infection during pregnancy is of particular concern because of the risk of transplacental transmission and potentially severe fetal consequences, including neurological and ophthalmological complications (11). Establishing whether primary maternal infection occurred during pregnancy requires careful interpretation of Toxoplasma-specific IgG and IgM antibodies together with IgG avidity and serial serological testing. Persistent IgM positivity alone does not necessarily indicate recent primary infection, whereas higher IgG avidity, particularly when detected early in pregnancy, may support infection acquired before conception. Therefore, serological findings should be interpreted together with their temporal evolution and, when indicated, fetal assessment and amniotic-fluid PCR. Acute toxoplasmosis is asymptomatic in more than 80% of immunocompetent individuals. When symptoms occur, they are typically mild and non-specific, including fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy. Cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common clinical manifestation and may persist for several weeks. Less frequently, hepatosplenomegaly and skin rash may be observed. Although hepatic involvement is uncommon, elevated liver enzymes and, rarely, clinically significant hepatitis have been described in patients with acute toxoplasmosis. Experimental studies further support a direct role of Toxoplasma gondii in hepatic injury. In a murine model of acute toxoplasmosis, T. gondii macrophage migration inhibitory factor (TgMIF) promoted hepatocyte pyroptosis and recruitment of proinflammatory macrophages, resulting in severe inflammatory liver damage. These findings suggest that parasite-induced immune activation may contribute to hepatocellular injury during acute toxoplasmosis (12). Consequently, toxoplasmosis should be considered among the differential diagnoses of unexplained liver injury, particularly when accompanied by compatible clinical and serological findings (9). At presentation, toxoplasmosis was considered in the differential diagnosis because several clinical and serological findings raised suspicion of maternal T. gondii infection. The patient presented with fatigue, pruritus, cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, markedly elevated Toxoplasma IgG titres, persistent Toxoplasma IgM positivity, and elevated liver enzymes. However, the timing of maternal infection could not be established. The initial Toxoplasma IgG avidity index was elevated (54.6%), suggesting that infection may have been acquired before conception rather than during pregnancy. Furthermore, serial serological testing demonstrated a progressive decline in Toxoplasma IgG titres. Repeated fetal ultrasonographic examinations remained unremarkable throughout pregnancy, showing no sonographic signs of congenital toxoplasmosis, and amniotic-fluid polymerase chain reaction testing for Toxoplasma gondii was negative. Importantly, liver enzyme levels continued to increase despite antiparasitic treatment, reaching peak values of ALT 1,734 U/L and AST 728 U/L. Spiramycin has been used clinically for decades and is generally considered well tolerated, with gastrointestinal adverse effects and mild cutaneous reactions being the most frequently reported side effects. Unlike several other macrolides, convincing evidence linking spiramycin monotherapy to clinically significant hepatitis remains limited (13). Hussein et al. described four patients who developed moderate-to-severe liver injury after exposure to a spiramycin-metronidazole combination, including one patient who required liver transplantation because of subacute massive hepatic necrosis (14). Because metronidazole was co-administered in these cases, causality could not be attributed specifically to spiramycin, and this report therefore provides only limited evidence for spiramycin-associated hepatotoxicity. Evidence regarding pyrimethamine-associated hepatotoxicity remains limited. However, pyrimethamine-containing regimens have been linked to rare cases of clinically apparent liver injury, including severe hepatocellular damage and acute liver failure (15). It remains unclear whether pyrimethamine alone can cause liver injury, as most reported cases occurred during combination therapy with sulfonamides. In an analysis of pediatric hepatic adverse events reported to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System, pyrimethamine was identified among several newly detected drugs potentially associated with liver injury. Although causality could not be established, these findings indicate a possible association between pyrimethamine-containing therapy and liver injury that warrants further investigation (16). Furthermore, the most pronounced biochemical deterioration occurred during prolonged antiparasitic therapy, while serological markers of toxoplasmosis were gradually improving. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis including more than 42 million pregnancies estimated the global incidence of ICP at 2.9%, although substantial geographical variation exists, with the highest incidence reported in Asia and lower rates observed in developed countries (19). Clinically, ICP is characterized by pruritus and elevated serum bile acid concentrations and is associated with an increased risk of adverse perinatal outcomes (20). However, although elevated aminotransferase levels are frequently observed in ICP, liver enzyme elevations are typically mild to moderate and are not considered the defining biochemical feature of the disease (21). At the same time, Tregs, MDSCs, M2-like macrophages, TGF-β, IL-10, hypoxia, lactate accumulation, and extracellular matrix barriers collectively restrict γδ T-cell trafficking, activation, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity. Under sustained suppressive conditions, γδ T cells may shift from cytotoxic effector states toward exhausted, regulatory, or IL-17-producing phenotypes, which may partially explain the inconsistent prognostic significance of γδ T-cell infiltration in cervical cancer. Although HPV vaccination and screening have reduced disease incidence, outcomes for advanced and recurrent cervical cancer remain poor, and conventional treatments provide limited benefit (2). However, their roles in cervical cancer are complex because γδ T-cell infiltration and function may vary according to subset composition and the tumor genomic landscape (4).Persistent HPV infection may further reshape γδ T-cell immunity through multiple immune-evasion mechanisms. Although direct evidence linking HPV oncoproteins to γδ T-cell dysfunction remains limited, HPV-associated changes in cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-18 may indirectly regulate γδ T-cell activation. Recent single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies now enable high-resolution characterization of γδ T-cell heterogeneity, functional states, and spatial interactions with tumor cells, CD8+ T cells, and dendritic cells (7). Their abundance in cervical mucosal tissues is relatively low under physiological conditions but may increase following inflammatory or tumor-associated recruitment (10). Vδ3 T cells are much less abundant under homeostatic conditions but may expand during chronic viral infection and in selected tumor microenvironments, although their biological significance remains insufficiently characterized (1). The differentiation and functional polarization of γδ T-cell subsets are further shaped by transcription factors such as RORγt, Eomes, and T-bet, together with cytokines including IL-7 and TGF-β, thereby influencing their tissue-homing and effector programs (11). full_text: PurposeRecurrent or second primary head and neck cancer (rsHNC) presents a radiotherapeutic challenge due to limited tolerance of previously irradiated tissues. These patients could benefit from dose painting (DP), which focuses on delivering maximal dose to areas of high tumor burden while respecting dose constraints to organs at risk. In this study, we compare clinical outcomes in one group receiving standard reirradiation with a group receiving 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT-guided DP.MethodsOur standard reirradiation regimen is hyperfractionated radiotherapy (RT) of 1.5 Gy x 40 (60 Gy total dose). For DP, we defined two FDG-based prescription volumes receiving at least 65 Gy and 70 Gy. Thirteen patients receiving standard RT were compared with 10 DP patients. Toxicity was scored using CTCAE v3.0. Disease-related endpoints were locoregional control (LRC), disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS).ResultsThe mean composite toxicity score was maximal at the end of RT, with varying patterns across the CTCAE items. No significant difference in toxicity was found between the groups except for dysphagia at 6 months, where the standard RT group had worse scores (p=0.01). No differences were found in LRC and DFS. Two-year OS was 50% in the DP group versus 15% in the standard group (p=0.04), although this may reflect higher comorbidity in the standard group.ConclusionDP of rsHNC did not increase toxicity compared with standard reirradiation. No evidence of improved disease control was found. However, DP may benefit selected patients, and future studies should focus on identifying these candidates.Clinical trial registrationhttps://clinicaltrials.gov, identifier NCT02921581. Materials and methodsPatientsThis sub-study is part of a larger prospective, longitudinal observational cohort study titled “RIOT - Reirradiation or Other Treatment of patients with Head and Neck cancer unsuited for radical RT, evaluation with patient reported outcomes (RIOT)” conducted at Oslo University Hospital (12). Inclusion criteria for the sub-study were histologically or cytologically confirmed squamous cell carcinoma in the head and neck region, planned hyperfractionated reirradiation (HFR) without concomitant systemic therapy, age ≥18 years, with ability to respond to questionnaires. The exclusion criterion was previous reirradiation. Reirradiation was not recommended within 6 months after primary RT and for patients with RT-related severe trismus, ulcerations or osteoradionecrosis. In the present sub-study, patients with inoperable disease planned for HFR were included and consisted of two groups: 1) A control group of 13 patients who received standard HFR (no DP). 2) Ten patients who received FDG-PET-guided DP (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT02921581). The primary endpoint was feasibility (success rate and workload) of implementing the DP technique. Secondary endpoints were toxicity and tumor response.This study was approved by the Regional Ethics Committee (Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics, Southeast Norway). Informed consent was obtained from all patients.Treatment planningAll imaging for treatment planning was performed on an RT-compatible flat table with head support and a radiotherapy fixation mask. The patients in the control group underwent a contrast-enhanced CT scan (Brilliance Big Bore CT, Philips Healthcare, Best, The Netherlands) from the skull base to mid chest with the arms down. The patients in the DP group had a contrast-enhanced FDG-PET/CT scan (Biograph 32, Siemens Healthcare, Munich, Germany). full_text_sections.abstract: PurposeRecurrent or second primary head and neck cancer (rsHNC) presents a radiotherapeutic challenge due to limited tolerance of previously irradiated tissues. These patients could benefit from dose painting (DP), which focuses on delivering maximal dose to areas of high tumor burden while respecting dose constraints to organs at risk. In this study, we compare clinical outcomes in one group receiving standard reirradiation with a group receiving 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT-guided DP.MethodsOur standard reirradiation regimen is hyperfractionated radiotherapy (RT) of 1.5 Gy x 40 (60 Gy total dose). For DP, we defined two FDG-based prescription volumes receiving at least 65 Gy and 70 Gy. Thirteen patients receiving standard RT were compared with 10 DP patients. Toxicity was scored using CTCAE v3.0. Disease-related endpoints were locoregional control (LRC), disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS).ResultsThe mean composite toxicity score was maximal at the end of RT, with varying patterns across the CTCAE items. No significant difference in toxicity was found between the groups except for dysphagia at 6 months, where the standard RT group had worse scores (p=0.01). No differences were found in LRC and DFS. Two-year OS was 50% in the DP group versus 15% in the standard group (p=0.04), although this may reflect higher comorbidity in the standard group.ConclusionDP of rsHNC did not increase toxicity compared with standard reirradiation. No evidence of improved disease control was found. However, DP may benefit selected patients, and future studies should focus on identifying these candidates.Clinical trial registrationhttps://clinicaltrials.gov, identifier NCT02921581.

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionDose painting in the reirradiation setting requires integration of PET/CT imaging, heterogeneous dose prescription, treatment planning, and patient-specific quality assurance while maintaining safe exposure of previously irradiated normal tissues. In this study, FDG-PET-guided DP was delivered successfully to all patients, meeting the prespecified feasibility endpoint. The additional planning and pre-treatment quality-assurance procedures were manageable and did not prevent treatment delivery. These findings show that DP can be incorporated into a clinical reirradiation workflow and support its further prospective evaluation.To improve the understanding of the clinical outcomes in the DP group, we included a control group of 13 patients from a larger observational cohort study. The patients in the control group had also received high-dose reirradiation for inoperable disease but with homogeneous target dose. The patients in the control group had poorer performance status and more comorbidity. After reirradiation, the acute and late toxicity in the two groups were comparable, lending support to the hypothesis that DP does not increase toxicity for the dose levels used in this study.Notably, fatal bleeding (carotid blow out) was the most serious late event, occurring in three patients in the control group, one of whom had no documented cancer progression at the time of the event.We have found two other DP reirradiation studies in the literature (10, 11). Schatteman et al. did a pilot study (n=10) similar to the current investigation, including rsHNC. The dose prescribed to the target volume was 60.0 - 100.5 Gy EQD2Gy (alfa/beta = 3 Gy) compared to 54.0-75.8 EQD2Gy in the present study. Concomitant cetuximab was given to six of the patients in the Schatteman study, and no control group was included. They reported similar toxicity rates as in our study, despite using a different late toxicity grading system (SOMA-LENT). Tan et al. presented a randomized reirradiation trial (n=150) on MRI-guided DP for patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma using a target dose of 60–68 Gy EQD2Gy compared to homogeneous dose of 60 EQD2Gy in the control group (11). The patients received induction chemotherapy with three cycles of gemcitabine and cisplatin. They reported eight patients with massive nasal bleeding and six of these died. There were no differences in grade 3 or higher toxicity.We did not find evidence of increased treatment effect in the DP group apart from increased OS, which we attribute to less comorbidity in the DP group. The 2-year LRC and OS observed in the present study were comparable to those reported by Langendijk et al, with 2-year LRC and OS rates of 27% and 28%, respectively (15). The study of Schatteman et al. (10) also found similar disease control rates as in the present study. In the randomized trial by Tan et al. (11) there was evidence of better disease outcome in the DP group, but this has less relevance for non-nasopharyngeal HNC as in our study.In the present study, the 2-year LRC was numerically lower in the DP group than in the standard group (22% vs. 45%), although this difference was not statistically significant. The 2-year LRC estimates should be interpreted with caution, as they are based on very few patients remaining at risk at this time point. Nevertheless, we chose to report the 2-year estimates to facilitate comparison with the results reported by Langendijk et al. (15).Most locoregional failures in the DP group occurred within the high-dose treatment volume. While this finding should be interpreted cautiously for such a small cohort, the dose escalation used in the present study may therefore have been insufficient to achieve control of aggressive recurrent disease. The two other reirradiation DP studies support further exploration of more intensive focal escalation (10, 11). However, potential gains in local control must be balanced against the narrow therapeutic window in previously irradiated tissues, where higher doses may increase the risk of severe late toxicity. Future approaches may therefore consider higher doses to smaller, anatomically confined subvolumes, with rigorous assessment of cumulative organ-at-risk doses and patient selection. Advanced optimization strategies such as multicriteria optimization (MCO) could potentially support such individualized planning by facilitating exploration of trade-offs between focal dose escalation and cumulative dose to previously irradiated organs at risk. However, while MCO has demonstrated dosimetric and workflow benefits in HNC planning (16), its clinical value specifically for reirradiation and DP remains to be established. Regarding patient selection, suitable candidates may be those with limited disease containing a well-defined FDG-avid subvolume that can be escalated without unacceptable cumulative dose to critical normal tissues. Favorable anatomy, including separation from the carotid arteries and other vulnerable structures may be particularly important. Clinical factors such as good performance status, limited comorbidity, a longer interval since previous radiotherapy, and absence of ulceration or vascular involvement may further support treatment selection.In conclusion, DP for rsHNC was feasible, although workload was moderately increased. DP did not increase toxicity compared with conventional reirradiation, but we found no evidence of improved disease control. Still, DP is expected to give a benefit in selected patients, and a challenge in future studies is to identify these cases.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionThirty to fifty percent of patients with locally advanced head and neck cancer (HNC) develop recurrence after primary treatment, which commonly includes radiotherapy (RT) (1). Many recurrences are unresectable, or patients are not candidates for further surgery. Outcomes remain poor, with fewer than 20% of patients with locoregional relapse surviving beyond 5 years (2). Second primary HNC represents a related clinical challenge, although prognosis is more favorable than for recurrent disease (3, 4).Reirradiation at high dose is challenging because previously irradiated normal tissues have limited residual tolerance, increasing the risk of severe acute and late toxicity. Advances in RT delivery, including volumetric-modulated arc therapy (VMAT), allow improved dose conformity and reduction of high-dose exposure to surrounding tissues. For recurrent and second primary HNC (rsHNC), these approaches have been associated with overall survival (OS) of around 30%, at the cost of increased late morbidity (5).Most local HNC recurrences arise within the original gross tumor volume (GTV), particularly in subregions with high 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake on positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) images (6–8). Dose painting (DP) may be used to escalate the dose to hypermetabolic regions within the recurrent tumor, based on the premise that FDG uptake reflects aggressive tumor biology. DP may be delivered by VMAT, which will normally limit exposure to organs at risk. FDG-PET-guided DP may be applicable both for primary and recurrent HNC.Clinical evidence for DP in the reirradiation setting remains limited. To our knowledge, in addition to our previous work (9), only two clinical studies have been reported (10, 11) warranting further investigations. In the current study, we aimed to assess the feasibility of FDG-PET-guided DP in patients with rsHNC and compare the clinical outcome with a group of patients receiving standard reirradiation in our institution. Treatment planningAll imaging for treatment planning was performed on an RT-compatible flat table with head support and a radiotherapy fixation mask. The patients in the control group underwent a contrast-enhanced CT scan (Brilliance Big Bore CT, Philips Healthcare, Best, The Netherlands) from the skull base to mid chest with the arms down. The patients in the DP group had a contrast-enhanced FDG-PET/CT scan (Biograph 32, Siemens Healthcare, Munich, Germany). Treatment planning was performed using Raystation (v. 4.5/5.0, RaySearch Laboratories, Stockholm, Sweden).Our standard reirradiation regimen consisted of 1.5 Gy twice daily to 60 Gy over 4 weeks. The GTV (defined as the macroscopic disease visible on CT) was expanded by either (i) 5 mm to generate the clinical target volume (CTV, accounting for microscopic disease) or (ii) 10 mm margin in which also limited elective lymph node areas were included. In the latter case, the CTV received a dose of 45 Gy over the first 3 weeks, followed by an additional boost of 15 Gy to the GTV. In the former case, the entire CTV received a dose of 60 Gy. Standard reirradiation was given with a homogenous dose to the CTV. Planning treatment volume margin was 3 mm.Our DP method has been described previously (9). In brief, two prescription volumes (PV33 and PV66) were identified from the PET-images using a linear dose prescription formula converting FDG uptake to dose (13). The span of FDG uptake in the tumor was divided into three. PV33 encompassed 2/3 of the intermediate to high intensities while PV66 encompassed the 1/3 highest intensities. PV33 and PV66 received 65 Gy and 70 Gy, respectively, with a maximum point dose of 75 Gy. DP was given the first 2 out of 4 weeks treatment with a dose per fraction to PV33 and PV66 of 1.75 Gy and 2.0 Gy (Dmax 2.25 Gy), respectively. During the last 2 weeks of the treatment, the CTV received a homogeneous dose per fraction of 1.5 Gy.Dose calculation was done by Raysearch’s implementation of collapsed cone v. 3.0/3.2 with a grid size of 2 mm. The plans were checked for dosimetric accuracy using an Arc Check phantom (Sun Nuclear Corporation, Melbourne, FL, USA). All plans were within the tolerance limit used at our hospital with a gamma pass rate above 95% for the 3%/3 mm criteria. Treatment was given on a Varian TrueBeam STx (Varian Medical Systems, Palo Alto, CA, USA) with a HD120 MLC (2.5 mm and 5 mm central and outer leaf thickness, respectively) and 6 MV photons. Follow-upToxicity (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, CTCAE v3.0) was scored for 13 (mucositis, dysphagia, taste, edema, hoarseness, dermatitis, xerostomia, fistula, trismus, osteoradionecrosis, fibrosis, bleeding, local pain) at baseline, at the end of RT, and 3, 6 and 12 months after baseline. Furthermore, a composite score; the mean value of all 13 scores was calculated. Disease-related endpoints were loco-regional control (LRC), disease-free survival (DFS) and OS. For the DP group, follow-up FDG-PET/CT was performed 5.5 months after inclusion (4 months after reirradiation), thereafter as clinically indicated. For the control group no per protocol imaging was specified but the institutional practice was to perform CT 3 months after RT and then as clinically indicated. StatisticsFrequencies in contingency tables were compared using Fisher’s exact test. The Mann–Whitney U test was used for group comparisons. Local, regional, and distant failure were determined by biopsy when available, or by radiological assessment if biopsy was not warranted. For calculation of survival, the Kaplan–Meier method was used. Time to event was measured from inclusion. For LRC, either local or regional failure was counted as an event; for DFS, distant failure and death were additionally counted. End of follow-up was December 24, 2025.P-values <0.05 (two-sided) were considered statistically significant. The data were analyzed using RStudio 2023.06.2 + 561 (14). ToxicityThere were no statistically significant differences between the DP and standard groups in the proportion of patients experiencing any grade 3 toxicity at any of the time points (Table 3). In Figure 2, the median CTCAE score for xerostomia and dysphagia and the mean composite score of all 13 CTCAE scores are shown. The CTCAE scores were highest at the end of RT, with some variation between specific toxicities. Comparing the two groups at each time point, no difference in toxicity was found except for worse dysphagia at 6 months in the standard group (p=0.01). full_text: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are heterogeneous stromal cells that influence extracellular matrix (ECM) organisation, tumour-cell state, immunity, and treatment response in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). This review synthesises evidence on CAF origins and states and on the transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and Hippo–YAP/TAZ networks that mediate fibroblast interactions with tumour and immune cells. Vestibular schwannoma (VS) is considered only as a hypothesis-generating benign stromal reference: both tumours contain fibroblast and ECM-remodelling compartments, but differ fundamentally in cell of origin, anatomy, oncogenic drivers, immune context, and invasive behaviour. VS stromal fibroblasts are not designated as CAFs unless a study has explicitly applied that term, and cross-tumour observations are not treated as evidence of biological equivalence. Single-cell and spatial studies reveal multiple HNSCC fibroblast states, including myofibroblastic, inflammatory, antigen-presenting and fibroblastic reticular cell (FRC)-like, and immune-regulatory populations, but nomenclature and marker sets remain inconsistent and most inferred functions require perturbational validation. Translational evidence is similarly uneven: broad CAF depletion can be harmful in some non-HNSCC models, whereas pathway- or state-selective modulation is supported mainly by preclinical studies. Early HNSCC trials of TGF-β/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) blockade and NADPH oxidase 1/4 (NOX1/4) inhibition provide feasibility signals but not definitive efficacy. Current evidence supports biomarker-guided investigation of functionally defined CAF states; stromal observations in VS remain hypothesis-generating and require direct experimental validation. ConclusionCAFs are heterogeneous and dynamic components of the HNSCC microenvironment. Their effects arise from state- and location-dependent interactions with tumour, immune, vascular, and matrix compartments; they cannot be reduced to a single uniformly tumour-promoting population. VS may serve as a benign stromal comparator, but differences in lineage, anatomy, oncogenic drivers, and immune context preclude biological equivalence or attribution of its non-metastatic behaviour to fibroblasts. The strongest HNSCC evidence concerns defined fibroblast states associated with invasion, immune exclusion, or immune support, whereas most therapeutic mechanisms remain preclinical. Early trials of TGF-β/PD-L1 and NOX1/4-directed combinations provide feasibility data and hypothesis-generating efficacy signals but do not define a standard of care. Progress will require spatially resolved state definitions, functional perturbation, paired treatment biopsies, and biomarkers that preserve homeostatic or antitumour fibroblast functions. Future studies should connect spatially defined CAF states to causal functions, pharmacodynamic responses, and clinical outcomes before stromal interventions are advanced into routine treatment. IntroductionHead and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is biologically heterogeneous and often clinically aggressive, particularly when locally advanced (Hu et al., 2023; Tsai et al., 2025). The tumour microenvironment (TME) contributes to progression and treatment response, and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a major but non-uniform stromal compartment (Hu et al., 2023; Sahai et al., 2020; Federspiel et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025). CAFs can remodel extracellular matrix (ECM), secrete growth factors and cytokines, regulate immune-cell localisation, and alter treatment sensitivity; however, these functions vary across fibroblast states and experimental contexts (Hu et al., 2023; Sahai et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2021). Interpretation depends on distinguishing direct HNSCC evidence from findings extrapolated from other tumour types.Benign stromal tumours are not interchangeable with HNSCC. Vestibular schwannoma (VS) arises from Schwann-lineage cells of the vestibular nerve and is usually non-metastatic, whereas HNSCC arises from mucosal epithelium in a carcinogen- and/or human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated field and can invade and metastasise. VS studies nevertheless identify fibroblast, ECM-remodelling, and immune–stromal compartments, together with candidate paracrine interactions, that can be interrogated using single-cell and spatial methods (Sung and Lee, 2024; Barrett et al., 2024; Gonzalez Castro et al., 2025; Huo et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2022). These shared analytical domains provide a limited rationale for comparison, whereas differences in cell lineage, anatomical constraints, oncogenic drivers, ECM composition, immune exposure, and treatment context preclude direct equivalence. The studies reviewed here do not include a matched comparison of HNSCC CAFs and VS fibroblasts. Accordingly, VS is treated as a hypothesis-generating stromal reference intended to define experimentally testable questions, not to explain the benign behaviour of VS or to model HNSCC malignancy. The term “VS fibroblasts” is used throughout; “CAF” or “CAF-like” is reserved for instances in which the cited VS study used that terminology, without implying equivalence to CAFs in malignant tumours.The review evaluates fibroblast origin and heterogeneity together with TGF-β, Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and Hippo–YAP/TAZ signalling, tumour behaviour, immune regulation, therapy resistance, and stromal therapeutic strategies. Evidence is classified as HNSCC-specific, VS-specific, or derived from other tumour types; transcriptomic associations and ligand–receptor predictions are distinguished from functional perturbation data, and preclinical findings are distinguished from clinical evidence. Origin and heterogeneity of CAFsCAFs arise from multiple cellular sources and activation trajectories rather than a single lineage (Sahai et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2021; LeBleu and Kalluri, 2018; Kalluri and Zeisberg, 2006). In carcinomas, resident tissue fibroblasts are a major source, while mesenchymal stromal cells, perivascular cells, and endothelial-derived mesenchymal cells can contribute in model- and tissue-dependent ways (LeBleu and Kalluri, 2018; Frisbie et al., 2022; Han et al., 2025; Guo and Xu, 2024). Partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition can produce tumour cells with mesenchymal features, but does not demonstrate their conversion into CAFs. Tumour-derived TGF-β, CXCL12, interleukins, and mechanical cues can recruit or activate stromal fibroblasts, echoing but not reproducing the wound-healing programme (Sahai et al., 2020; Dvorak, 2019).CAF populations may also receive contributions from sources beyond local fibroblasts. In model-dependent settings, bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells can migrate to tumours and adopt fibroblast-like programmes (Frisbie et al., 2022). Some carcinoma cells undergo partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition and acquire mesenchymal features, but this is not equivalent to proven conversion into CAFs (LeBleu and Kalluri, 2018). Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, perivascular cells, and adipocyte-derived stromal cells have been proposed as additional sources (Han et al., 2025; Guo and Xu, 2024). These routes are not mutually exclusive, and their quantitative contribution in human HNSCC remains uncertain (Figure 1a) (Sahai et al., 2020; LeBleu and Kalluri, 2018).FIGURE 1Origins and heterogeneity of CAFs. (a) Proposed cellular origins of CAFs, including resident fibroblasts, mesenchymal stem cells, endothelial cells, pericytes, adipocytes, and epithelial cells undergoing partial EMT. (b) Major CAF states and representative programmes: myofibroblastic, inflammatory, antigen-presenting-like, and ECM-rich. VS clusters are shown as transcriptional observations rather than functional equivalents of HNSCC CAF states. Created in BioRender. Zhang, X. (2026) https://BioRender.com/0mhsfwx.Diagram divided into panels illustrating the origins and subtypes of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). Panel a shows CAFs deriving from resting fibroblasts, adipocytes, capillary pericytes, endothelial cells, epithelial cells, and bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells by processes including activation, reprogramming, migration, differentiation, and transitions, acting like chronic wounds. Panel b depicts four CAF subtypes: myCAFs with high ACTA2 promoting tumor invasion via ECM stiffness; iCAFs with low ACTA2 and cytokine secretion aiding tumor progression; apCAFs interacting with CD4+ T cells affecting immune response; and ecmCAFs involved in tissue repair versus tumor invasion.Single-cell studies have resolved substantial fibroblast diversity in HNSCC and schwannoma, but their datasets are not directly comparable. Puram et al. profiled approximately 6,000 cells from 18 HNSCC specimens and linked a partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition programme at the invasive edge to stromal interactions (Puram et al., 2017). Subsequent HNSCC studies identify myofibroblastic, inflammatory, immune-regulatory, and fibroblastic-reticular-cell-like states, with spatial position and HPV/immune context influencing their abundance (Jenkins et al., 2025; Furudate et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2025; Li C. et al., 2024; Obra et al., 2022). By contrast, VS studies have profiled small cohorts or re-analysed published datasets: Huo et al. analysed seven VS and two normal nerves; Sung and Lee re-analysed three VS; and a broader schwannoma atlas sampled 22 cranial and peripheral tumours across genetic backgrounds (Sung and Lee, 2024; Barrett et al., 2024; Gonzalez Castro et al., 2025; Huo et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2022). VS datasets reveal heterogeneity and nominate candidate cell–cell interactions, but do not establish one-to-one correspondence between HNSCC CAF subsets and VS fibroblasts.Myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs) are generally enriched for ACTA2/alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), contractile genes, collagen and fibronectin production, and ECM organisation, often near tumour nests (Elyada et al., 2019; Biffi and Tuveson, 2021). TGF-β and mechanical tension can stabilise this programme. In oral squamous cell carcinoma, spatial analysis placed a myCAF population at the invasive front and linked ECM–CD44 interactions with lymph-node metastasis (Furudate et al., 2025). Nevertheless, α-SMA is neither exclusive to CAFs nor sufficient to define a tumour-promoting function; pericytes and wound-associated myofibroblasts can share this marker.Inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs) are characterised by cytokine and chemokine programmes that may include IL-6, IL-8, CXCL12, or IL-11, usually with lower contractile-gene expression (Elyada et al., 2019; Biffi and Tuveson, 2021). In HNSCC, Jenkins et al. identified six fibroblast subtypes across HPV-negative, HPV-positive, and non-malignant tissues, including IL11-positive inflammatory and CCL19-positive fibroblastic-reticular-cell-like populations (Jenkins et al., 2025). The latter were associated with immune-hot niches, tertiary lymphoid structures, and favourable immunotherapy response. The reported immune-hot association of CCL19-positive FRC-like fibroblasts illustrates why inflammatory and immune-associated fibroblast states cannot be assumed to be uniformly immunosuppressive; association, spatial colocalisation, and ex vivo function represent distinct levels of evidence.Antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs) express major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II and antigen-processing genes, but their consequences depend on co-stimulation, location, and immune context. They were first functionally characterised in pancreatic cancer (Elyada et al., 2019). MHC-II-expressing stromal or tumour-associated populations have also been reported in schwannoma datasets (Sung and Lee, 2024; Gonzalez Castro et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025), but this does not show that they are equivalent to pancreatic apCAFs or that they activate versus tolerise CD4+ T cells. Their identity and function in HNSCC remain incompletely resolved.Additional labels—including ECM-rich, cycling, fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-positive, leucine-rich repeat-containing protein 15 (LRRC15)-positive, MHC-I-high/Galectin-9-positive, and FRC-like fibroblasts—capture partly overlapping states (Li C. et al., 2024; Cords et al., 2024; Krishnamurty et al., 2022; Dominguez et al., 2020). A pan-cancer LRRC15-positive myofibroblast programme is TGF-β-associated and correlated with poor checkpoint-blockade response, while selective depletion enhanced anti-PD-L1 activity in pancreatic mouse models (Krishnamurty et al., 2022; Dominguez et al., 2020). In HNSCC, an MHC-I-high/Galectin-9-positive CAF subset spatially restricted CD8+ T-cell infiltration and function (Li C. et al., 2024), whereas immunostimulatory HNCAF-0/HNCAF-3 populations predicted response in a small discovery cohort (Obra et al., 2022). These apparently conflicting observations likely reflect true state diversity plus differences in sampling, annotation, and assay design (Figure 1b).No universal marker panel yet separates tumour-promoting from tumour-restraining fibroblasts, and the same marker can occur in several states or in normal stromal cells (Sahai et al., 2020; Biffi and Tuveson, 2021; Cords et al., 2024). Most single-cell studies are cross-sectional, contain limited patient numbers, and infer function from transcription or ligand–receptor databases. Within this evidence hierarchy, transcriptomic association defines a candidate state; spatial colocalisation supports proximity but not signalling direction; ligand–receptor analysis generates hypotheses; perturbation or co-culture provides model-specific functional evidence; and trial outcomes constitute clinical evidence. Lineage tracing and treatment-linked longitudinal sampling remain necessary before a transcriptomic cluster can be treated as a therapeutic target.Classifications that integrate fibroblast state, spatial location, and function are more clinically informative than fixed cell categories. full_text_sections.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are heterogeneous stromal cells that influence extracellular matrix (ECM) organisation, tumour-cell state, immunity, and treatment response in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). This review synthesises evidence on CAF origins and states and on the transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and Hippo–YAP/TAZ networks that mediate fibroblast interactions with tumour and immune cells. Vestibular schwannoma (VS) is considered only as a hypothesis-generating benign stromal reference: both tumours contain fibroblast and ECM-remodelling compartments, but differ fundamentally in cell of origin, anatomy, oncogenic drivers, immune context, and invasive behaviour. VS stromal fibroblasts are not designated as CAFs unless a study has explicitly applied that term, and cross-tumour observations are not treated as evidence of biological equivalence. Single-cell and spatial studies reveal multiple HNSCC fibroblast states, including myofibroblastic, inflammatory, antigen-presenting and fibroblastic reticular cell (FRC)-like, and immune-regulatory populations, but nomenclature and marker sets remain inconsistent and most inferred functions require perturbational validation. Translational evidence is similarly uneven: broad CAF depletion can be harmful in some non-HNSCC models, whereas pathway- or state-selective modulation is supported mainly by preclinical studies. Early HNSCC trials of TGF-β/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) blockade and NADPH oxidase 1/4 (NOX1/4) inhibition provide feasibility signals but not definitive efficacy. Current evidence supports biomarker-guided investigation of functionally defined CAF states; stromal observations in VS remain hypothesis-generating and require direct experimental validation.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionCAFs are heterogeneous and dynamic components of the HNSCC microenvironment. Their effects arise from state- and location-dependent interactions with tumour, immune, vascular, and matrix compartments; they cannot be reduced to a single uniformly tumour-promoting population. VS may serve as a benign stromal comparator, but differences in lineage, anatomy, oncogenic drivers, and immune context preclude biological equivalence or attribution of its non-metastatic behaviour to fibroblasts. The strongest HNSCC evidence concerns defined fibroblast states associated with invasion, immune exclusion, or immune support, whereas most therapeutic mechanisms remain preclinical. Early trials of TGF-β/PD-L1 and NOX1/4-directed combinations provide feasibility data and hypothesis-generating efficacy signals but do not define a standard of care. Progress will require spatially resolved state definitions, functional perturbation, paired treatment biopsies, and biomarkers that preserve homeostatic or antitumour fibroblast functions. Future studies should connect spatially defined CAF states to causal functions, pharmacodynamic responses, and clinical outcomes before stromal interventions are advanced into routine treatment.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHead and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is biologically heterogeneous and often clinically aggressive, particularly when locally advanced (Hu et al., 2023; Tsai et al., 2025). The tumour microenvironment (TME) contributes to progression and treatment response, and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a major but non-uniform stromal compartment (Hu et al., 2023; Sahai et al., 2020; Federspiel et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025). CAFs can remodel extracellular matrix (ECM), secrete growth factors and cytokines, regulate immune-cell localisation, and alter treatment sensitivity; however, these functions vary across fibroblast states and experimental contexts (Hu et al., 2023; Sahai et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2021). Interpretation depends on distinguishing direct HNSCC evidence from findings extrapolated from other tumour types.Benign stromal tumours are not interchangeable with HNSCC. Vestibular schwannoma (VS) arises from Schwann-lineage cells of the vestibular nerve and is usually non-metastatic, whereas HNSCC arises from mucosal epithelium in a carcinogen- and/or human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated field and can invade and metastasise. VS studies nevertheless identify fibroblast, ECM-remodelling, and immune–stromal compartments, together with candidate paracrine interactions, that can be interrogated using single-cell and spatial methods (Sung and Lee, 2024; Barrett et al., 2024; Gonzalez Castro et al., 2025; Huo et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2022). These shared analytical domains provide a limited rationale for comparison, whereas differences in cell lineage, anatomical constraints, oncogenic drivers, ECM composition, immune exposure, and treatment context preclude direct equivalence. The studies reviewed here do not include a matched comparison of HNSCC CAFs and VS fibroblasts. Accordingly, VS is treated as a hypothesis-generating stromal reference intended to define experimentally testable questions, not to explain the benign behaviour of VS or to model HNSCC malignancy. The term “VS fibroblasts” is used throughout; “CAF” or “CAF-like” is reserved for instances in which the cited VS study used that terminology, without implying equivalence to CAFs in malignant tumours.The review evaluates fibroblast origin and heterogeneity together with TGF-β, Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and Hippo–YAP/TAZ signalling, tumour behaviour, immune regulation, therapy resistance, and stromal therapeutic strategies. Evidence is classified as HNSCC-specific, VS-specific, or derived from other tumour types; transcriptomic associations and ligand–receptor predictions are distinguished from functional perturbation data, and preclinical findings are distinguished from clinical evidence. Origin and heterogeneity of CAFsCAFs arise from multiple cellular sources and activation trajectories rather than a single lineage (Sahai et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2021; LeBleu and Kalluri, 2018; Kalluri and Zeisberg, 2006). In carcinomas, resident tissue fibroblasts are a major source, while mesenchymal stromal cells, perivascular cells, and endothelial-derived mesenchymal cells can contribute in model- and tissue-dependent ways (LeBleu and Kalluri, 2018; Frisbie et al., 2022; Han et al., 2025; Guo and Xu, 2024). Partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition can produce tumour cells with mesenchymal features, but does not demonstrate their conversion into CAFs. Tumour-derived TGF-β, CXCL12, interleukins, and mechanical cues can recruit or activate stromal fibroblasts, echoing but not reproducing the wound-healing programme (Sahai et al., 2020; Dvorak, 2019).CAF populations may also receive contributions from sources beyond local fibroblasts. In model-dependent settings, bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells can migrate to tumours and adopt fibroblast-like programmes (Frisbie et al., 2022). Some carcinoma cells undergo partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition and acquire mesenchymal features, but this is not equivalent to proven conversion into CAFs (LeBleu and Kalluri, 2018). Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, perivascular cells, and adipocyte-derived stromal cells have been proposed as additional sources (Han et al., 2025; Guo and Xu, 2024). These routes are not mutually exclusive, and their quantitative contribution in human HNSCC remains uncertain (Figure 1a) (Sahai et al., 2020; LeBleu and Kalluri, 2018).FIGURE 1Origins and heterogeneity of CAFs. full_text: Gynecologic diseases, including infectious disorders, endocrine-related conditions, gynecologic malignancies, and pregnancy complications, are clinically diverse yet frequently share features of hormonal imbalance, microbial dysbiosis, and dysregulated inflammation. Current research has largely examined these processes separately, limiting integrated understanding of their potential interactions. This review synthesizes current evidence and proposes a hormone–microbiota–neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) framework as a conceptual tool for understanding common and disease-specific mechanisms across gynecologic disorders. We first summarize the core molecular basis of NET formation, with emphasis on peptidylarginine deiminase 4 as a candidate regulatory node. We then examine the effects of sex hormones on NET regulation, the role of the microbiota in shaping mucosal immune responses, and potential mechanistic links between microbial products, extracellular matrix components, and NET dysregulation. Evidence is further integrated across representative infectious, endocrine-related, malignant, and pregnancy-associated conditions, including pelvic inflammatory disease, bacterial vaginosis, endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, and preeclampsia. The available literature indicates that hormone-dependent immune modulation, pathogen- or microbiota-associated inflammatory signaling, and NET-related tissue injury may converge in multiple gynecologic settings, although the strength of evidence differs substantially across specific pathways and diseases. Direct support is strongest for selected hormone–NET effects in defined experimental or pregnancy-associated settings and for pathogen/microbial product–NET interactions in infectious contexts, whereas the complete hormone–microbiota–NET framework and the proposed glycosaminoglycan–peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (GAG–PAD4) bridge remain insufficiently validated. Overall, this review provides an evidence-based integrative framework for organizing current knowledge, identifying mechanistic gaps, and informing future biomarker development, patient stratification, and translational research in gynecologic disease. 6.7Non-uniform sample sources and NET detection methods limit cross-study comparabilityAnother important but often underestimated problem is the methodological heterogeneity of NET research. Different studies use peripheral blood, vaginal secretions, ascites, lesion tissue, placental tissue, and follicular fluid, among other sample sources, yet these specimens reflect different biological levels and are not necessarily directly comparable. In addition, NET detection methods are not standardized: some studies use cell-free DNA, whereas others assess MPO–DNA complexes, CitH3, NE, or tissue immunostaining, and these markers do not necessarily represent the same biological process. Some are more reflective of general cell damage or inflammatory burden, whereas others are more specific to NETosis itself. Without standardized sampling strategies and combined biomarker systems, it is difficult to establish a truly comparable “axis signature,” which is one of the most practical current barriers to moving from mechanistic discussion toward clinical translation (108–110). 2.3The hypothesis-generating GAG–PAD4 mechanism: in vitro findings and an in vivo hypothesis awaiting validation2.3.1Biochemical evidence for GAG-mediated modulation of PAD4A recent primary biochemical study provided evidence that GAGs can enhance PAD4 activation at sub-saturating calcium concentrations. Bereta et al. demonstrated high-affinity binding between PAD4 and heparin and showed that heparin increased the calcium sensitivity of PAD4 in several purified biochemical assays. In peptide-substrate calcium-response experiments, 0.025 μM heparin lowered the calcium concentration required for half-maximal activation. In a BAEE-based assay, 1 μM heparin reduced the Ca0.5 from 370 ± 26 μM to 101 ± 19 μM, and 1 μM heparin also enhanced histone H3 citrullination at lower calcium concentrations. Heparan sulfate, dermatan sulfate, and several chondroitin sulfates showed varying PAD4-activating capacities. The effect depended on GAG chain length and negative charge and required PAD4 dimerization (31).Importantly, these findings were obtained primarily in purified biochemical systems, and we did not identify an independent primary study directly replicating the GAG-mediated reduction in the calcium requirement of PAD4. These observations therefore establish biochemical plausibility but do not by themselves demonstrate that GAG-dependent PAD4 sensitization occurs in neutrophils or gynecologic mucosal tissues in vivo.2.3.2Physiological relevance of the experimental GAG concentrationsThe physiological relevance of the concentrations and molecular species used in these biochemical assays remains uncertain. Bereta et al. used 0.025 μM heparin in peptide-based calcium-response experiments and 1 μM heparin in BAEE- and histone-based assays, while other natural GAGs were generally evaluated at micromolar concentrations. These experimental conditions cannot currently be assumed to reproduce the concentration, molecular size, sulfation pattern, or bioavailability of free GAG species in the cervicovaginal microenvironment.Importantly, the study by Myers et al. quantified sulfated GAGs in human cervical tissue rather than free GAG concentrations in vaginal secretions. A recent human study has provided more direct evidence that heparan sulfate is measurable in the vaginal environment: Yano et al. reported higher heparan sulfate concentrations in vaginal swab-derived conditioned medium from women with symptomatic vulvovaginal candidiasis than in asymptomatic and healthy groups. However, because the vaginal swabs were eluted into 1 mL of medium and because heparan sulfate is structurally heterogeneous, these measurements cannot be directly converted into an in situ molar concentration comparable with the purified heparin concentrations used in the PAD4 assays (58, 59). Thus, whether GAG concentrations sufficient to sensitize PAD4 occur locally in vivo remains unresolved.2.3.3Alternative interpretations of the GAG–PAD4 interactionSeveral alternative interpretations should be considered before assigning the GAG–PAD4 interaction a causal role in gynecologic NETosis. First, because the core calcium sensitization experiments were performed using purified PAD4, GAG-mediated activation may be particularly relevant to extracellular PAD4 and extracellular protein citrullination rather than necessarily reflecting intracellular PAD4 activation during NETosis. Second, the strong dependence of the effect on polymer length, negative charge, and PAD4 oligomerization raises the possibility that GAGs act as polyanionic allosteric scaffolds rather than through a highly specific disease-related GAG signaling pathway. Third, altered GAG abundance or sulfation may arise downstream of epithelial injury, inflammation, or extracellular matrix remodeling, creating the possibility of reverse causality rather than a unidirectional microbiota → GAG → PAD4 sequence. Finally, GAGs may influence neutrophil function independently of PAD4. For example, elevated vaginal heparan sulfate has been associated with impaired neutrophil–Candida albicans interactions and reduced antifungal activity (59).Accordingly, the microbiota–GAG–PAD4–NET sequence should currently be regarded as one testable mechanistic model among several alternatives rather than as an established causal pathway. 8Conclusion and outlookThe hormone–microbiota–NET framework proposed in this review is intended as a testable heuristic framework for understanding shared pathogenic mechanisms across gynecologic diseases. The central premise is that gynecologic disorders—whether infectious diseases, endocrine disturbances, gynecologic malignancies, or pregnancy-related complications—may be more coherently interpreted through multidirectional interactions among hormones, microbiota, and NETs, provided that supported component-level observations are clearly separated from untested causal bridges.8.1Organizational value of the framework and its current limitationsThis framework attempts to bridge several disciplines that have traditionally been studied in relative isolation—including reproductive endocrinology, microbiology, immunology, and oncology—and thus offers a shared language for interdisciplinary research in gynecologic diseases. It also suggests that distinct disease categories may be linked by certain underlying mechanisms. From acute infection, such as pelvic inflammatory disease, to chronic inflammatory conditions, such as endometriosis, and further to malignant transformation, as exemplified by ovarian cancer, NETs may represent a recurring mechanistic thread. This perspective may help overcome research boundaries imposed by disease-specific classification. In addition, the framework provides a new conceptual direction for clinical investigation, including combined assessment based on framework-related signatures and the idea of multimodal intervention targeting hormones, microbiota, and NETs, thereby reflecting an exploratory shift from symptom management toward etiologic intervention (37, 38, 126, 127). However, these organizational advantages remain largely conceptual at present. For this framework to truly advance the field, the priority is to identify the hypotheses most worthy of direct testing and the research directions most deserving of early investment.8.2The GAG–PAD4 mechanism as one falsifiable research hypothesisThe GAG–PAD4 mechanism is one hypothesis-generating component of this framework, rather than its established molecular center. Biochemical evidence justifies testing whether relevant GAG species influence PAD4 under gynecologic conditions, but does not establish that microbiota-dependent GAG changes regulate intracellular PAD4 or NET release in vivo. Testing should distinguish three questions: whether microbial status relates to local GAG composition, whether the relevant GAG species alter PAD4 activity in the appropriate compartment, and whether PAD4-dependent changes contribute to NET formation and disease-related outcomes. Negative results at any step would limit this proposed route without invalidating separately supported hormonal, microbial, or NET-related observations.8.3Research directions that should be prioritizedBased on the above hierarchy of hypotheses, the following research directions merit priority consideration.Direction 1: Test the compartment-specific relevance of the GAG–PAD4 hypothesisCore question: Do the relevant local GAG species affect PAD4 activity and NET formation in the disease compartment under study?Suggested research strategy: Evaluate the proposed links separately, beginning with characterization of local GAG species and controlled biochemical or cellular tests. Distinguish extracellular PAD4 activity from intracellular PAD4-dependent NET formation, and include appropriate controls for PAD4-independent effects. Tissue and secretion sampling should match the intended disease compartment; vaginal measurements should not be assumed to represent endometriotic lesions, ovarian tumors, or the placenta. Subsequent disease-model studies can test whether manipulating the candidate link changes both the mechanistic readouts and a relevant phenotype. Negative findings should be used to revise or reject the proposed connection (128–130).Direction 2: Prioritize analytical validation and harmonization of NET-related measurementsCore question: How can NET-related measurements be made analytically reliable, biologically interpretable, and comparable across laboratories?Suggested research strategy: Method-development studies should prioritize analyte definition, specimen-specific pre-analytical procedures, antibody specificity, suitable calibration materials, precision, recovery, dilutional behavior, and inter-laboratory reproducibility (110, 114). Soluble measurements should be evaluated alongside independent structural or functional NET assessments in representative samples (108). Automation may subsequently be investigated to improve throughput and workflow consistency, but it should not be assumed to improve NET specificity or replace analytical and clinical validation. Well-characterized cohorts should be used to investigate physiological variation and candidate reference distributions using validated assays before clinical decision thresholds are proposed.Technical challenges: Major challenges include specimen-dependent interference, heterogeneity in analytes and assay formats, harmonization across laboratories, and the distinction between physiological variation, disease association, and clinical utility.Direction 3: Conduct prospective cohort studies based on framework-related signaturesCore question: Do framework-related signatures, defined by hormones plus microbiota plus NETs, have independent clinical predictive value?Suggested research strategy: Establish multicenter prospective cohorts including patients with representative diseases such as endometriosis, PCOS, and preeclampsia, together with healthy controls. Baseline samples should be collected using standardized procedures, with simultaneous assessment of hormones (E2, P4, and E2/P4), microbiota features (16S rRNA sequencing and Lactobacillus abundance), and NET-related markers (CitH3, NE, and MPO–DNA). Clinical endpoints, including disease progression, treatment response, recurrence, and pregnancy outcomes, should then be longitudinally followed to evaluate the independent predictive value of these framework-related signatures. Unsupervised approaches such as clustering analysis may help identify disease subtypes based on framework characteristics and explore their association with clinical outcomes.Technical challenges: Multicenter coordination is organizationally demanding; large sample sizes are needed to preserve statistical power under multiple-testing conditions; follow-up periods are long, especially for recurrence and pregnancy outcomes; and the costs of microbiota and NETs analyses remain a practical concern.8.4Closing remarksThe value of this framework lies in distinguishing supported component-level observations from untested connections across gynecologic diseases. Future work should combine disease-specific and compartment-resolved studies, reliable NET measurements, and prospective human research to determine which links are reproducible and clinically relevant. The GAG–PAD4 mechanism is one candidate for such testing, not a prerequisite for the validity of all hormonal, microbial, or NET-related observations. The framework should be revised as evidence supports, limits, or refutes its proposed connections. 1IntroductionThe spectrum of gynecologic diseases encompasses a wide range of conditions, including infectious disorders, endocrine disturbances, malignancies, and pregnancy-related complications. Population-level analyses from the Global Burden of Disease studies indicate that diseases of the female reproductive system contribute substantially to morbidity and disability worldwide, although estimates vary according to disease definitions, age groups, and analytic categories (Y. 1, 2). Endometriosis, uterine fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), and gynecologic malignancies also exert substantial effects on patients’ quality of life (3). Despite their heterogeneous clinical manifestations, these diseases share several common pathogenic features, notably immune dysregulation, endocrine imbalance, and alterations in the microbiota (4, 5).The immune system plays a central role in gynecologic diseases (6, 7). Pelvic inflammatory disease is characterized by an acute inflammatory response triggered by pathogens, endometriotic lesions exhibit a chronic inflammatory microenvironment, and gynecologic tumors often display immune evasion. Although these three disease settings present distinct immune phenotypes, all involve dysfunctional immune regulation (5, 8–10). The endocrine system is also closely implicated in gynecologic disorders. Endometriosis is estrogen-dependent, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is characterized by hyperandrogenism, and premature ovarian insufficiency manifests as a decline in endocrine function (11, 12). In recent years, major advances have also been made in research on the reproductive tract microecology. Existing evidence suggests that vaginal dysbiosis is associated with a range of gynecologic conditions, including bacterial vaginosis, persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, pelvic inflammatory disease, and preterm birth. These findings indicate that the microbiota may play an important role in the onset and progression of gynecologic diseases (13–16).The discovery of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) has provided a new perspective for understanding these complex mechanisms. NETs are web-like fibrous structures released by activated neutrophils and consist of a DNA scaffold decorated with histones and granular proteins such as neutrophil elastase (NE) and myeloperoxidase (MPO).
