full_text_sections.abstract: Gynecologic diseases, including infectious disorders, endocrine-related conditions, gynecologic malignancies, and pregnancy complications, are clinically diverse yet frequently share features of hormonal imbalance, microbial dysbiosis, and dysregulated inflammation. Current research has largely examined these processes separately, limiting integrated understanding of their potential interactions. This review synthesizes current evidence and proposes a hormone–microbiota–neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) framework as a conceptual tool for understanding common and disease-specific mechanisms across gynecologic disorders. We first summarize the core molecular basis of NET formation, with emphasis on peptidylarginine deiminase 4 as a candidate regulatory node. We then examine the effects of sex hormones on NET regulation, the role of the microbiota in shaping mucosal immune responses, and potential mechanistic links between microbial products, extracellular matrix components, and NET dysregulation. Evidence is further integrated across representative infectious, endocrine-related, malignant, and pregnancy-associated conditions, including pelvic inflammatory disease, bacterial vaginosis, endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, and preeclampsia. The available literature indicates that hormone-dependent immune modulation, pathogen- or microbiota-associated inflammatory signaling, and NET-related tissue injury may converge in multiple gynecologic settings, although the strength of evidence differs substantially across specific pathways and diseases. Direct support is strongest for selected hormone–NET effects in defined experimental or pregnancy-associated settings and for pathogen/microbial product–NET interactions in infectious contexts, whereas the complete hormone–microbiota–NET framework and the proposed glycosaminoglycan–peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (GAG–PAD4) bridge remain insufficiently validated. Overall, this review provides an evidence-based integrative framework for organizing current knowledge, identifying mechanistic gaps, and informing future biomarker development, patient stratification, and translational research in gynecologic disease.
full_text_sections.methods: 6.7Non-uniform sample sources and NET detection methods limit cross-study comparabilityAnother important but often underestimated problem is the methodological heterogeneity of NET research. Different studies use peripheral blood, vaginal secretions, ascites, lesion tissue, placental tissue, and follicular fluid, among other sample sources, yet these specimens reflect different biological levels and are not necessarily directly comparable. In addition, NET detection methods are not standardized: some studies use cell-free DNA, whereas others assess MPO–DNA complexes, CitH3, NE, or tissue immunostaining, and these markers do not necessarily represent the same biological process. Some are more reflective of general cell damage or inflammatory burden, whereas others are more specific to NETosis itself. Without standardized sampling strategies and combined biomarker systems, it is difficult to establish a truly comparable “axis signature,” which is one of the most practical current barriers to moving from mechanistic discussion toward clinical translation (108–110).
full_text_sections.results: 2.3The hypothesis-generating GAG–PAD4 mechanism: in vitro findings and an in vivo hypothesis awaiting validation2.3.1Biochemical evidence for GAG-mediated modulation of PAD4A recent primary biochemical study provided evidence that GAGs can enhance PAD4 activation at sub-saturating calcium concentrations. Bereta et al. demonstrated high-affinity binding between PAD4 and heparin and showed that heparin increased the calcium sensitivity of PAD4 in several purified biochemical assays. In peptide-substrate calcium-response experiments, 0.025 μM heparin lowered the calcium concentration required for half-maximal activation. In a BAEE-based assay, 1 μM heparin reduced the Ca0.5 from 370 ± 26 μM to 101 ± 19 μM, and 1 μM heparin also enhanced histone H3 citrullination at lower calcium concentrations. Heparan sulfate, dermatan sulfate, and several chondroitin sulfates showed varying PAD4-activating capacities. The effect depended on GAG chain length and negative charge and required PAD4 dimerization (31).Importantly, these findings were obtained primarily in purified biochemical systems, and we did not identify an independent primary study directly replicating the GAG-mediated reduction in the calcium requirement of PAD4. These observations therefore establish biochemical plausibility but do not by themselves demonstrate that GAG-dependent PAD4 sensitization occurs in neutrophils or gynecologic mucosal tissues in vivo.2.3.2Physiological relevance of the experimental GAG concentrationsThe physiological relevance of the concentrations and molecular species used in these biochemical assays remains uncertain. Bereta et al. used 0.025 μM heparin in peptide-based calcium-response experiments and 1 μM heparin in BAEE- and histone-based assays, while other natural GAGs were generally evaluated at micromolar concentrations. These experimental conditions cannot currently be assumed to reproduce the concentration, molecular size, sulfation pattern, or bioavailability of free GAG species in the cervicovaginal microenvironment.Importantly, the study by Myers et al. quantified sulfated GAGs in human cervical tissue rather than free GAG concentrations in vaginal secretions. A recent human study has provided more direct evidence that heparan sulfate is measurable in the vaginal environment: Yano et al. reported higher heparan sulfate concentrations in vaginal swab-derived conditioned medium from women with symptomatic vulvovaginal candidiasis than in asymptomatic and healthy groups. However, because the vaginal swabs were eluted into 1 mL of medium and because heparan sulfate is structurally heterogeneous, these measurements cannot be directly converted into an in situ molar concentration comparable with the purified heparin concentrations used in the PAD4 assays (58, 59). Thus, whether GAG concentrations sufficient to sensitize PAD4 occur locally in vivo remains unresolved.2.3.3Alternative interpretations of the GAG–PAD4 interactionSeveral alternative interpretations should be considered before assigning the GAG–PAD4 interaction a causal role in gynecologic NETosis. First, because the core calcium sensitization experiments were performed using purified PAD4, GAG-mediated activation may be particularly relevant to extracellular PAD4 and extracellular protein citrullination rather than necessarily reflecting intracellular PAD4 activation during NETosis. Second, the strong dependence of the effect on polymer length, negative charge, and PAD4 oligomerization raises the possibility that GAGs act as polyanionic allosteric scaffolds rather than through a highly specific disease-related GAG signaling pathway. Third, altered GAG abundance or sulfation may arise downstream of epithelial injury, inflammation, or extracellular matrix remodeling, creating the possibility of reverse causality rather than a unidirectional microbiota → GAG → PAD4 sequence. Finally, GAGs may influence neutrophil function independently of PAD4. For example, elevated vaginal heparan sulfate has been associated with impaired neutrophil–Candida albicans interactions and reduced antifungal activity (59).Accordingly, the microbiota–GAG–PAD4–NET sequence should currently be regarded as one testable mechanistic model among several alternatives rather than as an established causal pathway.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 8Conclusion and outlookThe hormone–microbiota–NET framework proposed in this review is intended as a testable heuristic framework for understanding shared pathogenic mechanisms across gynecologic diseases. The central premise is that gynecologic disorders—whether infectious diseases, endocrine disturbances, gynecologic malignancies, or pregnancy-related complications—may be more coherently interpreted through multidirectional interactions among hormones, microbiota, and NETs, provided that supported component-level observations are clearly separated from untested causal bridges.8.1Organizational value of the framework and its current limitationsThis framework attempts to bridge several disciplines that have traditionally been studied in relative isolation—including reproductive endocrinology, microbiology, immunology, and oncology—and thus offers a shared language for interdisciplinary research in gynecologic diseases. It also suggests that distinct disease categories may be linked by certain underlying mechanisms. From acute infection, such as pelvic inflammatory disease, to chronic inflammatory conditions, such as endometriosis, and further to malignant transformation, as exemplified by ovarian cancer, NETs may represent a recurring mechanistic thread. This perspective may help overcome research boundaries imposed by disease-specific classification. In addition, the framework provides a new conceptual direction for clinical investigation, including combined assessment based on framework-related signatures and the idea of multimodal intervention targeting hormones, microbiota, and NETs, thereby reflecting an exploratory shift from symptom management toward etiologic intervention (37, 38, 126, 127). However, these organizational advantages remain largely conceptual at present. For this framework to truly advance the field, the priority is to identify the hypotheses most worthy of direct testing and the research directions most deserving of early investment.8.2The GAG–PAD4 mechanism as one falsifiable research hypothesisThe GAG–PAD4 mechanism is one hypothesis-generating component of this framework, rather than its established molecular center. Biochemical evidence justifies testing whether relevant GAG species influence PAD4 under gynecologic conditions, but does not establish that microbiota-dependent GAG changes regulate intracellular PAD4 or NET release in vivo. Testing should distinguish three questions: whether microbial status relates to local GAG composition, whether the relevant GAG species alter PAD4 activity in the appropriate compartment, and whether PAD4-dependent changes contribute to NET formation and disease-related outcomes. Negative results at any step would limit this proposed route without invalidating separately supported hormonal, microbial, or NET-related observations.8.3Research directions that should be prioritizedBased on the above hierarchy of hypotheses, the following research directions merit priority consideration.Direction 1: Test the compartment-specific relevance of the GAG–PAD4 hypothesisCore question: Do the relevant local GAG species affect PAD4 activity and NET formation in the disease compartment under study?Suggested research strategy: Evaluate the proposed links separately, beginning with characterization of local GAG species and controlled biochemical or cellular tests. Distinguish extracellular PAD4 activity from intracellular PAD4-dependent NET formation, and include appropriate controls for PAD4-independent effects. Tissue and secretion sampling should match the intended disease compartment; vaginal measurements should not be assumed to represent endometriotic lesions, ovarian tumors, or the placenta. Subsequent disease-model studies can test whether manipulating the candidate link changes both the mechanistic readouts and a relevant phenotype. Negative findings should be used to revise or reject the proposed connection (128–130).Direction 2: Prioritize analytical validation and harmonization of NET-related measurementsCore question: How can NET-related measurements be made analytically reliable, biologically interpretable, and comparable across laboratories?Suggested research strategy: Method-development studies should prioritize analyte definition, specimen-specific pre-analytical procedures, antibody specificity, suitable calibration materials, precision, recovery, dilutional behavior, and inter-laboratory reproducibility (110, 114). Soluble measurements should be evaluated alongside independent structural or functional NET assessments in representative samples (108). Automation may subsequently be investigated to improve throughput and workflow consistency, but it should not be assumed to improve NET specificity or replace analytical and clinical validation. Well-characterized cohorts should be used to investigate physiological variation and candidate reference distributions using validated assays before clinical decision thresholds are proposed.Technical challenges: Major challenges include specimen-dependent interference, heterogeneity in analytes and assay formats, harmonization across laboratories, and the distinction between physiological variation, disease association, and clinical utility.Direction 3: Conduct prospective cohort studies based on framework-related signaturesCore question: Do framework-related signatures, defined by hormones plus microbiota plus NETs, have independent clinical predictive value?Suggested research strategy: Establish multicenter prospective cohorts including patients with representative diseases such as endometriosis, PCOS, and preeclampsia, together with healthy controls. Baseline samples should be collected using standardized procedures, with simultaneous assessment of hormones (E2, P4, and E2/P4), microbiota features (16S rRNA sequencing and Lactobacillus abundance), and NET-related markers (CitH3, NE, and MPO–DNA). Clinical endpoints, including disease progression, treatment response, recurrence, and pregnancy outcomes, should then be longitudinally followed to evaluate the independent predictive value of these framework-related signatures. Unsupervised approaches such as clustering analysis may help identify disease subtypes based on framework characteristics and explore their association with clinical outcomes.Technical challenges: Multicenter coordination is organizationally demanding; large sample sizes are needed to preserve statistical power under multiple-testing conditions; follow-up periods are long, especially for recurrence and pregnancy outcomes; and the costs of microbiota and NETs analyses remain a practical concern.8.4Closing remarksThe value of this framework lies in distinguishing supported component-level observations from untested connections across gynecologic diseases. Future work should combine disease-specific and compartment-resolved studies, reliable NET measurements, and prospective human research to determine which links are reproducible and clinically relevant. The GAG–PAD4 mechanism is one candidate for such testing, not a prerequisite for the validity of all hormonal, microbial, or NET-related observations. The framework should be revised as evidence supports, limits, or refutes its proposed connections.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionThe spectrum of gynecologic diseases encompasses a wide range of conditions, including infectious disorders, endocrine disturbances, malignancies, and pregnancy-related complications. Population-level analyses from the Global Burden of Disease studies indicate that diseases of the female reproductive system contribute substantially to morbidity and disability worldwide, although estimates vary according to disease definitions, age groups, and analytic categories (Y. 1, 2). Endometriosis, uterine fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), and gynecologic malignancies also exert substantial effects on patients’ quality of life (3). Despite their heterogeneous clinical manifestations, these diseases share several common pathogenic features, notably immune dysregulation, endocrine imbalance, and alterations in the microbiota (4, 5).The immune system plays a central role in gynecologic diseases (6, 7). Pelvic inflammatory disease is characterized by an acute inflammatory response triggered by pathogens, endometriotic lesions exhibit a chronic inflammatory microenvironment, and gynecologic tumors often display immune evasion. Although these three disease settings present distinct immune phenotypes, all involve dysfunctional immune regulation (5, 8–10). The endocrine system is also closely implicated in gynecologic disorders. Endometriosis is estrogen-dependent, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is characterized by hyperandrogenism, and premature ovarian insufficiency manifests as a decline in endocrine function (11, 12). In recent years, major advances have also been made in research on the reproductive tract microecology. Existing evidence suggests that vaginal dysbiosis is associated with a range of gynecologic conditions, including bacterial vaginosis, persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, pelvic inflammatory disease, and preterm birth. These findings indicate that the microbiota may play an important role in the onset and progression of gynecologic diseases (13–16).The discovery of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) has provided a new perspective for understanding these complex mechanisms. NETs are web-like fibrous structures released by activated neutrophils and consist of a DNA scaffold decorated with histones and granular proteins such as neutrophil elastase (NE) and myeloperoxidase (MPO). They were initially described as an antimicrobial mechanism that contributes to host defense by trapping and killing pathogens (17). However, subsequent studies have shown that excessive NET formation or impaired NET clearance may result in tissue injury, promote fibrosis, and even contribute to tumor progression (18–21).In the field of gynecology, the involvement of NETs has been reported in multiple settings, although the quality and directness of evidence differ across diseases. NET-related tissue injury has been described in experimental PID/SPID-related settings, NET deposition or NET-associated markers have been reported in endometriosis, NET-related inflammatory changes have been linked to PCOS in exploratory clinical and animal studies, and aberrant NET-related activity has also been implicated in pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia (22–24). Given the broad involvement of NETs in gynecologic diseases, efforts have increasingly turned toward the development of integrative theoretical frameworks. Recently, Wu et al., in a review published in Frontiers in Medicine, integrated NETs into gynecologic endocrinology and proposed the conceptual framework of a “NET–sex hormone axis,” suggesting that sex hormones, particularly estrogen and progesterone, regulate NET formation, while NETs may, in turn, influence the progression of hormone-related diseases (5, 25, 26). This framework provides a theoretical basis for understanding the role of NETs in hormone-dependent gynecologic diseases.The reproductive tract microbiota is a dynamic ecosystem that is profoundly regulated by sex hormones (13, 27). Estrogen promotes glycogen deposition and the growth of Lactobacillus, thereby helping maintain an acidic pH and mucosal barrier function, whereas progesterone alters the colonization environment of the microbiota by affecting the properties of cervical mucus (28, 29). The microbiota may regulate local immune responses through multiple mechanisms, including potential effects on neutrophil activation and NET formation (21, 30). Recent in vitro studies suggest that microbial metabolites may influence the composition and sulfation patterns of mucosal glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), while GAGs can bind to peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4), a key enzyme in NETosis, and modulate its calcium sensitivity in vitro (31–33). This in vitro finding offers a new molecular perspective for understanding the link between the microbiota and NETs. At the same time, NETs themselves may exert feedback effects on the endocrine microenvironment through several possible routes, including protease-mediated degradation of the extracellular matrix, inflammatory factor-mediated effects on the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis, and fibrosis-associated alterations in local hormone metabolism. However, these pathways are currently supported mainly by correlative studies or in vitro experiments, and their causal relationships remain to be clarified (18–20).Terminologically, “microbiota” refers here to microbial communities, whereas “microbiome” is used only when referring to the broader microbial ecosystem, microbial genetic content, or the wording of cited literature. Because the proposed framework focuses primarily on microbial communities and host immune responses, “microbiota” is used throughout for the mechanistic framework.Accumulating evidence suggests that inflammatory imbalance in gynecologic diseases is unlikely to be driven by a single factor alone, but may involve interactions among hormonal changes, local microbiota dysbiosis, defined pathogens or microbial products, and aberrant NET formation. From this perspective, examining gynecologic diseases through the lens of a hormone–microbiota–NET framework may help organize shared inflammatory regulatory mechanisms across different disease categories. Current evidence on the hormonal regulation of NETs is derived primarily from in vitro studies and animal models outside the gynecologic field, indicating that estrogenic signaling may enhance NETosis under selected conditions, whereas progesterone may restrain selected stages of NET formation; however, direct evidence in gynecologic patients remains relatively limited. Moreover, although pathogen- or microbial product-induced NET formation through pathogen-associated molecular pattern–Toll-like receptor (PAMP–TLR) pathways has been investigated to some extent in acute infection, its role in chronic inflammatory gynecologic disorders remains to be further defined. The proposed framework is illustrated in Figure 1.Figure 1Evidence framework of hormone–microbiota–NET interactions in gynecologic diseases and their translational implications. This figure summarizes the current evidence landscape linking hormonal regulation, reproductive tract microbiota, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) across gynecologic diseases. Rather than representing a unified causal pathway, the framework distinguishes experimentally supported relationships from hypothesis-generating connections. Hormonal effects on NET formation are context-dependent and are supported mainly by experimental systems, pregnancy-associated studies, and non-gynecologic inflammatory models. Microbial stimulation of NET formation through pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) represents a relatively established mechanism in infectious settings. By contrast, the potential regulation of NET formation through microbiota-associated alterations in glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and PAD4 remains a hypothesis-generating mechanism supported p…

full_text: AbstractDirect evidence for a continuous immune-priming defect in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) remains incomplete. This Review therefore does not treat failed priming as an established LSCC mechanism. Instead, it separates direct LSCC observations from evidence derived from mixed-site head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cohorts and mechanistic studies in other tumors, using this hierarchy to identify supported pathway nodes and unresolved connections. Direct LSCC studies support recurrent loss of MHC class I antigen-processing components, favorable associations between tumor HLA-DR and clinical outcome, accumulation of PD-L2-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, remodeling of dendritic cell states, and an association between tumor-cell STING abundance and advanced disease. None of these findings demonstrates antigen-specific priming. Cross-tumor evidence provides mechanistic context for cDC1 cross-presentation, CCR7-dependent migration, tumor-draining lymph-node priming, and functional cGAS-STING signaling, but these links require LSCC-specific validation. We therefore distinguish MHC class I from MHC class II presentation, cross-presentation from tumor-cell HLA-DR expression, lymph-node priming from intratumoral restimulation, and STING abundance from activation, downstream output, and function. Translational priorities are grouped into evidence-based tiers according to the strength of LSCC evidence and intervention tractability. The MHC-I antigen-processing machinery, PD-L2-positive pDC states, and functional cGAS-STING competence merit the earliest LSCC-specific validation, whereas CLEC9A-, XCR1-, and FLT3L-directed cDC1 strategies remain mechanistically compelling but rely mainly on evidence from other tumor systems. Future multicenter studies should incorporate HLA genotype, population diversity, paired tumor and draining-node sampling, functional assays, and bioinformatic or artificial-intelligence integration with external validation. The proposed sensing-low, presentation-deficient, regulatory-DC-dominant, and signal-present but functionally disconnected phenotypes remain research constructs rather than clinical selection tools. The framework is intended to test where priming fails, if it fails at all, without presenting an unproven LSCC-specific pathway as established biology.Keywords: antigen presentation, cGAS-STING, cross-presentation, dendritic cells, HLA-DR, immune checkpoint resistance, laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, tumor-draining lymph nodes 7.2.2.Validation of single-cell and spatial findingsLSCC atlases should report donor numbers and characteristics alongside cell counts, separate discovery from validation, and disclose reused datasets or overlapping specimens. Donor-level subsite, stage, treatment, handling, and batch should be reported. Cell annotations need convergent markers and orthogonal validation where possible. LAMP3-positive or mature regulatory programs should be described as states unless lineage is resolved. Ligand and receptor scores and spatial proximity generate interaction hypotheses, not evidence of signaling, antigen transfer, priming, or suppression. Trajectory and migration claims require longitudinal, lineage, or perturbational evidence (9, 10, 66). 7.Discussion7.1.Prioritizing actionable nodes within the LSCC immune-priming axisTarget prioritization should reflect both the strength of LSCC evidence and intervention tractability rather than pathway prominence alone. We therefore separate candidates supported by direct LSCC observations from those transferred from broader HNSCC or other tumor systems, and we distinguish antibody-accessible surface molecules from intracellular pathways that require pharmacological or genetic modulation. The hierarchy below defines research priorities for mechanistic and translational validation. It is not a clinical treatment recommendation. Candidates within the same tier are not ranked further because their evidence types and intervention modalities are not directly comparable.The highest LSCC-specific validation priority includes the MHC-I antigen-processing machinery, PD-L2-positive pDC states, and functional cGAS-STING competence. Recurrent loss of HLA class I and antigen-processing components provides the strongest direct evidence for a potentially actionable presentation bottleneck (3, 4). Restoration strategies may involve reversible transcriptional or epigenetic regulators such as LSD1, but success must be judged by recovered peptide display and cognate T cell recognition rather than by HLA abundance alone (25). PD-L2-positive pDCs are directly associated with nodal disease, adverse outcome, and lower CD8-positive T cell infiltration in LSCC (8). PD-L2 is antibody accessible, but separate PD-L2 blockade cannot yet be prioritized clinically because PD-1 blockade already interrupts PD-L2 signaling and causality remains unproven. STING is similarly a high-priority functional stratification node rather than an expression-selected drug target. Agonism is most defensible when cell-resolved activation, downstream output, and immune rescue are demonstrable (11, 57, 58).Second-tier candidates are cDC1-directed strategies centered on CLEC9A, XCR1, and FLT3L. CLEC9A and XCR1 represent candidate receptors for cDC1-directed antigen-delivery strategies; however, their antibody-targeting utility and functional relevance have not been validated in LSCC. FLT3L can expand cDC1 populations and strengthen draining-node priming in experimental systems (18, 22, 29), but this strategy also lacks direct functional validation in LSCC. CCR7 is better viewed as a migration-enabling node than as a conventional blockade target because inhibiting CCR7 could impair the trafficking required for priming (19, 21).Lower-priority exploratory candidates include the LAMP3 or mature regulatory dendritic-cell program and the tumor HLA-DR or CIITA axis. LAMP3 marks a mature state that may arise from several dendritic-cell lineages and is not a sufficiently specific surface target by itself (9, 10, 20). Tumor HLA-DR has reproducible prognostic and immune-context associations in LSCC (5, 6), but its current value is greater as a biomarker or functional readout than as a direct therapeutic target. HNSCC dendritic-cell vaccines and innate adjuvants remain developmental, and their relevance to LSCC depends on evidence that they restore antigen-specific priming rather than inflammation alone (67, 68).TRIM29 should also remain a Tier 3 exploratory intracellular mediator. Its inhibition could, in principle, stabilize STING or relieve PERK/ROS-associated suppression of TBK1 signaling, and SB24011 provides preclinical proof of concept for disrupting the STING-TRIM29 interaction (77–80). However, no LSCC study has established the relevant dependency, and no clinically validated TRIM29-directed intervention is available.Table 3 summarizes this evidence-to-intervention hierarchy and explicitly separates functional nodes, actionable mediators, and modality or classification. Actionable mediator: none established. Modality/classification: state-specific investigation or perturbation after lineage and spatial resolution.LSCC-related single-cell studies identify LAMP3-positive states, but lineage origin and function remain uncertain. Selection/functional readouts: lineage-resolved LAMP3 state, spatial localization, migration, and cognate T-cell effects.LAMP3 alone is not lineage specific and is not an ideal stand-alone surface target.Tier 3Functional node: tumor HLA-DR/CIITA axis. Actionable mediator: none established; CIITA is a candidate regulatory mediator. Modality/classification: biomarker stratification and functional perturbation or restoration studies.Direct LSCC cohorts associate tumor HLA-DR with favorable outcome and greater CD4 T-cell infiltration. Selection/functional readouts: tumor-cell HLA-DR and CIITA status, MHC-II peptidomics, and HLA-DR-dependent cognate CD4 T-cell activation.HLA-DR may mark an interferon-rich state and does not establish professional APC function.7.2.From evidence gaps to LSCC-specific validationPaired sampling across anatomical compartments. A multicenter prospective validation cohort would provide the clearest test of the compartment-resolved model by linking primary tumor, adjacent mucosa, blood, and anatomically mapped draining cervical nodes from the same patients. Nodal tissue is most informative when linked to metastatic status and pretreatment state. The design should preserve laryngeal subsite and record HPV testing method, tobacco and alcohol exposure, treatment history, stage, nodal basin, HLA genotype, self-reported race or ethnicity where appropriate, and genetically inferred ancestry when genomic data permit. Untreated primary disease should not be merged with treatment-exposed recurrence. Broader HNSCC evidence demonstrates site and treatment heterogeneity (1, 2), while current LSCC atlases do not connect tumor observations to priming in mapped nodes (9, 10, 66).7.2.1.Integration of molecular profiling with functional assaysImmunopeptidomics requires matched HLA typing. Fresh tissue assays should measure dendritic cell antigen uptake, maturation, costimulation, and CCR7-dependent migration. Systems using defined antigens can test cross-presentation and cognate T cell activation with peptide-loaded MHC multimers, ELISpot assays, cytokine measurements, or cytotoxicity assays. Paired tumor and node T cell receptor sequencing can identify clonotype expansion, although shared clonotypes do not prove antigen specificity. Blockade, genetic interruption, or rescue should test whether cGAS-STING, antigen-processing machinery, or a dendritic cell state is necessary for the effect. Cross-tumor studies support these measurements (19, 21, 22, 69, 70), but their LSCC relevance remains unproven.7.2.2.Validation of single-cell and spatial findingsLSCC atlases should report donor numbers and characteristics alongside cell counts, separate discovery from validation, and disclose reused datasets or overlapping specimens. Donor-level subsite, stage, treatment, handling, and batch should be reported. Cell annotations need convergent markers and orthogonal validation where possible. LAMP3-positive or mature regulatory programs should be described as states unless lineage is resolved. Ligand and receptor scores and spatial proximity generate interaction hypotheses, not evidence of signaling, antigen transfer, priming, or suppression. Trajectory and migration claims require longitudinal, lineage, or perturbational evidence (9, 10, 66).7.2.3.Candidate phenotypes remain provisionalA sensing-low phenotype would lack activation and downstream output after an appropriate stimulus. A presentation-deficient phenotype would show impaired peptide and MHC display. A regulatory-DC-dominant phenotype would inhibit cognate T cell activation in functional assays. A signal-present but functionally disconnected phenotype would show innate activation or HLA expression without migration, cross-presentation, node priming, or tumor-directed T cell output. These overlapping research categories require prespecified criteria and independent reproduction. They are not validated LSCC subtypes. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractDirect evidence for a continuous immune-priming defect in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) remains incomplete. This Review therefore does not treat failed priming as an established LSCC mechanism. Instead, it separates direct LSCC observations from evidence derived from mixed-site head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cohorts and mechanistic studies in other tumors, using this hierarchy to identify supported pathway nodes and unresolved connections. Direct LSCC studies support recurrent loss of MHC class I antigen-processing components, favorable associations between tumor HLA-DR and clinical outcome, accumulation of PD-L2-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells, remodeling of dendritic cell states, and an association between tumor-cell STING abundance and advanced disease. None of these findings demonstrates antigen-specific priming. Cross-tumor evidence provides mechanistic context for cDC1 cross-presentation, CCR7-dependent migration, tumor-draining lymph-node priming, and functional cGAS-STING signaling, but these links require LSCC-specific validation. We therefore distinguish MHC class I from MHC class II presentation, cross-presentation from tumor-cell HLA-DR expression, lymph-node priming from intratumoral restimulation, and STING abundance from activation, downstream output, and function. Translational priorities are grouped into evidence-based tiers according to the strength of LSCC evidence and intervention tractability. The MHC-I antigen-processing machinery, PD-L2-positive pDC states, and functional cGAS-STING competence merit the earliest LSCC-specific validation, whereas CLEC9A-, XCR1-, and FLT3L-directed cDC1 strategies remain mechanistically compelling but rely mainly on evidence from other tumor systems. Future multicenter studies should incorporate HLA genotype, population diversity, paired tumor and draining-node sampling, functional assays, and bioinformatic or artificial-intelligence integration with external validation. The proposed sensing-low, presentation-deficient, regulatory-DC-dominant, and signal-present but functionally disconnected phenotypes remain research constructs rather than clinical selection tools. The framework is intended to test where priming fails, if it fails at all, without presenting an unproven LSCC-specific pathway as established biology.Keywords: antigen presentation, cGAS-STING, cross-presentation, dendritic cells, HLA-DR, immune checkpoint resistance, laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, tumor-draining lymph nodes

full_text_sections.discussion: 7.Discussion7.1.Prioritizing actionable nodes within the LSCC immune-priming axisTarget prioritization should reflect both the strength of LSCC evidence and intervention tractability rather than pathway prominence alone. We therefore separate candidates supported by direct LSCC observations from those transferred from broader HNSCC or other tumor systems, and we distinguish antibody-accessible surface molecules from intracellular pathways that require pharmacological or genetic modulation. The hierarchy below defines research priorities for mechanistic and translational validation. It is not a clinical treatment recommendation. Candidates within the same tier are not ranked further because their evidence types and intervention modalities are not directly comparable.The highest LSCC-specific validation priority includes the MHC-I antigen-processing machinery, PD-L2-positive pDC states, and functional cGAS-STING competence. Recurrent loss of HLA class I and antigen-processing components provides the strongest direct evidence for a potentially actionable presentation bottleneck (3, 4). Restoration strategies may involve reversible transcriptional or epigenetic regulators such as LSD1, but success must be judged by recovered peptide display and cognate T cell recognition rather than by HLA abundance alone (25). PD-L2-positive pDCs are directly associated with nodal disease, adverse outcome, and lower CD8-positive T cell infiltration in LSCC (8). PD-L2 is antibody accessible, but separate PD-L2 blockade cannot yet be prioritized clinically because PD-1 blockade already interrupts PD-L2 signaling and causality remains unproven. STING is similarly a high-priority functional stratification node rather than an expression-selected drug target. Agonism is most defensible when cell-resolved activation, downstream output, and immune rescue are demonstrable (11, 57, 58).Second-tier candidates are cDC1-directed strategies centered on CLEC9A, XCR1, and FLT3L. CLEC9A and XCR1 represent candidate receptors for cDC1-directed antigen-delivery strategies; however, their antibody-targeting utility and functional relevance have not been validated in LSCC. FLT3L can expand cDC1 populations and strengthen draining-node priming in experimental systems (18, 22, 29), but this strategy also lacks direct functional validation in LSCC. CCR7 is better viewed as a migration-enabling node than as a conventional blockade target because inhibiting CCR7 could impair the trafficking required for priming (19, 21).Lower-priority exploratory candidates include the LAMP3 or mature regulatory dendritic-cell program and the tumor HLA-DR or CIITA axis. LAMP3 marks a mature state that may arise from several dendritic-cell lineages and is not a sufficiently specific surface target by itself (9, 10, 20). Tumor HLA-DR has reproducible prognostic and immune-context associations in LSCC (5, 6), but its current value is greater as a biomarker or functional readout than as a direct therapeutic target. HNSCC dendritic-cell vaccines and innate adjuvants remain developmental, and their relevance to LSCC depends on evidence that they restore antigen-specific priming rather than inflammation alone (67, 68).TRIM29 should also remain a Tier 3 exploratory intracellular mediator. Its inhibition could, in principle, stabilize STING or relieve PERK/ROS-associated suppression of TBK1 signaling, and SB24011 provides preclinical proof of concept for disrupting the STING-TRIM29 interaction (77–80). However, no LSCC study has established the relevant dependency, and no clinically validated TRIM29-directed intervention is available.Table 3 summarizes this evidence-to-intervention hierarchy and explicitly separates functional nodes, actionable mediators, and modality or classification. full_text_sections.conclusion: 8.ConclusionsLSCC contains several observations that make defective immune priming a credible but unproven research question. These include loss of MHC class I antigen-processing components, favorable associations with tumor HLA-DR, accumulation of PD-L2-positive pDCs, altered dendritic-cell states, and stage-associated tumor-cell STING abundance (3–6, 8–11). Yet no LSCC study identified in this Review demonstrates the complete sequence from innate danger sensing and peptide presentation to dendritic-cell migration, tumor-draining lymph-node priming, and antigen-specific T cell entry into the tumor. The compartment-resolved model should therefore be read as an evidence-organizing and hypothesis-testing framework, not as an established LSCC-specific mechanism.Progress will require compartment-resolved and temporally defined studies that pair tumor tissue with adjacent mucosa, blood, and anatomically mapped draining lymph nodes. Molecular atlases should be linked to immunopeptidomics, dendritic-cell function, perturbation or rescue experiments, and antigen-specific T cell assays. Among translational candidates, the MHC-I antigen-processing machinery has the strongest direct LSCC evidence for a potentially reversible presentation bottleneck. PD-L2-positive pDC states and cell-resolved STING competence merit high-priority mechanistic validation, whereas CLEC9A, XCR1, FLT3L, and related cDC1 strategies are compelling but currently supported mainly by HNSCC or cross-tumor evidence. Multicenter studies should incorporate HLA genotype and population diversity, and computational or AI models should be externally validated and linked to functional assays. Until these findings are prospectively reproduced, the proposed pathway nodes and priming phenotypes should remain research variables rather than clinical selection tools. TRIM29 is an exploratory intracellular modifier of STING/TBK1 output, but its expression, pathway dependence, and therapeutic tractability remain untested in LSCC.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionLaryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) presents an unusual immunological problem. It arises in a mucosal organ that is repeatedly exposed to inhaled particles, microbial products, tobacco-associated injury, and treatment-related tissue damage, yet clinically meaningful antitumor immunity is not assured. This Review treats checkpoint inhibitor evidence from recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) as contextual evidence from an anatomically heterogeneous population rather than as an LSCC-specific estimate of efficacy. This distinction matters because HPV-negative HNSCCs from different anatomical sites have non-equivalent genomic, transcriptional, hypoxic, and immune profiles (1). More recent profiling of recurrent or metastatic HNSCC also indicates that anatomical site and the number of prior treatment lines can shape the molecular and immune landscape (2). Direct LSCC studies point to defects at earlier stages of the cancer immunity cycle. Downregulation of HLA class I and several antigen-processing machinery components has been associated with reduced CD8-positive T cell infiltration and unfavorable survival (3). A separate immunohistochemical series also reported frequent loss or reduction of TAP1, LMP7, and HLA class I (4). These findings justify closer examination of antigen display in LSCC. They do not, however, indicate a uniform presentation defect across tumors or a single cause of treatment resistance.The usual description of an inflamed or non-inflamed tumor based on tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density cannot resolve this problem. T cell presence does not necessarily indicate tumor antigen recognition, and antigen recognition does not necessarily reflect productive priming or subsequent effector killing. A tumor section containing CD8-positive cells cannot identify the peptides recognized by their T cell receptors or determine where these cells first encountered antigen. Nor can it show that a professional antigen-presenting cell supplied adequate costimulation and differentiation signals. LSCC observations illustrate this interpretive gap. Tumor cell HLA-DR expression has been associated with better clinical outcomes in two cohorts (5, 6). In one 56-patient series, HLA-DR was detected on tumor cells in 18 cases and was associated with favorable disease-specific and relapse-free survival, although the imprecision of some hazard estimates limits strong inference (5). A later study linked high tumor HLA-DR expression to greater CD4-positive T cell infiltration and favorable outcomes (6). These associations may reflect an interferon-exposed or otherwise inflamed tumor state, or a functionally relevant MHC class II program. Neither possibility has been confirmed by evidence of peptide loading, antigen-specific CD4-positive T cell activation, or de novo priming of naive T cells. Mixed-site HNSCC data strengthen the plausibility of the biomarker hypothesis because a malignant cell interferon and MHC class II program was associated with pembrolizumab response (7). Such evidence is generalizable in principle but not specific to LSCC and cannot by itself validate tumor HLA-DR as a predictive biomarker in laryngeal cancer.Observations involving dendritic cells and innate sensing provide further evidence of disconnected immune states. In LSCC, increased tumor-infiltrating plasmacytoid dendritic cells were associated with nodal disease, adverse outcome, and lower CD8-positive T cell infiltration (8). The same study found a higher proportion of PD-L2-positive pDCs in tumor than in paired adjacent non-tumor tissue and an inverse association between PD-L2-positive pDC abundance and CD8-positive T cell infiltration, but it did not test causality (8). Single-cell studies of vocal cord leukoplakia and LSCC have identified immune remodeling before or during malignant transition (9). One analysis reported abundant LAMP3-positive dendritic cells in leukoplakia and correlations with regulatory T cells and exhausted CD8-positive T cell states (10). LAMP3 expression alone does not prove lineage origin, migration to tumor-draining lymph nodes, or suppressive function. Likewise, tumor cell STING abundance was associated with advanced stage, higher grade, and nodal positivity in a 59-sample LSCC series (11). Protein abundance is not equivalent to recent pathway activation, downstream interferon output, or effective dendritic cell cross-priming. A detectable immune pathway may nevertheless remain disconnected from antigen-specific T cell immunity. Spatial evidence from mixed-site HNSCC offers a useful comparison. CCR7-positive dendritic cell niches were associated with survival in a pretreatment pembrolizumab cohort (12). However, comparable evidence for LSCC-specific dendritic cell trafficking and lymph node priming has not been identified in the current literature.This Review addresses a question that lies upstream of the dominant explanations for immune failure in LSCC. Two recent companion reviews examined cancer-associated fibroblasts and myeloid-derived suppressor cells as mediators of stromal remodeling, immune exclusion, myeloid suppression, and checkpoint inhibitor resistance (13, 14). The present Review does not duplicate those downstream frameworks, nor does it assume that LSCC possesses a unique or uniform failure-to-prime phenotype. Instead, it asks whether danger sensing, antigen processing, peptide presentation, dendritic cell maturation, lymphatic migration, and tumor-draining lymph-node priming are functionally connected in LSCC. Tumor-intrinsic MHC class I presentation is separated from MHC class II presentation, cross-presentation from tumor-cell HLA-DR expression, naive T cell priming from intratumoral restimulation, and STING expression from activation, output, and function. Direct LSCC observations are treated as the primary evidence layer. Mixed-site HNSCC studies are used as anatomical and clinical context, whereas studies in other tumors and experimental systems are used only to establish mechanistic plausibility. This hierarchy is intended to prevent cross-tumor mechanisms from being presented as LSCC findings. The central model is deliberately conditional: in some LSCCs, detectable innate signals and HLA molecules may remain disconnected from competent antigen processing, professional dendritic-cell activation, migration to draining lymph nodes, and tumor-specific T cell priming. “Failure to prime” is therefore a falsifiable organizing framework rather than an established disease mechanism. The purpose of the Review is to define which nodes are supported in LSCC, which links remain untested, and which translational candidates justify prioritized validation. 2.A compartment-resolved framework for sensing, presentation, and priming2.1.Step 1: danger sensing is distinct from antigen sensingThe first step is detection of danger, not recognition of a tumor peptide. cGAS detects aberrantly localized double-stranded DNA and generates cyclic GMP-AMP, which engages STING to activate IRF3 and induce type I interferon and NF-κB-associated outputs (15, 16). These signals may promote chemokine production, dendritic cell recruitment, and acquisition of an activated state. They do not identify which tumor antigen will be processed or which T cell receptor will recognize it. This separation is especially important in LSCC because the available direct study measured tumor cell cGAS and STING abundance rather than pathway activation or antigen-specific immunity (11). Innate sensing should therefore be treated as a potentially enabling condition. Its immune consequence depends on the responding cell type, signal duration, downstream competence, and connection to professional antigen-presenting cells.2.2.Step 2: antigen processing and MHC presentationAntigen visibility requires more than HLA expression. full_text: BackgroundOral cancer remains a major global health challenge, with delayed diagnosis contributing to poor prognosis and reduced survival. Dental students play an important role in early detection; however, deficiencies in preparedness and diagnostic confidence have been reported. This study assessed oral cancer knowledge, oral potentially malignant disorder (OPMD) awareness, and diagnostic confidence among Saudi dental students.MethodsA quantitative cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 354 dental students and interns from governmental and private dental schools in Saudi Arabia. The questionnaire assessed oral cancer knowledge, OPMD knowledge, and self-reported diagnostic confidence related to screening and biopsy procedures. Participants were classified as meeting or not meeting a study-defined minimum operational threshold of ≥60% of the maximum possible score in each domain; this cutoff was not interpreted as a definition of “good” performance or clinical competence. Associations between participant characteristics and study outcomes were examined using chi-square tests and multivariable binary logistic regression analyses.ResultsOverall, 81.9% of participants met the oral cancer knowledge threshold, 55.4% met the OPMD knowledge threshold, and 24.0% met the diagnostic confidence threshold. Most participants correctly identified major oral cancer risk factors, including tobacco smoking (97.2%), alcohol consumption (92.7%), and human papillomavirus infection (86.7%). However, clinically oriented response patterns highlighted areas for educational attention. 20.1% selected the prespecified specialist-referral response for management of a persistent suspicious lesion, while 35.6% recognized factors associated with increased malignant transformation risk in leukoplakia. Intern status remained independently associated with meeting the oral cancer knowledge and diagnostic confidence thresholds in multivariable analyses. The diagnostic-confidence outcome reflected self-perceived preparedness rather than observed screening, referral, or procedural competence.ConclusionA high proportion of Saudi dental students met the study-defined oral cancer knowledge threshold; however, self-reported diagnostic confidence and preparedness for early detection remained considerably lower. Strengthening competency-based oral cancer education and clinical training may improve early detection preparedness and referral practices among future dental practitioners. Because the domains assessed different constructs and had different effective cutoffs, their threshold proportions should not be compared directly; the diagnostic-confidence findings represent perceived preparedness only. Materials and methodsStudy design and participantsA quantitative observational cross-sectional survey was carried out among dental students and interns enrolled in Saudi dental schools. The study was designed to evaluate participants’ understanding of oral cancer, knowledge of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), and confidence in performing oral cancer screening and managing suspicious oral lesions.Participants were recruited using nonprobability convenience sampling. Data were collected from April 2024 through the end of December 2024. The target population comprised third-, fourth-, and fifth-year undergraduate dental students and dental interns at governmental and private dental schools in Saudi Arabia. A structured, self-administered questionnaire was hosted on Google Forms, and the survey link was distributed electronically through WhatsApp, Telegram, X, and student discussion groups to facilitate participation from dental institutions in different regions of the country. As invitations were disseminated through these channels without an individually tracked invitation list, the number of unique eligible students who received the invitation could not be established. Consequently, a conventional response rate could not be calculated. Participation was entirely voluntary, and responses were submitted anonymously after electronic consent was provided. To minimize duplicate submissions, the Google Forms ‘Limit to 1 response’ setting was enabled during data collection, restricting submissions to one per signed-in Google account. All questionnaire items were mandatory, and respondents were required to answer every item before the form could be submitted. The final analytical sample comprised 354 eligible respondents from 20 reported institutional-affiliation categories, including governmental and private institutions. Of these respondents, 251 were undergraduate dental students and 103 were interns. Institutional affiliation and university type were based on information reported by participants. Responses from the 30 participants involved in pilot testing were excluded from the final analysis.Reporting of the study was guided by the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines (16) and the Checklist for Reporting Results of Internet E-Surveys (CHERRIES) (17). A completed CHERRIES checklist is provided as Supplementary Material. Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University (Approval No. SCBR-373/2024). All procedures were performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Participant anonymity was ensured, and all collected data were treated with strict confidentiality. This study involved human participants. Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants before questionnaire completion, and participation was voluntary and anonymous.Questionnaire development, validation, and data collectionData were gathered using a structured self-administered questionnaire distributed electronically through online platforms. The survey instrument was developed after reviewing previously published studies related to oral cancer awareness, oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), and diagnostic preparedness among dental students and dental practitioners (18–21).The questionnaire consisted of four sections:Sociodemographic information.Knowledge related to oral cancer.Knowledge regarding oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs).Diagnostic confidence and preparedness for oral cancer screening and biopsy-related procedures.The questionnaire items were presented in multiple-choice format with predefined response options. No adaptive questioning or branching logic was used. All participants were presented with the same questionnaire items. The survey evaluated participants’ understanding of oral cancer risk factors, clinical manifestations, lesion monitoring, biopsy procedures, identification of OPMDs, malignant transformation potential, and self-perceived confidence in oral cancer examination and early detection practices.The complete questionnaire, original response options, designated scoring key, and supporting clinical references are provided in the Supplementary Questionnaire. For the item addressing management of a persistent suspicious lesion, “Consultation to a Specialist” was the prespecified scoring key. Because this was an educational survey of third-, fourth-, and fifth-year dental students and dental interns, the item was intended to assess referral-related decision-making and recognition of the need for escalation to specialist evaluation rather than to define the full range of management actions available to an appropriately trained clinician. Current evidence-based guidance supports either immediate biopsy by an appropriately trained clinician or immediate referral to an appropriate specialist when an oral mucosal lesion is clinically suspicious (22). For the follow-up item, 3 weeks was the prespecified scoring key, reflecting NICE guidance that unexplained oral ulceration persisting for more than 3 weeks warrants referral on a suspected-cancer pathway. In this student/intern educational context, the item is interpreted as recognition of a persistence threshold rather than as a recommendation to observe an already clinically suspicious lesion for 3 weeks; such lesions require prompt biopsy or specialist referral (23). For the malignant-transformation item, erosive oral lichen planus was designated as the lowest-risk option among the listed choices; this comparative classification is consistent with the relatively low absolute malignant-transformation rate reported for oral lichen planus compared with several higher-risk OPMDs, while erosive/red forms still warrant continued surveillance (7, 44).Content validity and face validity were assessed by three experts in the field of oral medicine and oral pathology to ensure the relevance, clarity, and appropriateness of the questionnaire items. A pilot study involving 30 participants was subsequently conducted to evaluate questionnaire clarity, comprehensibility, and feasibility. Based on participant feedback obtained during the pilot phase, minor modifications were made to improve the wording and structure of several items. Responses collected during the pilot study were excluded from the final statistical analysis (17).Scoring and operational definitionsEach response matching the prespecified scoring key in the oral cancer and OPMD knowledge domains was assigned one point. Diagnostic confidence items were dichotomized. For the three Poor/Fair/Good self-rating items, the response option “Good” was coded as a favorable item-level response; for the oral-biopsy knowledge self-rating item, “Yes” was coded as favorable. These item-level favorable responses were distinct from the aggregate domain classification and did not mean that participants meeting the ≥60% study-defined threshold had “good” diagnostic competence.Bloom’s taxonomy provides a framework for educational objectives (24); it was not used to validate a numerical cutoff for the present questionnaire. A threshold of ≥60% was applied as a pragmatic, study-defined operational criterion for descriptive comparisons and binary logistic regression analyses. This choice has precedent in healthcare questionnaire research: Raab et al. (25) classified knowledge using a threshold of at least three of five questions answered correctly or sufficiently. In Saudi dental hygiene students, Mulla (26) categorized scores <60% as poor, 60%–80% as average, and >80% as good. These studies provide precedent for using a 60% boundary, rather than validation of the present domain classifications. Accordingly, aggregate outcomes are described as meeting or not meeting the study-defined threshold and are not interpreted as evidence of clinical competence.Because the domain scores were based on whole items, the nominal ≥60% rule did not produce an exact 60% cutoff in any domain. Participants meeting the study-defined threshold scored ≥8/12 for oral cancer knowledge (66.7%) and ≥9/14 for OPMD knowledge (64.3%). For diagnostic confidence, the same rule required ≥3/4 favorable self-reported responses (75.0%). Thus, the effective operational cutoffs ranged from 64.3% to 75.0%. Because diagnostic confidence was self-reported rather than performance-based, this classification represents perceived preparedness and was not validated against an external measure of clinical competence.Reliability analysisInternal consistency reliability was evaluated in the main study sample using Cronbach’s alpha coefficient in IBM SPSS Statistics version 25. Reliability testing was performed on item-level responses within each questionnaire domain, with reverse coding applied where appropriate prior to analysis. The questionnaire demonstrated acceptable internal consistency reliability. Domain-specific Cronbach’s alpha coefficients were 0.72 for oral cancer knowledge, 0.74 for knowledge of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), and 0.71 for diagnostic confidence. Cronbach’s alpha values of ≥0.70 were considered indicative of acceptable reliability for the study instrument (27).Sample size calculationThe theoretical sample size requirement for estimating a single proportion was assessed using the single-proportion formula implemented in OpenEpi software (Open Source Epidemiologic Statistics for Public Health, version 3.01) (28). The value of 50% used in the calculation did not represent the prevalence of oral cancer or OPMDs. Rather, because no sufficiently reliable prior estimate was available for the proportion of Saudi dental students expected to meet the study outcomes across the assessed domains, an anticipated proportion of 50% (p = 0.50) was selected as a conservative assumption. This value maximizes p(1 - p) and therefore yields the largest required sample size for a fixed confidence level and margin of error. Using n = Z2p(1 - p)/d2, with a 95% confidence level (Z = 1.96), p = 0.50, and an absolute precision of 5%, the calculation yielded 384.16, rounded upward to 385 participants. The final analytical sample comprised 354 dental students and interns. Under the same simple-random-sampling assumptions, this sample corresponds to a nominal margin of error of approximately ±5.21 percentage points. This precision estimate represents a theoretical benchmark given the study’s nonprobability convenience sampling approach.A supplementary assessment evaluated the available sample relative to the complexity of the multivariable logistic regression models. Each model included three binary predictors: gender, study level, and university type, corresponding to three predictor parameters excluding the intercept. The smaller outcome categories contained 64 participants for oral cancer knowledge, 158 for OPMD knowledge, and 85 for diagnostic confidence. Dividing these counts by three yielded ratios of 21.3, 52.7, and 28.3 observations per predictor parameter, respectively. These ratios exceeded the conventional benchmark of 10 events per predictor parameter (29), supporting the limited complexity of the fitted models. Nevertheless, this assessment does not establish statistical power for individual adjusted associations or guarantee model adequacy (30).Statistical analysisData analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Descriptive statistics were applied to summarize participants’ demographic characteristics and questionnaire responses. Categorical variables were reported as frequencies and percentages.Item scores were summed within each domain, and participants were classified as meeting or not meeting a study-defined minimum threshold of ≥60% of the maximum possible domain score. This boundary was used as an operational classification criterion, informed by previous questionnaire research (22, 23), and was not considered a validated standard of good performance. Because whole-item scoring was used, the corresponding effective thresholds were ≥8/12 (66.7%) for oral cancer knowledge, ≥9/14 (64.3%) for OPMD knowledge, and ≥3/4 (75.0%) favorable self-reported responses for diagnostic confidence. full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundOral cancer remains a major global health challenge, with delayed diagnosis contributing to poor prognosis and reduced survival. Dental students play an important role in early detection; however, deficiencies in preparedness and diagnostic confidence have been reported. This study assessed oral cancer knowledge, oral potentially malignant disorder (OPMD) awareness, and diagnostic confidence among Saudi dental students.MethodsA quantitative cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 354 dental students and interns from governmental and private dental schools in Saudi Arabia. The questionnaire assessed oral cancer knowledge, OPMD knowledge, and self-reported diagnostic confidence related to screening and biopsy procedures. Participants were classified as meeting or not meeting a study-defined minimum operational threshold of ≥60% of the maximum possible score in each domain; this cutoff was not interpreted as a definition of “good” performance or clinical competence. Associations between participant characteristics and study outcomes were examined using chi-square tests and multivariable binary logistic regression analyses.ResultsOverall, 81.9% of participants met the oral cancer knowledge threshold, 55.4% met the OPMD knowledge threshold, and 24.0% met the diagnostic confidence threshold. Most participants correctly identified major oral cancer risk factors, including tobacco smoking (97.2%), alcohol consumption (92.7%), and human papillomavirus infection (86.7%). However, clinically oriented response patterns highlighted areas for educational attention. 20.1% selected the prespecified specialist-referral response for management of a persistent suspicious lesion, while 35.6% recognized factors associated with increased malignant transformation risk in leukoplakia. Intern status remained independently associated with meeting the oral cancer knowledge and diagnostic confidence thresholds in multivariable analyses. The diagnostic-confidence outcome reflected self-perceived preparedness rather than observed screening, referral, or procedural competence.ConclusionA high proportion of Saudi dental students met the study-defined oral cancer knowledge threshold; however, self-reported diagnostic confidence and preparedness for early detection remained considerably lower. Strengthening competency-based oral cancer education and clinical training may improve early detection preparedness and referral practices among future dental practitioners. Because the domains assessed different constructs and had different effective cutoffs, their threshold proportions should not be compared directly; the diagnostic-confidence findings represent perceived preparedness only.
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsStudy design and participantsA quantitative observational cross-sectional survey was carried out among dental students and interns enrolled in Saudi dental schools. The study was designed to evaluate participants’ understanding of oral cancer, knowledge of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), and confidence in performing oral cancer screening and managing suspicious oral lesions.Participants were recruited using nonprobability convenience sampling. Data were collected from April 2024 through the end of December 2024. The target population comprised third-, fourth-, and fifth-year undergraduate dental students and dental interns at governmental and private dental schools in Saudi Arabia. A structured, self-administered questionnaire was hosted on Google Forms, and the survey link was distributed electronically through WhatsApp, Telegram, X, and student discussion groups to facilitate participation from dental institutions in different regions of the country. As invitations were disseminated through these channels without an individually tracked invitation list, the number of unique eligible students who received the invitation could not be established. Consequently, a conventional response rate could not be calculated. Participation was entirely voluntary, and responses were submitted anonymously after electronic consent was provided. To minimize duplicate submissions, the Google Forms ‘Limit to 1 response’ setting was enabled during data collection, restricting submissions to one per signed-in Google account. All questionnaire items were mandatory, and respondents were required to answer every item before the form could be submitted. The final analytical sample comprised 354 eligible respondents from 20 reported institutional-affiliation categories, including governmental and private institutions. Of these respondents, 251 were undergraduate dental students and 103 were interns. Institutional affiliation and university type were based on information reported by participants. Responses from the 30 participants involved in pilot testing were excluded from the final analysis.Reporting of the study was guided by the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines (16) and the Checklist for Reporting Results of Internet E-Surveys (CHERRIES) (17). A completed CHERRIES checklist is provided as Supplementary Material. Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University (Approval No. SCBR-373/2024). All procedures were performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Participant anonymity was ensured, and all collected data were treated with strict confidentiality. This study involved human participants. Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants before questionnaire completion, and participation was voluntary and anonymous.Questionnaire development, validation, and data collectionData were gathered using a structured self-administered questionnaire distributed electronically through online platforms. The survey instrument was developed after reviewing previously published studies related to oral cancer awareness, oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), and diagnostic preparedness among dental students and dental practitioners (18–21).The questionnaire consisted of four sections:Sociodemographic information.Knowledge related to oral cancer.Knowledge regarding oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs).Diagnostic confidence and preparedness for oral cancer screening and biopsy-related procedures.The questionnaire items were presented in multiple-choice format with predefined response options. No adaptive questioning or branching logic was used. All participants were presented with the same questionnaire items. The survey evaluated participants’ understanding of oral cancer risk factors, clinical manifestations, lesion monitoring, biopsy procedures, identification of OPMDs, malignant transformation potential, and self-perceived confidence in oral cancer examination and early detection practices.The complete questionnaire, original response options, designated scoring key, and supporting clinical references are provided in the Supplementary Questionnaire. For the item addressing management of a persistent suspicious lesion, “Consultation to a Specialist” was the prespecified scoring key. Because this was an educational survey of third-, fourth-, and fifth-year dental students and dental interns, the item was intended to assess referral-related decision-making and recognition of the need for escalation to specialist evaluation rather than to define the full range of management actions available to an appropriately trained clinician. Current evidence-based guidance supports either immediate biopsy by an appropriately trained clinician or immediate referral to an appropriate specialist when an oral mucosal lesion is clinically suspicious (22). For the follow-up item, 3 weeks was the prespecified scoring key, reflecting NICE guidance that unexplained oral ulceration persisting for more than 3 weeks warrants referral on a suspected-cancer pathway. In this student/intern educational context, the item is interpreted as recognition of a persistence threshold rather than as a recommendation to observe an already clinically suspicious lesion for 3 weeks; such lesions require prompt biopsy or specialist referral (23). For the malignant-transformation item, erosive oral lichen planus was designated as the lowest-risk option among the listed choices; this comparative classification is consistent with the relatively low absolute malignant-transformation rate reported for oral lichen planus compared with several higher-risk OPMDs, while erosive/red forms still warrant continued surveillance (7, 44).Content validity and face validity were assessed by three experts in the field of oral medicine and oral pathology to ensure the relevance, clarity, and appropriateness of the questionnaire items. A pilot study involving 30 participants was subsequently conducted to evaluate questionnaire clarity, comprehensibility, and feasibility. Based on participant feedback obtained during the pilot phase, minor modifications were made to improve the wording and structure of several items. Responses collected during the pilot study were excluded from the final statistical analysis (17).Scoring and operational definitionsEach response matching the prespecified scoring key in the oral cancer and OPMD knowledge domains was assigned one point. Diagnostic confidence items were dichotomized. For the three Poor/Fair/Good self-rating items, the response option “Good” was coded as a favorable item-level response; for the oral-biopsy knowledge self-rating item, “Yes” was coded as favorable. These item-level favorable responses were distinct from the aggregate domain classification and did not mean that participants meeting the ≥60% study-defined threshold had “good” diagnostic competence.Bloom’s taxonomy provides a framework for educational objectives (24); it was not used to validate a numerical cutoff for the present questionnaire. A threshold of ≥60% was applied as a pragmatic, study-defined operational criterion for descriptive comparisons and binary logistic regression analyses. This choice has precedent in healthcare questionnaire research: Raab et al. (25) classified knowledge using a threshold of at least three of five questions answered correctly or sufficiently. In Saudi dental hygiene students, Mulla (26) categorized scores <60% as poor, 60%–80% as average, and >80% as good. These studies provide precedent for using a 60% boundary, rather than validation of the present domain classifications. Accordingly, aggregate outcomes are described as meeting or not meeting the study-defined threshold and are not interpreted as evidence of clinical competence.Because the domain scores were based on whole items, the nominal ≥60% rule did not…
