full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionStrengths and methodological contributions of the present studyThis multicenter study assessed oral cancer knowledge, knowledge of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), and self-reported diagnostic confidence within a single analytical framework. Participants were drawn from governmental and private dental institutions across Saudi Arabia, broadening institutional representation without implying population representativeness because recruitment was based on convenience sampling and institutional participation was unequal (19, 20). The questionnaire was informed by previous literature, reviewed by experts for face and content validity, pilot tested, and demonstrated acceptable internal consistency, supporting interpretation of the measured domains (17, 32, 33).Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine independent associations with the study-defined thresholds. Academic level and university type were independently associated with oral cancer knowledge, whereas academic level and gender were associated with diagnostic confidence. No significant adjusted associations were identified for OPMD knowledge (9, 11).Knowledge, OPMD awareness, and diagnostic confidenceThe three measured domains showed distinct patterns: 81.9% of participants met the oral cancer knowledge threshold, 55.4% met the OPMD knowledge threshold, and 24.0% met the diagnostic confidence threshold (Table 4). These proportions are not directly comparable because the domains assess different constructs and have different effective cutoffs. Importantly, diagnostic confidence reflects self-perceived preparedness rather than objectively demonstrated clinical performance and should not be interpreted as evidence of diagnostic accuracy or clinical competence. The continuous score summaries were therefore used only as within-domain descriptive complements to the dichotomized outcomes and not as evidence of equivalent performance across domains.Although knowledge of major oral cancer risk factors was generally high, clinically oriented areas for educational attention remained. 20.1% selected the prespecified specialist-referral response for a persistent suspicious lesion, 35.6% identified factors associated with increased malignant transformation risk in leukoplakia, and 33.1% answered “Yes” to having sufficient knowledge about oral biopsy techniques (Table 4). Referral and biopsy-related preparedness has likewise been identified as an educational concern internationally (9, 10), underscoring the value of training in clinical decision-making.These clinically oriented items should be interpreted within the educational context of a survey of dental students and interns and according to their prespecified scoring keys: specialist referral is a guideline-concordant response for a clinically suspicious lesion, although immediate biopsy by an appropriately trained clinician is also an acceptable pathway (22); the 3-week item represents a referral threshold for unexplained oral ulceration rather than a recommended delay for an already suspicious lesion (23); and erosive oral lichen planus was scored as the lowest-risk option among the disorders listed in that question, rather than as a lesion with negligible malignant potential (7, 44).OPMD knowledge was lower than oral cancer knowledge. Gaps in understanding malignant transformation are clinically important because recognition and risk assessment of OPMDs are central to prevention and early intervention (5, 6). Comparable OPMD-related knowledge gaps have been reported among dental students in other settings (18, 20).The Türkiye literature provides a useful regional parallel for these educational gaps. In a study comparing third- and fifth-year dental students, recognition of leukoplakia and erythroplakia as lesions with high carcinogenic potential was substantially more frequent among fifth-year students (13). This supports the relevance of academic progression to awareness of potentially malignant lesions, but the different instruments and sampled populations preclude direct comparison of percentages with the present study.Factors associated with study outcomesAcademic progression was related to both oral cancer knowledge and diagnostic confidence. Interns were more likely than undergraduate students to meet the corresponding thresholds, and these associations remained significant after adjustment (Tables 1, 2). Greater clinical exposure during internship may contribute to these differences, consistent with studies linking advanced training and practical experience to improved oral cancer knowledge and confidence (7, 11, 34). However, because the study was cross-sectional, these associations should not be interpreted as evidence that academic progression or clinical exposure caused the observed differences.This pattern is also consistent with recent evidence from Türkiye. The multicenter study by Yüksel et al. included students from 10 dental faculties and found significant variation across both academic grades and faculties (45), while Yildirim et al. reported higher oral cancer knowledge, screening awareness, and appropriate referral behavior among fifth-year than first-year students (47). These findings support examining training stage and institutional context, although differences in questionnaire content, sampling, and outcome definitions mean that the numerical results should not be treated as directly comparable.Students from governmental universities were more likely than those from private universities to meet the oral cancer knowledge threshold, whereas university type was not associated with OPMD knowledge or diagnostic confidence after adjustment. Gender was not associated with either knowledge outcome; however, male participants were more likely to meet the self-reported diagnostic confidence threshold. These associations may also be influenced by unmeasured educational or participant-level factors and by the voluntary convenience-based recruitment strategy. As confidence was self-reported, the observed gender difference should be interpreted as a difference in perceived preparedness rather than objective clinical ability (10, 11).Educational, clinical, and public health implicationsThe findings support greater emphasis on competency-based oral cancer education, including structured oral mucosal examination, referral decision-making, assessment of malignant transformation risk, and biopsy-related training. Supervised clinical exposure, simulation-based learning, and practical workshops may help translate theoretical knowledge into greater clinical preparedness (35–37).These priorities are clinically relevant because dentists are frontline providers for oral mucosal examination and early referral. Strengthening practical training during undergraduate education and internship may improve future screening and referral practices and help reduce diagnostic delay (38–43).
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionThe present study found that a high proportion of Saudi dental students met the study-defined oral cancer knowledge threshold, whereas a smaller proportion met the OPMD knowledge threshold. Self-reported diagnostic confidence was lower, and clinically oriented areas for educational attention remained, particularly in responses to suspicious-lesion management items, malignant transformation risk assessment, and biopsy-related procedures. Intern status was associated with meeting the oral cancer knowledge and diagnostic confidence thresholds. However, given the cross-sectional design, voluntary online convenience recruitment, and reliance on self-reported measures, these findings should be interpreted as descriptive and associational rather than causal, and diagnostic confidence should not be regarded as equivalent to objectively demonstrated clinical competence. The diagnostic-confidence findings therefore describe self-perceived preparedness rather than observed competence, and the threshold proportions across the three domains should not be interpreted as directly comparable because their effective cutoffs differed.These findings emphasize the need to strengthen competency-based oral cancer education within undergraduate dental curricula in Saudi Arabia through greater incorporation of supervised oral examination training, oral mucosal lesion assessment, biopsy-related education, and simulation-based clinical learning. Improving practical preparedness among future dental practitioners may contribute to earlier oral cancer detection, more effective referral practices, and improved public health outcomes.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionOral cancer is widely regarded as one of the most serious malignancies of the head and neck because of its substantial disease burden, the profound functional impairment it causes, and the poor survival rates associated with late-stage diagnosis. Although diagnostic and therapeutic modalities have advanced considerably, many patients still present at advanced stages, resulting in extensive tissue destruction, more complex treatment requirements, and diminished survival outcomes (1). As a result, strengthening early detection efforts has become a central priority in modern oral healthcare and cancer-prevention initiatives (2).Dental practitioners serve as key frontline providers in oral cancer prevention, as routine dental appointments offer repeated opportunities for comprehensive oral mucosal screening and early detection of suspicious lesions A recent multicountry survey of 4, 197 adults across 13 Middle Eastern and North African countries found limited public awareness of oral cancer and showed that receiving oral cancer education from a dentist was strongly associated with higher knowledge across the assessed domains (3). Therefore, dental students must develop strong foundational knowledge and clinical competence during their undergraduate training to recognize potentially malignant changes, conduct systematic oral examinations, and make timely referrals for specialist evaluation or biopsy. Inadequate preparation at the undergraduate level may contribute to diagnostic delays and missed opportunities for early intervention (4).A substantial proportion of oral cancers develop from pre-existing oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) (5). Conditions such as leukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis, and oral lichen planus carry varying degrees of malignant transformation risk and therefore require meticulous clinical evaluation and long-term surveillance. Early identification of these disorders is critical, as timely intervention during the premalignant phase may support earlier recognition of malignant change and timely management (6).Research conducted among dental students and dental professionals in different countries has demonstrated inconsistent levels of oral cancer awareness and diagnostic preparedness. Although awareness of major risk factors is often satisfactory (7, 8), deficiencies continue to be reported in practical areas such as biopsy-related procedures, management of suspicious lesions, referral pathways, and confidence in oral cancer screening practices (9). These findings indicate that acceptable theoretical understanding may not always correspond to adequate clinical readiness (10).Educational progression appears to significantly influence oral cancer-related competence among dental students. Advanced academic levels and greater clinical exposure have been associated with improved diagnostic confidence and better recognition of oral mucosal abnormalities, suggesting that clinical training plays an important role in strengthening early detection capabilities (11).Relevant studies from Türkiye provide regional educational context. A 2025 multicenter survey of 603 third-, fourth-, and fifth-year dental students from 10 faculties reported variation in oral cancer knowledge, self-perceived preparedness, and responses across both academic grades and faculties (12). Academic-level comparisons from Türkiye have also identified differences in recognition of oral cancer and potentially malignant/precancerous lesions: fifth-year students in Van more often recognized leukoplakia and erythroplakia as lesions with high carcinogenic potential than third-year students (13), and a recent first- versus fifth-year comparison found higher knowledge, screening awareness, and referral-related awareness among senior students (13). Because these studies used different questionnaires, populations, and academic-level definitions, their reported percentages are best used as contextual evidence rather than as directly comparable estimates.In Saudi Arabia, evidence regarding oral cancer knowledge, awareness of OPMDs, and diagnostic confidence among dental students remains limited, particularly in relation to oral lesion management and biopsy-associated practices. Evaluating these aspects is important for identifying educational deficiencies and guiding curriculum development aimed at improving oral cancer screening competencies among future dental practitioners (14, 15).Therefore, the present study aimed to assess oral cancer knowledge, knowledge of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), and diagnostic confidence among Saudi dental students. In addition, the study sought to examine demographic and academic factors associated with meeting the study-defined oral cancer knowledge, OPMD knowledge, and diagnostic confidence thresholds, with particular attention to the discrepancy between theoretical knowledge and clinical preparedness related to oral cancer screening and early detection. The contribution of this study is the integrated assessment of these three domains, including clinically oriented referral and biopsy items, within a common analytical framework across 20 reported institutional-affiliation categories. Questionnaire development, validation, and data collectionData were gathered using a structured self-administered questionnaire distributed electronically through online platforms. full_text: Cancer immunotherapy and adoptive cell therapy have transformed modern oncology, yet durable benefits remain limited by tumor heterogeneity, immune escape mechanisms, biomarker variability, and the dynamic remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment. Current biomarker strategies, including PD-L1 (programmed death-ligand 1) expression, microsatellite instability (MSI), tumor mutational burden (TMB), immune gene signatures, liquid biopsy measurements, and target antigen profiles, provide clinically useful information but are often static and insufficient to capture longitudinal tumor–immune–therapy interactions. Digital twin technology offers a computational paradigm for integrating multi-omics, immune profiling, clinical variables, imaging, and treatment-response data into patient-linked virtual models. Generative artificial intelligence, including generative adversarial networks (GANs), may enrich sparse biomarker-defined state spaces and support the simulation of underrepresented treatment response or toxicity trajectories. This mini review critically compares mechanistic quantitative systems pharmacology, spatial and agent-based modeling, data-driven prediction, and emerging digital twin approaches and proposes a platform-agnostic architecture that can be implemented in MATLAB/Simulink or other computational environments. The adoptive cell therapy scope focuses on chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T), chimeric antigen receptor natural killer cell (CAR-NK), and T-cell receptor-engineered T-cell (TCR-T) therapies, with related principles applicable to tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy. We describe conditional and longitudinal GAN strategies, dynamic tumor–immune state modeling, biomarker integration, validation metrics, governance, and prospective implementation pathways. The proposed framework is conceptual and has not yet been clinically validated; synthetic data are treated as methodological support rather than clinical evidence. Its intended near-term uses are hypothesis generation, virtual-cohort enrichment, trial design, and uncertainty-aware decision support. 4GAN-enhanced patient state enrichmentA major obstacle in biomarker-driven immunotherapy modeling is the scarcity, imbalance, and inconsistent longitudinal depth of high-quality datasets. Cell therapy cohorts are commonly small, disease-specific, and heterogeneous in prior treatment exposure. Rare but clinically important states, including early relapse after CAR-T therapy, severe cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, and acquired checkpoint-inhibitor resistance, are therefore underrepresented (7–9, 45, 46).Candidate generative approaches include conditional GANs for outcome- or treatment-conditioned biomarker profiles, tabular GANs for mixed clinical and molecular variables, longitudinal adversarial models for serial trajectories, Wasserstein formulations with gradient penalties to improve training stability, and privacy-preserving variants for restricted data sharing (16, 17, 47–52). Conditioning variables include tumor type, treatment class, response state, antigen status, immune phenotype, time from infusion, and toxicity grade. Potential outputs include baseline multimodal profiles, serial biomarker trajectories, virtual-cohort parameter distributions, and rare response or toxicity states.Synthetic data should not be interpreted as replacement evidence or used to create an apparent increase in clinical sample size for inferential claims. Evaluation must cover statistical fidelity, downstream utility, biological plausibility, subgroup robustness, temporal coherence, and privacy. Appropriate tests include train-on-synthetic/test-on-real and train-on-real/test-on-synthetic analyses, maintenance of pathway and marker co-expression constraints, outlier review, the calibration of downstream predictions, membership-inference risk, and performance in independent real cohorts. Risks include mode collapse, memorization and privacy leakage, hallucinated biomarker combinations, reinforcement of source-cohort bias, and overconfident predictions under distribution shift. Generated records should be labeled, versioned, auditable, and rejected when augmentation worsens calibration or minority group performance. 8ConclusionGAN-enhanced digital twins are a promising but still conceptual approach to biomarker-guided cancer immunotherapy and adoptive cell therapy. Their value depends on a disciplined separation of synthetic data generation, mechanistic or hybrid modeling, longitudinal patient updates, and independent clinical validation. A platform-agnostic modular architecture can support research on checkpoint blockade, CAR-T, CAR-NK, TCR-T, TIL, combination therapy, and toxicity, but its near-term role is virtual-cohort enrichment, trial design, and uncertainty-aware decision support rather than autonomous treatment prescription. 1IntroductionCancer immunotherapy and adoptive cell therapy have generated durable responses in several malignancies; however, the clinical benefit remains uneven across tumor types and patient populations. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, T-cell receptor-engineered therapy, and natural killer cell-based therapies are influenced by tumor antigenicity, antigen presentation, immune infiltration, effector cell fitness, immune escape, suppressive microenvironmental programs, and treatment-associated toxicity (1–3). This heterogeneity has made biomarker-driven decision-making central to precision immuno-oncology. In this review, adoptive cell therapy refers primarily to CAR-T, CAR-NK, and T-cell receptor-engineered T-cell (TCR-T) therapies; tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy is considered a related platform when the same biomarker and dynamic modeling principles apply.Clinically approved or widely investigated biomarkers, such as PD-L1 expression, microsatellite instability, tumor mutational burden, circulating immune parameters, immune gene-expression signatures, and target antigen expression, provide useful but incomplete information (1). Many biomarkers are measured at a single time point, whereas tumor–immune interactions are dynamic. A baseline biopsy may not show treatment-induced antigen loss, immune editing, effector cell exhaustion, cytokine amplification, stromal remodeling, or acquired resistance. This gap is particularly important for cell therapy because therapeutic efficacy depends not only on tumor target expression but also on the trafficking, expansion, persistence, exhaustion, and survival of engineered immune cells (4–7).Digital twin technology has emerged as a computational strategy to represent a patient or biological system as a continuously updated virtual counterpart. In oncology, digital twins may combine mechanistic modeling, quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP), artificial intelligence, multi-omics, and clinical monitoring to simulate tumor progression and treatment response (8–15). Generative artificial intelligence, including generative adversarial networks (GANs), may further address sparse-data problems by generating synthetic patient state profiles that preserve selected statistical and biological properties of real patient cohorts (16, 17). This mini review critically synthesizes recent evidence and proposes a translational, platform-agnostic architecture for biomarker-guided cancer immunotherapy and adoptive cell therapy. MATLAB/Simulink is retained as an interpretable implementation option rather than as a required platform, and no original computational or clinical validation results are presented.Existing literature spans QSP virtual patients, spatial and agent-based models, multimodal predictive artificial intelligence, and early oncology digital twin concepts, but these strands are often evaluated separately. Recent AI immunotherapy reviews also emphasize therapeutic formulation and combination design rather than longitudinal patient-state updating (18, 19). The specific contribution of this mini review is to distinguish a dynamically updated digital twin from static prediction, define a restricted and auditable role for synthetic data, map clinically relevant biomarker domains to model states, and outline staged validation for checkpoint blockade and engineered cell therapies. 2Biomarker domains requiring dynamic integrationBiomarkers in immuno-oncology can be organized into functional domains. The first domain involves tumor antigenicity. In checkpoint blockade, neoantigen burden, tumor mutational burden, and mismatch repair deficiency may indicate immunogenic potential, although predictive performance varies across tumor types (20–23). In cell therapy, target antigen expression is even more direct. CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) have supported major progress in hematological malignancies, whereas HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2), EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor), mesothelin, CLDN18.2 (claudin 18.2), MUC1 (mucin 1), GD2 (disialoganglioside 2), and viral antigens, such as HPV (human papillomavirus) E6/E7, are being explored in solid tumors (4, 5, 7). Antigen heterogeneity and antigen loss, however, remain major mechanisms of resistance.The second domain involves antigen presentation and interferon signaling. HLA (human leukocyte antigen) expression, B2M (beta-2-microglobulin) integrity, TAP1/TAP2 function, and interferon response programs influence whether tumor antigens can be effectively presented to T cells (24, 25). Defects in these pathways can produce primary or acquired resistance to checkpoint blockade and may influence TCR-engineered therapies. The third domain involves effector immune activity, including CD8A (CD8 alpha), GZMB (granzyme B), PRF1 (perforin 1), NKG7 (natural killer cell granule protein 7), GNLY (granulysin), and IFNG (interferon gamma)-associated cytotoxicity signatures. These markers capture immune attack more directly than tumor-intrinsic variables alone (1, 24).The fourth domain involves checkpoint activation and immune exhaustion. PDCD1 (programmed cell death 1), CD274 (cluster of differentiation 274), CTLA4 (cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4), LAG3 (lymphocyte-activation gene 3), TIGIT (T-cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains), HAVCR2 (hepatitis A virus cellular receptor 2), TOX (thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box), and related exhaustion programs can indicate both an inflamed tumor state and functional impairment of effector lymphocytes (26–28). This dual interpretation is clinically important: Checkpoint expression may identify tumors susceptible to immunotherapy, but deep exhaustion, suppressive cytokines, and poor metabolic conditions may limit durable response. The fifth domain involves the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, tumor-associated macrophages, cancer-associated fibroblasts, TGF-β (transforming growth factor) signaling, hypoxia, adenosine metabolism, and abnormal vasculature may restrict immune infiltration and effector function (3, 24, 29, 30). Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies increasingly show that response or resistance depends not only on the presence of immune cells but also on their spatial organization, functional states, and interactions with malignant and stromal compartments (29–32). These biomarker layers are interdependent and dynamic, which makes them suitable inputs for digital twin modeling rather than isolated static predictors.Additional longitudinal biomarker domains include circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) kinetics, circulating tumor cells (CTCs), T-cell receptor repertoire features, microbiome-associated signals, and metabolic fingerprints. Circulating genomic profiles may capture resistance and subsequent immunotherapy response, while recent multimodal and metabolic studies illustrate how imaging and metabolomics could broaden the observation layer of future digital twins (33–36). These studies are enabling examples rather than evidence that the corresponding data streams are already validated for digital twin-guided immunotherapy.Clinical feasibility requires a tiered input strategy. A minimum layer may include tumor burden, treatment history, routine laboratory measurements, target antigen or HLA status, and selected liquid biopsy variables. Single-cell, spatial, microbiome, and metabolomic assays should remain optional research layers until their incremental value, reproducibility, and turnaround time are proven. Integration also requires time-stamped provenance, assay-specific quality control, unit harmonization, batch correction, explicit alignment to treatment events, and models that account for informative missingness. Platform-specific measurement uncertainty should propagate into the digital twin rather than being removed by preprocessing alone. 3Digital twin modeling in immuno-oncologyA cancer digital twin is a patient-linked computational system that integrates biological data, clinical observations, and treatment inputs to simulate disease evolution and is updated when new measurements become available (10–15 56, 57). This definition differs from related terms. A virtual patient is a parameterized in silico individual sampled from a mechanistic model; a synthetic patient is a generated data record intended to resemble a source distribution; and a predictive model may provide a static or episodic estimate without bidirectional longitudinal updating. Maintaining these distinctions prevents synthetic cohorts or one-time risk models from being mislabeled as digital twins.Current computational approaches can be grouped into mechanistic QSP or ordinary differential equation models, spatial or agent-based models, data-driven multimodal predictors, and hybrid digital twin architectures. QSP models provide interpretable links among pathway biology, dosing, immune cell dynamics, and response, but parameter identifiability and simplified biological assumptions limit personalization (11, 37–40). Spatial and agent-based models capture trafficking, tumor architecture, and local suppression but are computationally intensive and difficult to calibrate with routine patient data (31, 38, 39, 41). Data-driven models can integrate high-dimensional variables and achieve strong discrimination; however, they are often static, vulnerable to dataset shift, and less suitable for counterfactual schedule simulation (21–23, 33–36, 42, 43). Hybrid digital twins seek to combine these strengths through longitudinal calibration, but the majority of oncology implementations remain proof-of-concept, retrospectively validated, or aspirational (10–15, 44).For biomarker-guided immunotherapy, a digital twin should include interacting representations of tumor burden and growth kinetics; target antigen and antigen presentation status; endogenous and engineered effector cell dynamics; suppressive microenvironmental signals; and treatment inputs such as checkpoint blockade, CAR-T or CAR-NK infusion, TCR-T therapy, lymphodepletion, cytokine support, or combination treatment. CAR-T and CAR-NK models require target density, trafficking, expansion, persistence, exhaustion, and cytokine toxicity states. TCR-T models additionally require HLA genotype, epitope presentation, B2M/TAP (transporter associated with antigen processing) integrity, and clonotype fitness. Such models could compare schedules and combinations, but clinically significant outputs must be calibrated to longitudinal observations and reported with uncertainty.The proposed architecture does not assume that GAN augmentation or a MATLAB/Simulink implementation creates a digital twin by itself. GANs are assigned a restricted role in rare-state enrichment and stress testing, whereas the patient-linked mechanistic or hybrid core remains anchored to real longitudinal measurements. This separation is essential to the novelty and safety of the framework. 5Implementation options and a MATLAB/Simulink-compatible architecture5.1Platform rationale and modular architectureMATLAB/Simulink is well suited to state-space modeling, ordinary differential equations, parameter estimation, feedback control, sensitivity analysis, modular visualization, and co-simulation. These features support transparent block-level representation of tumor growth, immune cell dynamics, treatment inputs, and measurement updates. However, the framework is not platform-dependent. Python-based environments provide open-source machine learning, probabilistic programming, workflow automation, and deployment ecosystems; specialized QSP tools support pharmacology-centered model development; and agent-based platforms may better represent spatial cell–cell interactions. MATLAB/Simulink can facilitate rapid prototyping and traceable model-based design, but proprietary licensing, accessibility, version control, and deployment costs may limit adoption. title: Embryonic yield-related serum proteomic analysis at bovine superovulation

source_records.title: Embryonic yield-related serum proteomic analysis at bovine superovulation

full_text: Superovulation is a key technology for accelerating genetic improvement in cattle, but its efficiency is limited by the unpredictable ovarian response among donors. A non-invasive method to predict this response could enhance superovulation outcomes. As serum proteome may mirror ovarian function, this study aimed to identify potential serum protein biomarkers at critical time points to predict embryo yield in donor cows. In this study, blood samples were collected from 33 donor cows undergoing superovulation at two time points: before FSH administration (designated BS) and at estrus detection (designated E). Based on the total number of embryos recovered, the cows were subsequently assigned to high embryonic yield (HEY) and low embryonic yield (LEY) groups. Proteomic sequencing was performed using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). A total of 352 embryos were collected. Proteomic analysis identified 1,620 proteins, corresponding to 11,726 annotated entries. A total of 154 and 102 differentially expressed proteins were identified between HEY and LEY at BS and E, respectively (|log2FC| ≥0.263, P < 0.05, FDR<0.01). Thirteen proteins were shared between the two time points, including consistently upregulated vitamin D-binding protein (GC). The enriched pathways were mainly metabolism-related. Notably, elevated TCN2 and DNMT1 at BS (AUC = 0.96 and 1.00, respectively), and AGRN, RCN3, and WNT7B at E (AUC = 1.00, 0.80, and 0.84, respectively), were associated with the HEY group, suggesting their potential as biomarkers for predicting embryo yield in bovine superovulation. Collectively, this study identified multiple serum protein biomarkers, providing novel molecular insights into the serum protein response to superovulation and laying a foundation for the development of non-invasive prediction strategies. 2Methods2.1Experimental location and cows' managementThis study was conducted at the Livestock Experimental Base of Inner Mongolia University in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, China (40°49′N, 111°41′E; elevation 1 050 m). This region has a mid-temperate, semi-arid continental monsoon climate, characterized by long dry winters, short rainy summers, an annual mean temperature of 7.2 °C, and an annual average precipitation of 392.2 mm. A cohort of 33 sexually mature, healthy Huaxi cows, aged 2–4 years and weighing 580 ± 20 kg, with no history of reproductive disorders and no record of two or more unsuccessful breeding attempts, were used as donors in this study. They were raised in free-stall barns and provided with water and shade ad libitum. full_text_sections.abstract: Superovulation is a key technology for accelerating genetic improvement in cattle, but its efficiency is limited by the unpredictable ovarian response among donors. A non-invasive method to predict this response could enhance superovulation outcomes. As serum proteome may mirror ovarian function, this study aimed to identify potential serum protein biomarkers at critical time points to predict embryo yield in donor cows. In this study, blood samples were collected from 33 donor cows undergoing superovulation at two time points: before FSH administration (designated BS) and at estrus detection (designated E). Based on the total number of embryos recovered, the cows were subsequently assigned to high embryonic yield (HEY) and low embryonic yield (LEY) groups. Proteomic sequencing was performed using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). A total of 352 embryos were collected. Proteomic analysis identified 1,620 proteins, corresponding to 11,726 annotated entries. A total of 154 and 102 differentially expressed proteins were identified between HEY and LEY at BS and E, respectively (|log2FC| ≥0.263, P < 0.05, FDR<0.01). Thirteen proteins were shared between the two time points, including consistently upregulated vitamin D-binding protein (GC). The enriched pathways were mainly metabolism-related. Notably, elevated TCN2 and DNMT1 at BS (AUC = 0.96 and 1.00, respectively), and AGRN, RCN3, and WNT7B at E (AUC = 1.00, 0.80, and 0.84, respectively), were associated with the HEY group, suggesting their potential as biomarkers for predicting embryo yield in bovine superovulation. Collectively, this study identified multiple serum protein biomarkers, providing novel molecular insights into the serum protein response to superovulation and laying a foundation for the development of non-invasive prediction strategies.

full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis study aimed to identify serum protein biomarkers for predicting superovulation efficiency in Huaxi cattle. Serum samples were collected at two critical time points during the superovulation protocol: BS (antral follicle status) and E (mature follicle status). Comparison of the serum proteomic profiles from the same donors at these two time points enables the assessment of dynamic changes in response to superovulation and their association with embryo yield. The proteomic profiling showed that a total of 1,620 proteins were identified from the serum samples of all donor cows, corresponding to 11,726 peptides. PCA revealed a clear clustering separation between the HEY and LEY groups at the BS time point; however, no distinct clustering was observed between the two groups at the E time point. Between HEY and LEY, more DEPs were identified at BS (154) than at E (102), with 80 up-regulated and 74 down-regulated at BS time point, and 58 up-regulated and 44 down-regulated at E time point. Among the DEPs, 7 proteins including GC, were commonly upregulated, while another 6 proteins were consistently downregulated. The DEPs at BS capture the pre-existing molecular differences that may pre-determine the donor's ovarian responsiveness, while those at E capture the molecular events associated with follicular maturation in response to superovulation treatment.While Amino acid metabolism and Carbohydrate metabolism were enriched at both time points, glycan biosynthesis and metabolism showed a notable BS-specific enrichment, indicating that high-yield donors may possess a more active protein glycosylation. This observation exemplifies the systemic divergence between HEY and LEY groups at the metabolic level. Protein glycosylation, specifically O-GlcNAcylation, acts as a nutrient-sensing mechanism regulating granulosa cell proliferation; its disruption impairs cell expansion and follicular growth in cattle (23). Therefore, the observed pathway enrichment in HEY cows likely reflect an enhanced capacity to sense and utilize energy supply, promoting granulosa cell proliferation and ultimately supporting the recruitment of a larger cohort of follicles and higher embryo yield. By comparison, the E time point featured enrichments in lipid metabolism and steroid biosynthesis. These enrichments align with the role of functional fatty acids in enhancing energy supply and providing hormone precursors to support follicular development (24). For example, Oleic acid, the most abundant free fatty acid in bovine follicular fluid, can directly modulate gonadotrophin receptor expression, steroidogenic enzyme activity, and estradiol-17β synthesis in granulosa cells (25). A proposed regulatory network involving the oocyte-secreted factor FGF10 and Oleic acid appears to modulate the estradiol dominance to progesterone dominance steroidogenic switch in the periovulatory follicle (26). Therefore, the lipid-related pathways enrichment in HEY cows may reflect a more efficient utilization of lipid supply to support the LH-induced steroid shift, thereby promoting oocyte maturation and ovulation.Among the consistently upregulated proteins in the HEY group, GC is of particular interest, with elevated expression at both time points and enrichment of the vitamin digestion and absorption pathway and high performance of ROC analysis. The sustained GC upregulation in HEY donors may contribute to a favorable peri-ovulatory environment through two potential mechanisms. First, by modulating free 25(OH)D bioavailability, GC may support AMH signaling, FSH sensitivity, and progesterone synthesis (27). Given the strong correlation between serum and follicular fluid 25(OH)D, and its association with improved pregnancy outcomes (28), this mechanism likely facilitates oocyte maturation and implantation. Second, GC may exert vitamin D-independent effects on tissue remodeling and inflammation (29), processes essential for ovulation and luteogenesis. The context-dependent nature of GC function is further supported by genetic evidence: GC enhancer copy number variation in dairy cattle is associated with reduced fertility despite high GC expression (30), whereas the Gc1f genotype in humans confers favorable pregnancy outcomes independent of 25(OH)D levels (31). As the transporter of vitamin B12, TCN2 upregulation suggests enhanced B12 availability in HEY donors. B12 supports oocyte maturation, embryo implantation, and placental development through its roles in folate cycling, one-carbon metabolism, and DNA synthesis (32). The cross-species relevance of this mechanism is supported by evidences from human follicular fluid studies, where B12 levels correlate with ovarian reserve and pregnancy probability (33), and from goat in vitro maturation (IVM) models, where B12 supplementation improves fertilization and embryo quality through normalization of DNA methylation (34). Consequently, a GWAS in Gir cattle identified TCN2 as a candidate gene associated with oocyte and embryo counts (35). Furthermore, TCN2 harbors functional variants associated with recurrent implantation failure and elevated estradiol levels in humans (36), further supporting its relevance to reproductive function. While these lines of evidence point to a potential role for TCN2 in superovulation, no functional studies have directly linked TCN2 to reproductive performance in cattle or sheep, warranting further investigation.DNMT1 was another significantly upregulated protein in the HEY group at the BS sampling time point, a finding supported by the enrichment of the cysteine and methionine metabolism pathway. This pathway generates S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), which serves as the methyl donor for DNMT1 in DNA methylation. DNA methylation plays a central role in gametogenesis, early embryonic development, and epigenetic reprogramming during fertilization. In young lamb donors, insufficient DNMT1 abundance leads to reduced global DNA methylation levels during gametogenesis and early embryonic development, underlying the compromised developmental competence of oocytes and resultant early embryos (37). Studies in yak have also demonstrated that DNMT1 expression in mature cumulus–oocyte complexes play an important role in optimizing sperm–oocyte interactions and DNA methylation patterns during fertilization (38). Notably, the synchronous elevation of DNMT1 and TCN2 (which provides methyl donors) at the BS time point suggests a pre-established cascade in HEY donors, from enhanced vitamin B12 transport to active one-carbon metabolism, sufficient DNMT1 activity, and consequently improved granulosa cell proliferation and epigenetic remodeling, which may underpin their superior superovulation response. ROC analysis also highlights the potential of DNMT1 and TCN2 as non-invasive biomarkers for predicting superovulation outcomes in cattle.NID2 was highly expressed in the LEY group but significantly downregulated in the HEY group at BS, suggesting that NID2 may serve as a negative selection factor. NID2 is a key component of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and participates in the construction and remodeling of the follicular basement membrane (39). In healthy bovine follicles, NID2 is predominantly localized to the basement membrane, but is aberrantly overexpressed in the granulosa cell layer in atretic follicles (40). full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionOur findings reveal distinct serum proteomic profiles between high- and low-embryo-yield donors, particularly in metabolism-related pathways. GC emerged as a consistent biomarker, with elevated expression at both time points in the HEY group. Moreover, high levels of TCN2 and DNMT1 at BS, and AGRN, RCN3, and WNT7B at E, were indicative of superior embryo yield, while low NID2 at BS and low MUC1 at E were similarly associated with favorable outcomes. ROC analysis supported the discriminative potential of these proteins as candidate biomarkers. In summary, GC along with other candidate proteins demonstrate potential as serum biomarkers for predicting superovulation outcomes, though their utility in larger populations and production settings awaits further validation.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionCattle of superior reproductive performance hold substantial economic value in modern livestock production. However, as monotocous animals, cattle exhibit inherently low reproductive efficiency under natural conditions. The application of superovulation technology enables the recovery of multiple fertilizable mature oocytes from elite donors within a single estrous cycle (1). When combined with artificial insemination and embryo transfer, this approach offers a powerful means for rapid genetic dissemination and accelerated breeding progress.Nevertheless, the ovarian response to superovulation protocols varies considerably among individual donors, leading to unpredictable embryo yields and, in many cases, inefficient use of hormonal preparations and associated costs (2). To improve superovulation efficiency, extensive efforts have been devoted to identifying predictive indicators based on ultrasonographic assessment of ovarian status, genotyping of reproduction-related loci, and analysis of circulating reproductive hormones, vitamins, metabolites, and biochemical parameters (3–11). These studies have generated valuable insights; however, most of the reported associations exhibit poor reproducibility across different breeds. Moreover, the relatively high cost and technical demands of these detection methods have hindered their routine application in breeding programs (12).The advent of high-throughput “omics” technologies has opened new avenues for deciphering the molecular mechanisms underlying reproductive performance and identifying biomarkers that can predict fertility outcomes in individual animals (13). Recently, transcriptomic analyses of bovine antral follicles have mapped ligand-receptor interactions that predict intrafollicular factors for improving oocyte quality (14), and single-cell RNA sequencing has revealed transcriptome dynamics during bovine oocyte growth from the secondary follicle to the mid-antral stage (15). Metabolomics and lipidomics have also become indispensable tools for elucidating the molecular basis of reproductive performance in livestock (16). A systematic review of oocyte competence in cattle identified nucleotide metabolism and extracellular matrix interactions as key pathways influencing oocyte quality (17).Proteomic profiling enables comprehensive comparative analysis of all proteins within a given biological sample, thereby facilitating the identification of molecular markers and regulatory pathways associated with specific physiological or pathological phenomena. In livestock studies, proteomic analyses have been increasingly utilized to elucidate the molecular events underlying critical reproductive processes, such as estrous cycling and gestation. For instance, N. G. Shashikumar et al. (11) identified potential stage-specific markers in the saliva of buffaloes across different estrous stages. Ankan De et al. (5) analyzed serum proteomic changes to reveal biomarkers during early pregnancy in pigs. Similarly, Wang et al. employed proteomic analysis in camels to identify potential indicators of reproductive capacity (18). Integrated proteomic profiling of serum, follicular fluid, and ovarian tissues has been used to identify molecular alterations linked to ovarian dysfunction and early pregnancy dynamics in cattle (19, 20). Despite these advances, the correlation between serum protein composition and superovulation yields in cattle has not yet been reported.To discover serum protein biomarkers associated with superovulation efficiency in cattle, blood samples were collected from Huaxi donor cattle on the day preceding FSH injection and at the time of estrus detection. Based on embryo production, the donors were classified into high-, medium-, and low-yield groups. Comparative serum proteomic analysis was performed between the high- and low-yield groups. This region has a mid-temperate, semi-arid continental monsoon climate, characterized by long dry winters, short rainy summers, an annual mean temperature of 7.2 °C, and an annual average precipitation of 392.2 mm. A cohort of 33 sexually mature, healthy Huaxi cows, aged 2–4 years and weighing 580 ± 20 kg, with no history of reproductive disorders and no record of two or more unsuccessful breeding attempts, were used as donors in this study. They were raised in free-stall barns and provided with water and shade ad libitum. The diet comprised 15.0% alfalfa hay, 50.0% whole-crop corn silage, and 35.0% concentrate supplement (582, Zhengda, China), yielding a forage-to-concentrate ratio of 65:35 (dry matter basis). 2.2Synchronized superovulation and embryo recovery protocolCows were synchronized and superovulated according to the schedule shown in Figure 1 (21). On Day 0 (D0), a controlled internal drug-release (CIDR) device containing 1.38 g progesterone (CIDR 1380, Zoetis, New Zealand) was inserted intravaginally. From D9 to D12, a total of 500 μg FSH (Stimufol®, Reprobiol, Belgium) was administered intramuscularly (i.m.) in eight step-down doses, each 10 % lower than the previous one. 300 μg prostaglandin F2α (010492201, GINTEN, China) was given concurrently with the fifth FSH injection on the morning of D11, and the CIDR was removed at the final FSH injection. Estrus was detected on D13, with the primary criterion being the cow's willingness to stand when mounted. Cows were inseminated twice at 12-h interval. On D20, embryos were recovered by non-surgical uterine flushing under caudal epidural anesthesia with 5 mL of lidocaine hydrochloride (H14024045, CSPC, China).Figure 1Schematic timeline of the superovulation protocol. From D9 to D12, 500 μg of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH; Stimufol®, Belgium) was administered intramuscularly in eight decreasing doses (10% reduction per dose). On the morning of D11 (the fifth FSH injection), 300 μg of prostaglandin F2α (PG; Reprobiol, New Zealand) was given concurrently. The CIDR was withdrawn with the last FSH injection on D12. full_text: The human body harbors highly diverse and complex microbial communities across various regions. Among these, the oral cavity and stomach are directly connected and engage in dynamic microbial interactions. Microorganisms capable of migrating between these two distinct niches are referred to as trans-organ microbes, which constitute a core component of the oral–gastric microbiome axis. In this review, we elucidate the mechanisms underlying microbial translocation along the oral-gastric axis. We further discuss how these cross-organ microbes exert bidirectional influences on health and disease in upper gastrointestinal environments. They contribute to mucosal homeostasis and modulate immune responses, yet under certain conditions, they can also promote pathologies such as gastritis, gastric cancer, and oral disorders. The migration and colonization patterns of microbes across organs also hold potential for developing diagnostic biomarkers, as well as for designing innovative microbiome-based interventions targeting the upper gastrointestinal tract. In summary, this review highlights the oral-gastric microbiome axis as a critical frontier for understanding and manipulating microbiome dynamics in human health and disease. 7DiscussionWith advancements in 16S rRNA gene sequencing technology and the exploration of cross-organ microbial axes such as the brain-gut axis, increasing research has revealed that bacterial translocation between the oral cavity and the stomach may exert profound effects on the digestive tract. This review comprehensively delineates the pivotal role of the oral-gastric microbiome axis in mediating gastrointestinal, with a specific focus on elucidating the mechanisms by which key oral microorganisms—including H. pylori, F. nucleatum, P. gingivalis, S. anginosus, and P. intermedia — translocate, colonize, and promote the pathogenesis of gastric disorders via this axis.We propose that various pathogenic bacteria and their metabolites within the oral-gastric microbial axis, similar to H. pylori, have the potential to serve as non-invasive biomarkers for predicting human diseases. In the future, this approach is expected to evolve into a non-invasive detection method akin to the 13C-urea breath test, enabling convenient screening for gastric diseases. For example, the enrichment of P. intermedia in gastric cancer holds significant clinical prognostic value. In terms of diagnostic application, P. intermedia can serve as a potential biomarker for gastric cancer. Detecting P. intermedia in saliva or gastric mucosa biopsy samples, in combination with other oral bacteria (such as S. anginosus and F. nucleatum), may assist in the early screening and risk stratification of gastric cancer (Sgamato et al., 2024). Nevertheless, the diagnostic specificity of such oral bacterial biomarkers may be substantially compromised by confounding factors that independently alter oral microbiota composition, including periodontal disease severity, oral hygiene practices, dietary habits, smoking, alcohol consumption, and proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use. Specifically, periodontal disease itself can markedly reshape the oral microbiome and shares multiple risk factors with gastric cancer, thereby potentially confounding the genuine association between microbiota and malignancy. PPIs raise gastric pH and facilitate oral bacterial colonization in the stomach, potentially creating spurious associations with gastric cancer in patients who receive PPIs for dyspeptic symptoms prior to diagnosis. Moreover, behavioural factors such as smoking, alcohol consumption, and dietary patterns exert profound influences on oral microbial community structure; if not adequately controlled, they may readily lead to false-positive or false-negative findings (Parsons et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019). To improve the clinical applicability of these biomarkers, we advocate the following strategies: (1) multivariate statistical adjustment for the aforementioned covariates in analytical models; (2) multiplexed detection combining oral microbiota profiling with serological markers (e.g., pepsinogen I/II ratio); and (3) integration of multi-omics data (e.g., metagenomics, metabolomics, and host immune parameters) to enhance diagnostic specificity and positive predictive value. Through such systematic adjustments and integrations, the reliability of oral-derived biomarkers in gastric cancer screening can be more robustly assessed in future clinical translation.On the other hand, eradicating pathogenic bacteria in the oral-gastric axis may serve as a novel therapeutic target for treating upper gastrointestinal diseases. Furthermore, the translocation of microorganisms in the oral-gastric microbial axis may also be the key to breaking through traditional probiotic therapy. Certain bacteria, such as Streptococcus sanguinis and S. mitis may become novel probiotics by modulating the oral-gastric microecological axis. Therefore, research on the oral-gastric microbiome axis holds significant prospects for clinical application (Figure 3).Figure 3Clinical implications of the oral–gastric microbial axis: a hypothetical framework for diagnosis, targeted therapy, and microbiome restoration. (1) early diagnosis and risk prediction using bacterial biomarkers; (2) targeted therapy by eradicating pathogenic bacteria via elimination of colonization, inhibition of translocation, and blockade of pathogenesis; and (3) microbiome restoration and prevention strategies, including competitive colonization, microenvironment modulation, biofilm regulation, and use of acid-resistant probiotics.Circular diagram illustrating the oral-gastric microbial axis, divided into three colored sections: light blue for predictive roles of bacteria, medium blue for therapeutic roles in eradicating pathogens, and dark blue for therapeutic probiotic roles. Each outer segment details a specific function, with associated bacterial species and concise labels such as risk stratification, competitive colonization, and gastric cancer enrichment biomarker. The diagram includes illustrative icons of bacteria and a color legend for the three thematic categories.Nevertheless, current research faces several limitations and challenges. Firstly, investigations into the oral-gastric microbiome axis predominantly rely on cross-sectional or retrospective analyses, lacking large-scale prospective cohort studies to establish causal relationships between specific microorganisms and gastric disease. Secondly, although animal models have confirmed that individual oral bacterial species can accelerate gastric lesion progression, the complexity of the human gastric microbiome surpasses that of experimental models, necessitating further exploration of synergistic or antagonistic interactions among multiple oral bacteria.In the future, novel technology and standardized metrics are needed to identify potential pathogenetic microbes and the core microbiota, location, interaction, effect, richness and colonization. In addition, current research on the oral-gastric biological axis is mostly confined to bacteria. However, as indispensable components of this axis, the dynamic changes of non-bacterial microorganisms such as fungi and viruses are equally crucial and urgently need in-depth exploration. It is essential to comprehensively incorporate the oral-gastric microbiome into the human microbiome research initiative and elucidate the intricate ecological interactions, structural relationships, physiological connections, and metabolic cross-species dynamics within it. 1IntroductionA diverse microbial community, made up of trillions of microorganisms, colonize the human body and its different habitats. These microbial communities have profound impacts on the host by activating the immune system, defending against pathogens, and can serve as triggers and drivers of chronic disease processes (Gilbert et al., 2018). The oral cavity serves as the entry point of the human digestive tract and represents a major reservoir of microbiota, which plays a significant role in upper gastrointestinal health and disease (Wade, 2013; Kunath et al., 2024). The interaction between oral microorganisms and gastric microorganisms and their pathogenic mechanisms are becoming a research hotspot. Oral pathogenic bacteria can transfer to the stomach through swallowing or co-aggregation, and damage the gastric mucosal barrier, promoting the occurrence of gastritis, gastric ulcers and gastric cancer (Chen et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2025). Conversely, gastric microorganisms can also influence oral health. For instance, Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) can colonize dental plaque and cavities, forming a symbiotic biofilm with Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) that exacerbates dental caries and periodontal disease (Zhang et al., 2018). In patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease, stomach acid entering the oral cavity can alter salivary pH. This change inhibits periodontal pathogens such as Porphyromonas while promoting the growth of acid-tolerant bacteria like Streptococcus, ultimately disrupting the oral microecosystem equilibrium (Kawar et al., 2021). The bidirectional exchange of microorganisms between the oral cavity and the stomach can reshape the microbial ecosystems of these two parts, forming oral–gastric microbiome axis (Figure 1).Figure 1The oral–gastric microbiome axis: bidirectional microbial exchange and translocation mechanisms. The oral microbiota comprises diverse bacterial and fungal species. These microorganisms can translocate to the stomach via multiple routes: direct swallowing, biofilm/coaggregation pathways, hematogenous dissemination, and virulence factor-mediated active invasion (including adhesin-receptor binding and secretion of proteases that degrade tight junctions). Key oral and gastric microbial taxa involved in this axis are listed in the figure, with arrows indicating their potential routes of transfer.Diagram illustrating the diversity of oral and gastric microbiota, pathways of their migration from the mouth to the stomach, including direct swallowing, biofilm-mediated transport, hematogenous dissemination, and active invasion, with implicated bacterial species, visual pathways, and cellular interactions on the gastric epithelium. 2Oral microbiota: composition and its role in oral health and disease2.1Composition of the oral microbiotaThe oral microbiome is the second-largest microbial ecosystem in the human body after the gut. More than 700 bacterial species have been identified, spanning nine major phyla (Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Fusobacteria, Spirochaetes, etc.), together with fungi (mainly Candida), archaea (methanogens) and a rich virome of bacteriophages (Dewhirst et al., 2010; Wade, 2013). The community can be grouped as follows: (1) Beneficial symbionts:Streptococcus salivarius has been shown to reduce the incidence of dental black stains, plaque, and tooth decay in children. It also decreases the occurrence of pharyngeal and recurrent streptococcal diseases (Al-Akel et al., 2024). Veillonella spp. are obligate anaerobes that convert Streptococcal lactate into the weaker acid propionate, buffering enamel demineralization and stabilizing dental-plaque homeostasis (Mashima and Nakazawa, 2015). Rothia and Corynebacterium colonize mucosal surfaces early, form a reticular matrix and create microoxic-to-anaerobic gradients that facilitate biofilm maturation and later colonization by strict anaerobes (Welch et al., 2016). (2) Opportunistic pathogenic bacteria (those enriched during dysbiosis): S. mutans and Lactobacillus have strong acid-producing and acid-tolerant properties, which drive enamel demineralization and are primary pathogens for dental caries (Takahashi and Nyvad, 2011). Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis) produces gingipain proteases and lipopolysaccharides that impair neutrophil phagocytosis and enhance bacterial survival within these cells (Ruan et al., 2023). Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum), as a bridge between early Gram-positive colonizing bacteria and late anaerobic pathogenic bacteria, promotes interspecies aggregation through co-aggregation, assisting strict anaerobic bacteria in surviving in oxygen-rich environments, thereby promoting the maturation of biofilms and dysbiosis (Bradshaw et al., 1998).2.2The impact of oral microbiota on oral diseases and its mechanismsThe oral microbiota is implicated in a range of oral conditions, including periodontal disease, dental caries and oral cancer (Baker et al., 2024). Periodontal disease, a chronic infectious disease affecting the supporting tissues of the teeth (including the gingiva, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone), arises from a disruption of host–microbial homeostasis within the periodontal pocket (Hajishengallis and Chavakis, 2021). Under conditions of oral health, the inflammatory response and the periodontal microbiome maintain a dynamic bidirectional equilibrium. In periodontitis, this balance is disrupted: Gram-negative bacteria proliferate extensively and ultimately displace the microbial communities associated with periodontal health (Holt and Ebersole, 2005). Among the enriched species are the classically recognized red-complex triad—comprising Treponema denticola, P. gingivalis and Tannerella forsythia —as well as other organisms such as Filifactor alocis, Peptoanaerobacter stomatis, and Saccharibacteria. Together, these microbial groups constitute the principal members of the periodontitis-associated microbial community (Curtis et al., 2020). Furthermore, proliferation of acidogenic and acid-tolerant species—such as S. mutans, lactobacilli, Veillonella, Candida albicans, Epstein-Barr virus, and Prevotella species also drive biofilm formation and ecological changes (Benseddik et al., 2025).Dental caries is an infectious, biofilm-mediated disease of the calcified tooth tissues, driven by acid production from bacterial fermentation of dietary carbohydrates. The disease process is characterized by phasic demineralization and remineralization; however, once cavitation occurs, the resultant structural damage is irreversible (Kutsch, 2014; Dayo et al., 2021). When the oral microecology is imbalanced, the cariogenic bacteria will dominate. The most prevalent cariogenic species include oral streptococci, notably S. mutans, and Lactobacilli (Szkaradkiewicz-Karpinska and Szkaradkiewicz, 2021). S. mutans is considered a primary pathogen in dental caries due to its ability to synthesize extracellular polysaccharides via glucosyltransferases, form biofilm matrices, and promote tooth demineralization through acid production coupled with inherent acid resistance (Ucuncu et al., 2025). Similarly, Lactobacillus acidophilus (L. acidophilus) exhibits strong acidogenic and acid-tolerant properties. It also produces extracellular polysaccharides that facilitate bacterial adhesion to enamel and dental plaque formation, ultimately contributing to tooth decay (Aas et al., 2008). Beyond these, other bacteria are associated with specific caries phenotypes. For example, Actinomyces naeslundii is closely linked to the development of root caries (Bergeron et al., 2000); Scardovia wiggsiae has been found to accumulate significantly in cases of severe early childhood caries (Kressirer et al., 2017).Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), the most prevalent head and neck cancer, constitutes about 90% of oral malignancies and impairs appearance, speech, swallowing, and taste perception (Tan et al., 2023). The significant role of tumor microenvironment in the initiation, development, and progression of OSCC has been widely recognized. A diverse range of oral microorganisms—including bacteria such as P. gingivalis and F. nucleatum, viruses like HPV and EBV, and fungi such as Candida albicans —have been linked to the development and progression of OSCC (Pignatelli et al., 2023; Starska-Kowarska, 2025). In addition, Parvimonas micra, which is enriched in OSCC tissues, interacts with the tumor cell receptor CKAP4 via its surface protein TmpC, activating HIF-1α-driven glycolysis and autophagy to facilitate epithelial–mesenchymal transition and lymph node metastasis (Qi et al., 2025). Moreover, emerging evidence has associated Fusobacterium periodonticum, Haemophilus influenzae, and Filifactor alocis with the onset and progression of OSCC (Stasiewicz and Karpiński, 2022).Furthermore, oral lichen planus and Behçet’s syndrome have also been confirmed to be associated with oral microbiota. H. pylori infection is closely related to erosive oral lichen planus, and the level of volatile sulfur compounds in patients with oral lichen planus is significantly higher than that in healthy individuals (Guan et al., 2024). In patients with Behçet’s syndrome, the H. pylori infection rate is higher, and symptoms such as oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and skin lesions can be improved after eradication therapy (Avci et al., 1999). 2.1Composition of the oral microbiotaThe oral microbiome is the second-largest microbial ecosystem in the human body after the gut.
