This review comprehensively delineates the pivotal role of the oral-gastric microbiome axis in mediating gastrointestinal, with a specific focus on elucidating the mechanisms by which key oral microorganisms—including H. pylori, F. nucleatum, P. gingivalis, S. anginosus, and P. intermedia — translocate, colonize, and promote the pathogenesis of gastric disorders via this axis.We propose that various pathogenic bacteria and their metabolites within the oral-gastric microbial axis, similar to H. pylori, have the potential to serve as non-invasive biomarkers for predicting human diseases. In the future, this approach is expected to evolve into a non-invasive detection method akin to the 13C-urea breath test, enabling convenient screening for gastric diseases. For example, the enrichment of P. intermedia in gastric cancer holds significant clinical prognostic value. In terms of diagnostic application, P. intermedia can serve as a potential biomarker for gastric cancer. Detecting P. intermedia in saliva or gastric mucosa biopsy samples, in combination with other oral bacteria (such as S. anginosus and F. nucleatum), may assist in the early screening and risk stratification of gastric cancer (Sgamato et al., 2024). Nevertheless, the diagnostic specificity of such oral bacterial biomarkers may be substantially compromised by confounding factors that independently alter oral microbiota composition, including periodontal disease severity, oral hygiene practices, dietary habits, smoking, alcohol consumption, and proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use. Specifically, periodontal disease itself can markedly reshape the oral microbiome and shares multiple risk factors with gastric cancer, thereby potentially confounding the genuine association between microbiota and malignancy. PPIs raise gastric pH and facilitate oral bacterial colonization in the stomach, potentially creating spurious associations with gastric cancer in patients who receive PPIs for dyspeptic symptoms prior to diagnosis. Moreover, behavioural factors such as smoking, alcohol consumption, and dietary patterns exert profound influences on oral microbial community structure; if not adequately controlled, they may readily lead to false-positive or false-negative findings (Parsons et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019). To improve the clinical applicability of these biomarkers, we advocate the following strategies: (1) multivariate statistical adjustment for the aforementioned covariates in analytical models; (2) multiplexed detection combining oral microbiota profiling with serological markers (e.g., pepsinogen I/II ratio); and (3) integration of multi-omics data (e.g., metagenomics, metabolomics, and host immune parameters) to enhance diagnostic specificity and positive predictive value. Through such systematic adjustments and integrations, the reliability of oral-derived biomarkers in gastric cancer screening can be more robustly assessed in future clinical translation.On the other hand, eradicating pathogenic bacteria in the oral-gastric axis may serve as a novel therapeutic target for treating upper gastrointestinal diseases. Furthermore, the translocation of microorganisms in the oral-gastric microbial axis may also be the key to breaking through traditional probiotic therapy. Certain bacteria, such as Streptococcus sanguinis and S. mitis may become novel probiotics by modulating the oral-gastric microecological axis. Therefore, research on the oral-gastric microbiome axis holds significant prospects for clinical application (Figure 3).Figure 3Clinical implications of the oral–gastric microbial axis: a hypothetical framework for diagnosis, targeted therapy, and microbiome restoration. (1) early diagnosis and risk prediction using bacterial biomarkers; (2) targeted therapy by eradicating pathogenic bacteria via elimination of colonization, inhibition of translocation, and blockade of pathogenesis; and (3) microbiome restoration and prevention strategies, including competitive colonization, microenvironment modulation, biofilm regulation, and use of acid-resistant probiotics.Circular diagram illustrating the oral-gastric microbial axis, divided into three colored sections: light blue for predictive roles of bacteria, medium blue for therapeutic roles in eradicating pathogens, and dark blue for therapeutic probiotic roles. Each outer segment details a specific function, with associated bacterial species and concise labels such as risk stratification, competitive colonization, and gastric cancer enrichment biomarker. The diagram includes illustrative icons of bacteria and a color legend for the three thematic categories.Nevertheless, current research faces several limitations and challenges. Firstly, investigations into the oral-gastric microbiome axis predominantly rely on cross-sectional or retrospective analyses, lacking large-scale prospective cohort studies to establish causal relationships between specific microorganisms and gastric disease. Secondly, although animal models have confirmed that individual oral bacterial species can accelerate gastric lesion progression, the complexity of the human gastric microbiome surpasses that of experimental models, necessitating further exploration of synergistic or antagonistic interactions among multiple oral bacteria.In the future, novel technology and standardized metrics are needed to identify potential pathogenetic microbes and the core microbiota, location, interaction, effect, richness and colonization. In addition, current research on the oral-gastric biological axis is mostly confined to bacteria. However, as indispensable components of this axis, the dynamic changes of non-bacterial microorganisms such as fungi and viruses are equally crucial and urgently need in-depth exploration. It is essential to comprehensively incorporate the oral-gastric microbiome into the human microbiome research initiative and elucidate the intricate ecological interactions, structural relationships, physiological connections, and metabolic cross-species dynamics within it.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionA diverse microbial community, made up of trillions of microorganisms, colonize the human body and its different habitats. These microbial communities have profound impacts on the host by activating the immune system, defending against pathogens, and can serve as triggers and drivers of chronic disease processes (Gilbert et al., 2018). The oral cavity serves as the entry point of the human digestive tract and represents a major reservoir of microbiota, which plays a significant role in upper gastrointestinal health and disease (Wade, 2013; Kunath et al., 2024). The interaction between oral microorganisms and gastric microorganisms and their pathogenic mechanisms are becoming a research hotspot. Oral pathogenic bacteria can transfer to the stomach through swallowing or co-aggregation, and damage the gastric mucosal barrier, promoting the occurrence of gastritis, gastric ulcers and gastric cancer (Chen et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2025). Conversely, gastric microorganisms can also influence oral health. For instance, Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) can colonize dental plaque and cavities, forming a symbiotic biofilm with Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) that exacerbates dental caries and periodontal disease (Zhang et al., 2018). In patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease, stomach acid entering the oral cavity can alter salivary pH. This change inhibits periodontal pathogens such as Porphyromonas while promoting the growth of acid-tolerant bacteria like Streptococcus, ultimately disrupting the oral microecosystem equilibrium (Kawar et al., 2021). The bidirectional exchange of microorganisms between the oral cavity and the stomach can reshape the microbial ecosystems of these two parts, forming oral–gastric microbiome axis (Figure 1).Figure 1The oral–gastric microbiome axis: bidirectional microbial exchange and translocation mechanisms. The oral microbiota comprises diverse bacterial and fungal species. These microorganisms can translocate to the stomach via multiple routes: direct swallowing, biofilm/coaggregation pathways, hematogenous dissemination, and virulence factor-mediated active invasion (including adhesin-receptor binding and secretion of proteases that degrade tight junctions). Key oral and gastric microbial taxa involved in this axis are listed in the figure, with arrows indicating their potential routes of transfer.Diagram illustrating the diversity of oral and gastric microbiota, pathways of their migration from the mouth to the stomach, including direct swallowing, biofilm-mediated transport, hematogenous dissemination, and active invasion, with implicated bacterial species, visual pathways, and cellular interactions on the gastric epithelium. 2Oral microbiota: composition and its role in oral health and disease2.1Composition of the oral microbiotaThe oral microbiome is the second-largest microbial ecosystem in the human body after the gut. More than 700 bacterial species have been identified, spanning nine major phyla (Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Fusobacteria, Spirochaetes, etc.), together with fungi (mainly Candida), archaea (methanogens) and a rich virome of bacteriophages (Dewhirst et al., 2010; Wade, 2013). The community can be grouped as follows: (1) Beneficial symbionts:Streptococcus salivarius has been shown to reduce the incidence of dental black stains, plaque, and tooth decay in children. It also decreases the occurrence of pharyngeal and recurrent streptococcal diseases (Al-Akel et al., 2024). Veillonella spp. are obligate anaerobes that convert Streptococcal lactate into the weaker acid propionate, buffering enamel demineralization and stabilizing dental-plaque homeostasis (Mashima and Nakazawa, 2015). Rothia and Corynebacterium colonize mucosal surfaces early, form a reticular matrix and create microoxic-to-anaerobic gradients that facilitate biofilm maturation and later colonization by strict anaerobes (Welch et al., 2016). (2) Opportunistic pathogenic bacteria (those enriched during dysbiosis): S. mutans and Lactobacillus have strong acid-producing and acid-tolerant properties, which drive enamel demineralization and are primary pathogens for dental caries (Takahashi and Nyvad, 2011). Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis) produces gingipain proteases and lipopolysaccharides that impair neutrophil phagocytosis and enhance bacterial survival within these cells (Ruan et al., 2023). Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum), as a bridge between early Gram-positive colonizing bacteria and late anaerobic pathogenic bacteria, promotes interspecies aggregation through co-aggregation, assisting strict anaerobic bacteria in surviving in oxygen-rich environments, thereby promoting the maturation of biofilms and dysbiosis (Bradshaw et al., 1998).2.2The impact of oral microbiota on oral diseases and its mechanismsThe oral microbiota is implicated in a range of oral conditions, including periodontal disease, dental caries and oral cancer (Baker et al., 2024). Periodontal disease, a chronic infectious disease affecting the supporting tissues of the teeth (including the gingiva, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone), arises from a disruption of host–microbial homeostasis within the periodontal pocket (Hajishengallis and Chavakis, 2021). Under conditions of oral health, the inflammatory response and the periodontal microbiome maintain a dynamic bidirectional equilibrium. In periodontitis, this balance is disrupted: Gram-negative bacteria proliferate extensively and ultimately displace the microbial communities associated with periodontal health (Holt and Ebersole, 2005). Among the enriched species are the classically recognized red-complex triad—comprising Treponema denticola, P. gingivalis and Tannerella forsythia —as well as other organisms such as Filifactor alocis, Peptoanaerobacter stomatis, and Saccharibacteria. Together, these microbial groups constitute the principal members of the periodontitis-associated microbial community (Curtis et al., 2020). Furthermore, proliferation of acidogenic and acid-tolerant species—such as S. mutans, lactobacilli, Veillonella, Candida albicans, Epstein-Barr virus, and Prevotella species also drive biofilm formation and ecological changes (Benseddik et al., 2025).Dental caries is an infectious, biofilm-mediated disease of the calcified tooth tissues, driven by acid production from bacterial fermentation of dietary carbohydrates. The disease process is characterized by phasic demineralization and remineralization; however, once cavitation occurs, the resultant structural damage is irreversible (Kutsch, 2014; Dayo et al., 2021). When the oral microecology is imbalanced, the cariogenic bacteria will dominate. The most prevalent cariogenic species include oral streptococci, notably S. mutans, and Lactobacilli (Szkaradkiewicz-Karpinska and Szkaradkiewicz, 2021). S. mutans is considered a primary pathogen in dental caries due to its ability to synthesize extracellular polysaccharides via glucosyltransferases, form biofilm matrices, and promote tooth demineralization through acid production coupled with inherent acid resistance (Ucuncu et al., 2025). Similarly, Lactobacillus acidophilus (L. acidophilus) exhibits strong acidogenic and acid-tolerant properties. It also produces extracellular polysaccharides that facilitate bacterial adhesion to enamel and dental plaque formation, ultimately contributing to tooth decay (Aas et al., 2008). Beyond these, other bacteria are associated with specific caries phenotypes. full_text: AbstractThe DEAD-box (DDX) protein family, constituting a critical subgroup of the Superfamily 2 (SF2) helicase family, plays extensive roles in nucleic acid metabolism, gene expression regulation and innate immune signaling, and exerts a key regulatory role during viral infection. During viral infection, DDX proteins function as both RNA helicases and host restriction factors, exerting antiviral effects by recognizing viral nucleic acids, regulating signaling pathways and maintaining the host immune response. Conversely, through complex and diverse mechanisms, viruses can hijack or antagonize DDX proteins to facilitate their replication, transcription, translation and immune evasion. Focusing on the DDX protein family, this review systematically elucidates their molecular mechanisms of action across the life cycles of various viruses. Specifically, it examines the regulation of viral nucleic acid metabolism by DDX proteins, their influence on innate immune signaling pathways, and the molecular strategies employed by viruses to antagonize DDX proteins, while synthesizing the functional similarities and differences among members of the DDX protein family across distinct viral infections. This review aims to establish a theoretical framework for the in-depth analysis of virus–host interactions and the discovery of novel antiviral targets.Keywords: DDX proteins, DNA viruses, innate immunity, RNA viruses, viral infection 5.Summary and outlookAs key members of the SF2 helicase family, DDX proteins play a central role in fundamental biological processes such as DNA replication, transcription, and translation. When viruses infect host cells, they often hijack various host factors, including DDX proteins, to facilitate their own replication, induce cellular damage, and evade the host’s innate immune defenses. The core of this process lies in exploiting the host’s RNA metabolism machinery to support viral proliferation and secure a replicative advantage during infection. A systematic examination of the interactions between diverse virus families and DDX proteins—whether through viral hijacking or DDX-mediated mechanisms—reveals that DDX proteins are not simply static antiviral “guardians” or passive “enablers” of viral replication. Instead, they function as dynamic regulators throughout viral infection. DDX proteins can influence viral nucleic acid structure, contribute to the assembly of viral complexes, act as a translation co-factor, and assist in immune evasion; they can also serve as a regulator or initiator of the innate immune response, activating relevant cellular signaling pathways and the interferon response (Figure 2; Table 3). These complex interactions and mutual constraints position DDX proteins as a “double-edged sword” in the regulation of viral infection: they can both promote viral infection and effectively suppress viral replication. Moreover, due to their inherent enzymatic activity and RNA regulatory capabilities, DDX proteins not only serve as a crucial tool for the host in orchestrating nucleic acid metabolism but also become a prime target for viral exploitation.Figure 2The viral replication process and the sites of interaction with the relevant DDX proteins. (A). The process of DNA virus replication and the sites of involvement of the relevant DDX proteins. (B). The process of RNA virus replication and the sites of involvement of the relevant DDX proteins. [(a) Receptor-mediated endocytosis. (b) Receptor-mediated membrane fusion. (c) Membrane fusion. (d) Budding. (e) Cell lysis. Orange sections: DDX proteins that can be utilized by viruses. this process drives IFN-β expression, which in turn upregulates ISGs such as Cig5 and IFIT1.Exert an antiviral effect(Chen et al., 2024)DDX11RIG-I-MAVSUpon specific binding to nucleic acids by RIG-I, the binding affinities of RIG-I for both double-stranded RNA and MAVS are consequently enhanced, thereby regulating RIG-I-MAVS-mediated interferon signaling.Activates potent interferon signaling and antiviral immunity(Zhang et al., 2024a)DDX4USP7-SOCS1By binding to the deubiquitinating enzyme ubiquitin-specific protease 7 (USP7), DDX4 disrupts the interaction between USP7 and suppressor of cytokine signaling 1 (SOCS1), leading to the degradation of SOCS1 and thereby enhancing the antiviral function of IFN-I.Boosting antiviral immunity(Miao et al., 2024)DDX54ALKBH5The virus modulates the cellular interferon-mediated antiviral response through the activation of the DDX54/m6A/ALKBH5 axis, thereby regulating m6A modifications on specific transcripts.Negative regulation of the antiviral action of interferon(Sun et al., 2025)DDX56IRF3, IFN-βBy directly targeting the MDA5-mediated signaling triggered by the virus, DDX56 activates KPNA3 and KPNA4 in the signaling cascade, thereby blocking the phosphorylation of IRF3 and its nuclear translocation, thus inhibiting IFN-β production.Promotes viral replication(Xu et al., 2022)Therefore, a comprehensive analysis of the interaction mechanisms between DDX proteins and viruses could provide valuable new insights into the prevention, treatment, and control of viral infections, particularly regarding refractory viruses as well as RNA viruses that exhibit high mutation rates. Although the mechanisms underlying the interactions between certain DDX proteins and viruses have already been clarified, this protein family consists of a large number of members, and many regulatory patterns and viral exploitation strategies remain uncharacterized. Moreover, most current findings are based exclusively on DDX protein-overexpressing or knockout cell lines, and these conclusions have not been validated in animal models or in vivo settings; whether unique interaction pathways exist between DDX proteins and viruses is still an open question. Additionally, it remains unclear whether functional interactions occur among different members of the DDX protein family, or whether other DDX proteins can compensate when a particular DDX protein is subverted by viral infection.Future research should aim to integrate high-throughput omics techniques, such as proteomics and transcriptomics, to systematically identify key DDX proteins associated with different viruses at various stages of their replication cycle, with a particular focus on viruses characterized by high infectivity, broad transmissibility, rapid mutation rates, and control challenges. Concurrently, employing advanced techniques such as single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) and cryo-electron microscopy will allow for a detailed elucidation of the binding dynamics between DDX proteins and viral nucleic acids, the regulatory principles governing ATPase activity, and the molecular basis by which these proteins influence viral proliferation—for instance, through remodeling the viral replication complex (RTC) or modulating host innate immune pathways. This approach will address existing gaps in our understanding of the multi-level interactions among “DDX proteins–viral nucleic acids–host factors”. With the rapid advancement of multi-omics technologies, it is now feasible to construct an “DDX protein–virus–host” interaction network model by integrating multi-dimensional data. Such integration would reveal the regulatory patterns of DDX proteins during viral infection at the systems level, while also exploring potential cooperative relationships among members of the DDX protein family.In summary, the role of DDX proteins as both regulators of host antiviral defenses and tools utilized by viruses extends beyond mere opposing functions, serving instead as a critical interface of interaction between the host and the virus. As research progresses, our understanding of the interactions and mechanisms between DDX proteins and viruses will become more systematic and in-depth, thereby establishing a robust theoretical framework for developing new, more efficient, and safer antiviral strategies based on these mechanisms. 1.IntroductionThe DEAD-box (DDX) protein family comprises a large and diverse group of highly conserved RNA helicases. The family derives its name from the conserved aspartic acid–glutamic acid–alanine–aspartic acid (Asp-Glu-Ala-Asp, DEAD) sequence within the Walker B motif of its core domain. This core domain comprises two RecA modules, each possessing ATP-binding and RNA-binding activities, and contains nine highly conserved sequence motifs. It is flanked by the N-terminal and C-terminal domains, which exhibit greater sequence diversity (Hirth et al., 2024; Tapescu and Cherry, 2024) and mediate key biological functions (Tanner et al., 2003; Song et al., 2023) (Figure 1). As central regulatory factors in RNA metabolism, DDX proteins are involved in several critical processes, including transcription, translation initiation, and messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) transport. Some DDX proteins can also interact with protein kinases; for example, by regulating the catalytic activity of microtubule affinity-regulating kinase 1 (MARK1), they participate in downstream signaling pathways (Chao et al., 2006; Soto-Rifo et al., 2012; Xing et al., 2019; Han et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023; Hirth et al., 2024).Figure 1Core domain of the DDX protein.Diagram of a protein with N-terminus and C-terminus labeled, showing RecA-like domains as colored boxes marked Q, I, Ia, Ib, II, III, IV, V, VI. A legend describes yellow boxes as regulating ATP binding and hydrolysis, blue boxes as coordinating ATP hydrolysis and RNA unwinding, green boxes as facilitating RNA binding, and a yellow “II” box as the DEAD (Walker B motif).During pathogen infection, DDX proteins act as host factors, participating in the intricate interactions between the host and the pathogen. Given this critical role, elucidating the interaction mechanisms between DDX proteins and viral pathogens is essential for understanding viral pathogenesis. These mechanistic insights represent a promising avenue for developing novel therapeutic strategies against viral pathogens. As strictly intracellular parasites, viruses utilize the host cell’s intrinsic molecules to carry out their life cycle and evade the host’s immune response. In this context, DDX proteins utilize their conserved catalytic cores to recognize RNA structural features in a sequence-independent manner (Tapescu et al., 2023; Tapescu and Cherry, 2024), thereby contributing to intracellular viral RNA unwinding, replication, transcription, translation, and assembly of viral particles (Linder and Jankowsky, 2011; Paine et al., 2019). Additionally, they regulate the host’s innate immune response by modulating relevant signaling pathways and protein expression (Ma et al., 2025a; Mao et al., 2024; Szappanos et al., 2018; Sandhu and Damania, 2025; Wu et al., 2026), thereby controlling viral infection. In the innate immune response, certain DDX proteins act as pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) to recognize viral nucleic acids and subsequently activate relevant signaling pathways (Miyashita et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011b, 2011a; Parthun et al., 2025). For example, DDX50 activates the Interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) signaling pathway upon stimulation by viral RNA or during infection with RNA and DNA viruses (Pallett et al., 2022). Furthermore, the DDX1-DDX21-DHX36 complex recognizes double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and utilizes the TIR domain-containing adaptor-inducing interferon-β (TRIF) pathway to activate the Type I Interferons (IFN-I) response (Zhang et al., 2011a), among other mechanisms. Moreover, in immune signaling cascades, DDX proteins not only act as sensors but also function as scaffold molecules to exert regulatory effects. For example, DDX3X, acting as a scaffold protein, directly facilitates the phosphorylation of IRF3 by IκB kinase-ε (IKKε), thereby contributing to the activation and regulation of the IRF3 pathway (Gu et al., 2013). Whether acting as PRRs or scaffold proteins, DDX proteins play a crucial role in regulating the host’s innate immune response.DDX proteins are not only key players in the innate immune system but also serve as vital tools for viruses to facilitate replication, reactivation, and immune evasion. Viruses can hijack DDX proteins to enhance viral replication or evade host immune surveillance, thereby enabling persistent infection or latent reactivation (Barra et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). For example, the Human papillomavirus regulatory protein E2 (HPV E2) hijacks DDX11 (ChlR1) to facilitate the binding of its own mitotic chromatin (Harris et al., 2016); the hepatitis C virus (HCV) hijacks DDX6 and the Processing body (P-body) to create conducive conditions for its own replication (Ariumi et al., 2011). It is precisely this dual role of DDX proteins in viral regulation that makes them a key battleground in the interplay between virus and host.DDX proteins and viruses share a complex, multifaceted relationship characterized by mutual influence and restraint, which is of great significance for the onset, progression, treatment and prevention of infectious diseases. Therefore, an in-depth investigation of the interactions between DDX proteins and viruses and their molecular mechanisms paves the way for the prevention and treatment of viral infectious diseases. This review will be organized primarily according to the type of viral nucleic acid, covering a range of viruses including hepatitis viruses, arboviruses, herpesviruses and oncoviruses. It will systematically summarize the mechanisms of their interactions with DDX proteins and the associated immune signaling pathways, and elucidate specific virus-DDX protein interactions, thereby offering novel theoretical insights into the prevention and control of viral infections. 2.DNA virus infection and DDX protein functionsAfter a host cell becomes infected, DNA viruses primarily rely on DNA polymerases to catalyze deoxyribonucleotide polymerization reactions. They also utilize enzymes encoded by either the host or the virus itself to carry out essential processes such as genome unwinding, primer synthesis, and damage repair (Gassmann et al., 1988; Tian et al., 2009; Lawler et al., 2024), with members of the DDX protein family playing a notable role in these activities. Viruses exploit DDX proteins to facilitate their own replication or to evade the host immune response. At the same time, upon detecting viral DNA, the host can activate classical signaling pathways like cyclic GMP-AMP synthase–stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING), Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9), and Retinoic acid-inducible gene I–mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (RIG-I-MAVS) to initiate an innate immune response (Ablasser et al., 2009; Fiola et al., 2010; Civril et al., 2013; Dansako et al., 2016; Hristova et al., 2024). In this context, DDX proteins act as pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), recognizing viral DNA and subsequently activating downstream signaling pathways, thereby triggering the host’s innate immune defenses. Given the differences in genomic structure, replication sites, and host exploitation strategies among DNA viruses, they have evolved diverse replication approaches. Moreover, as key host regulatory factors, DDX proteins are extensively involved in both viral infection and the host immune response, performing distinct functions throughout the life cycles of different DNA viruses and in the activation of various signaling pathways. The following sections will discuss several DNA viruses individually.2.1.Hepatitis B virusThe hepatitis B virus (HBV) primarily infects the liver, leading to hepatitis, and its replication cycle is critically dependent on the formation of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) within the cell nucleus (Wei and Ploss, 2020; Gómez-Moreno and Ploss, 2024). Additionally, HBV exhibits unique spatiotemporal dynamics, leading to distinct mechanisms through which DDX proteins mediate its replication compared to other hepatitis viruses. full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionThe DEAD-box (DDX) protein family comprises a large and diverse group of highly conserved RNA helicases. The family derives its name from the conserved aspartic acid–glutamic acid–alanine–aspartic acid (Asp-Glu-Ala-Asp, DEAD) sequence within the Walker B motif of its core domain. This core domain comprises two RecA modules, each possessing ATP-binding and RNA-binding activities, and contains nine highly conserved sequence motifs. It is flanked by the N-terminal and C-terminal domains, which exhibit greater sequence diversity (Hirth et al., 2024; Tapescu and Cherry, 2024) and mediate key biological functions (Tanner et al., 2003; Song et al., 2023) (Figure 1). As central regulatory factors in RNA metabolism, DDX proteins are involved in several critical processes, including transcription, translation initiation, and messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) transport. Some DDX proteins can also interact with protein kinases; for example, by regulating the catalytic activity of microtubule affinity-regulating kinase 1 (MARK1), they participate in downstream signaling pathways (Chao et al., 2006; Soto-Rifo et al., 2012; Xing et al., 2019; Han et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023; Hirth et al., 2024).Figure 1Core domain of the DDX protein.Diagram of a protein with N-terminus and C-terminus labeled, showing RecA-like domains as colored boxes marked Q, I, Ia, Ib, II, III, IV, V, VI. A legend describes yellow boxes as regulating ATP binding and hydrolysis, blue boxes as coordinating ATP hydrolysis and RNA unwinding, green boxes as facilitating RNA binding, and a yellow “II” box as the DEAD (Walker B motif).During pathogen infection, DDX proteins act as host factors, participating in the intricate interactions between the host and the pathogen. Given this critical role, elucidating the interaction mechanisms between DDX proteins and viral pathogens is essential for understanding viral pathogenesis. These mechanistic insights represent a promising avenue for developing novel therapeutic strategies against viral pathogens. As strictly intracellular parasites, viruses utilize the host cell’s intrinsic molecules to carry out their life cycle and evade the host’s immune response. In this context, DDX proteins utilize their conserved catalytic cores to recognize RNA structural features in a sequence-independent manner (Tapescu et al., 2023; Tapescu and Cherry, 2024), thereby contributing to intracellular viral RNA unwinding, replication, transcription, translation, and assembly of viral particles (Linder and Jankowsky, 2011; Paine et al., 2019). Additionally, they regulate the host’s innate immune response by modulating relevant signaling pathways and protein expression (Ma et al., 2025a; Mao et al., 2024; Szappanos et al., 2018; Sandhu and Damania, 2025; Wu et al., 2026), thereby controlling viral infection. In the innate immune response, certain DDX proteins act as pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) to recognize viral nucleic acids and subsequently activate relevant signaling pathways (Miyashita et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011b, 2011a; Parthun et al., 2025). For example, DDX50 activates the Interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) signaling pathway upon stimulation by viral RNA or during infection with RNA and DNA viruses (Pallett et al., 2022). Furthermore, the DDX1-DDX21-DHX36 complex recognizes double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and utilizes the TIR domain-containing adaptor-inducing interferon-β (TRIF) pathway to activate the Type I Interferons (IFN-I) response (Zhang et al., 2011a), among other mechanisms. Moreover, in immune signaling cascades, DDX proteins not only act as sensors but also function as scaffold molecules to exert regulatory effects. For example, DDX3X, acting as a scaffold protein, directly facilitates the phosphorylation of IRF3 by IκB kinase-ε (IKKε), thereby contributing to the activation and regulation of the IRF3 pathway (Gu et al., 2013). Whether acting as PRRs or scaffold proteins, DDX proteins play a crucial role in regulating the host’s innate immune response.DDX proteins are not only key players in the innate immune system but also serve as vital tools for viruses to facilitate replication, reactivation, and immune evasion. Viruses can hijack DDX proteins to enhance viral replication or evade host immune surveillance, thereby enabling persistent infection or latent reactivation (Barra et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). For example, the Human papillomavirus regulatory protein E2 (HPV E2) hijacks DDX11 (ChlR1) to facilitate the binding of its own mitotic chromatin (Harris et al., 2016); the hepatitis C virus (HCV) hijacks DDX6 and the Processing body (P-body) to create conducive conditions for its own replication (Ariumi et al., 2011). It is precisely this dual role of DDX proteins in viral regulation that makes them a key battleground in the interplay between virus and host.DDX proteins and viruses share a complex, multifaceted relationship characterized by mutual influence and restraint, which is of great significance for the onset, progression, treatment and prevention of infectious diseases. Therefore, an in-depth investigation of the interactions between DDX proteins and viruses and their molecular mechanisms paves the way for the prevention and treatment of viral infectious diseases. This review will be organized primarily according to the type of viral nucleic acid, covering a range of viruses including hepatitis viruses, arboviruses, herpesviruses and oncoviruses. It will systematically summarize the mechanisms of their interactions with DDX proteins and the associated immune signaling pathways, and elucidate specific virus-DDX protein interactions, thereby offering novel theoretical insights into the prevention and control of viral infections. 2.DNA virus infection and DDX protein functionsAfter a host cell becomes infected, DNA viruses primarily rely on DNA polymerases to catalyze deoxyribonucleotide polymerization reactions. They also utilize enzymes encoded by either the host or the virus itself to carry out essential processes such as genome unwinding, primer synthesis, and damage repair (Gassmann et al., 1988; Tian et al., 2009; Lawler et al., 2024), with members of the DDX protein family playing a notable role in these activities. Viruses exploit DDX proteins to facilitate their own replication or to evade the host immune response. At the same time, upon detecting viral DNA, the host can activate classical signaling pathways like cyclic GMP-AMP synthase–stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING), Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9), and Retinoic acid-inducible gene I–mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (RIG-I-MAVS) to initiate an innate immune response (Ablasser et al., 2009; Fiola et al., 2010; Civril et al., 2013; Dansako et al., 2016; Hristova et al., 2024). In this context, DDX proteins act as pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), recognizing viral DNA and subsequently activating downstream signaling pathways, thereby triggering the host’s innate immune defenses. Given the differences in genomic structure, replication sites, and host exploitation strategies among DNA viruses, they have evolved diverse replication approaches. Moreover, as key host regulatory factors, DDX proteins are extensively involved in both viral infection and the host immune response, performing distinct functions throughout the life cycles of different DNA viruses and in the activation of various signaling pathways. full_text: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the most common malignant tumor in the head and neck region. In locally advanced patients, neoadjuvant chemotherapy centered on cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil often leads to primary/acquired resistance, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 50%. Tumor microenvironment (TME) immunosuppressive remodeling is the core cause of chemotherapy failure. Adipokines secreted by cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs) are the key mediators that link metabolic disorders, immune polarization and chemotherapy resistance. The adipokines leptin, adiponectin, chemerin, resistin, and GDF15 signal through pathways such as JAK2/STAT3, PI3K/AKT, NF-κB, and PPARγ to bidirectionally regulate the polarization phenotypes of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), CD4+/CD8+ T cells, and NK cells. Pro-cancer adipokines induce M2-type TAMs, MDSCs expansion, Th2/Th17 polarization, and effector T cell exhaustion, constructing an immunosuppressive microenvironment, upregulating DNA damage repair, drug efflux, and anti-apoptotic genes, and reducing cisplatin/5-FU chemosensitivity. The tumor-suppressive adipokine adiponectin promotes M1 macrophage and CD8+ effector T cell infiltration, reverses immunosuppression, and sensitizes chemotherapy. This article systematically reviews the origin and classification of adipokines, the polarization patterns of immune cells in the OSCC microenvironment, the molecular pathways by which various adipokines regulate immune polarization, and the complete mechanism by which immune polarization mediates chemotherapy resistance. It summarizes the value of clinical markers and targeted reversal strategies, points out current research bottlenecks, and looks forward to the translational prospects of metabolism-immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy, aiming to provide new metabolism-immune targets for overcoming chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer. 7Discussion7.1Full text summaryAdipokines secreted by CAAs are the key bridge connecting metabolic disorders in obesity, OSCC immune polarization and chemotherapy resistance: Pro-tumor adipokines such as leptin, chemerin, and resistin activate STAT3, NF-κB, and PPARγ pathways, induce TAMs M2 polarization, MDSCs and Treg amplification, CD8+ T cell exhaustion, construct an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and upregulate DNA repair, drug efflux, and anti-apoptotic genes, dual mediating cisplatin/5-FU chemotherapy resistance (19, 26, 30, 31). Adiponectin acts as a protective adipokine, reversing immunosuppression through the AMPK pathway, reprogramming M1 macrophages with functional cytotoxic T cells, and significantly enhancing chemosensitivity (15, 32).The combined strategy of targeting the tumor-promoting adipokine pathway, supplementing adiponectin, and reprogramming immune polarization has shown efficacy in reversing chemotherapy resistance in vitro and in animal models, providing a promising therapeutic approach for locally advanced, recurrent and metastatic oral cancer (2). Future clinical validation is warranted to translate these preclinical findings into patient benefit.7.2Future research directionsAt the basic mechanism level: Construct a three-dimensional OSCC organoid containing CAAs, oral microbiota, and multiple subsets of immune cells, and analyze the transcriptome dynamic changes of adipokines regulating immune polarization in combination with single-cell RNA sequencing. Use leptin and AdipoR1 gene knockout 4NQO oral cancer mice to stratify and verify the specific resistance pathways of each adipokine. Elucidate the interregulatory mechanism between oral periodontal pathogenic bacteria and CAAs adipokines.At the clinical translational level: Conduct multicenter prospective cohorts, unify serum adipokine detection standards, and establish OSCC chemotherapy risk prediction models. Develop a tumor-targeted nanodelivery system to wrap adiponectin and leptin siRNA and reduce systemic toxic side effects. Conduct Phase II clinical studies to verify the real benefits of metformin/JAK2 inhibitors combined with standard chemotherapy in improving survival in obese OSCC patients.At the individualized treatment level: Construct stratified treatment regimens based on BMI, HPV status, serum adipokine profile, and tumor tissue immune polarization markers, and give priority to metabolism-immune-chemotherapy triple regimens for high leptin resistance population to achieve precise individualized treatment of oral cancer. 6.2Summary of the study conclusionsThe study systematically explored the effect of adipokines regulating the polarization of immune cells in oral cancer on chemosensitivity and revealed the key role of adipokines in the occurrence, development and chemoresistance of oral cancer (1). Preclinical evidence indicates that adipokines are significantly highly expressed in oral cancer tissues, and their expression levels are positively correlated with the malignancy of the tumor (1). Further studies have shown that adipokines can regulate the polarization state of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) by activating signaling pathways such as PI3K/Akt, promoting their transformation to a pro-tumor phenotype (M2 type), thereby suppressing anti-tumor immune responses and enhancing tumor cell resistance to chemotherapy drugs (16, 26). In addition, adipokines can also affect the immune microenvironment by regulating abnormal lipid metabolism, leading to dysfunction of tumor-infiltrating immune cells and further exacerbating tumor immune escape (2). These findings not only provide a new perspective for understanding the molecular mechanisms of chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer, but also lay a theoretical foundation for developing treatment strategies based on the regulation of adipokines (32).The significance of the study lies in the first organic combination of adipokines, immune cell polarization and oral cancer chemosensitivity, revealing the complex regulatory network among the three (50). This discovery offers a potential new target for overcoming chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer. For example, by targeting adipokines or their downstream signaling pathways, it is possible to effectively reverse the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and enhance the cytotoxic efficiency of chemotherapy drugs against tumor cells. At the same time, the study highlights the importance of multidisciplinary intersections, combining research methods from tumor biology, immunology and metabolomics to provide new ideas for further exploration of the complex pathological mechanisms of oral cancer (2, 18). In conclusion, the study not only expanded the scope of research on adipokines in the field of tumor immunology, but also provided an important theoretical basis for individualized treatment of oral cancer (26). 7.1Full text summaryAdipokines secreted by CAAs are the key bridge connecting metabolic disorders in obesity, OSCC immune polarization and chemotherapy resistance: Pro-tumor adipokines such as leptin, chemerin, and resistin activate STAT3, NF-κB, and PPARγ pathways, induce TAMs M2 polarization, MDSCs and Treg amplification, CD8+ T cell exhaustion, construct an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and upregulate DNA repair, drug efflux, and anti-apoptotic genes, dual mediating cisplatin/5-FU chemotherapy resistance (19, 26, 30, 31). Adiponectin acts as a protective adipokine, reversing immunosuppression through the AMPK pathway, reprogramming M1 macrophages with functional cytotoxic T cells, and significantly enhancing chemosensitivity (15, 32).The combined strategy of targeting the tumor-promoting adipokine pathway, supplementing adiponectin, and reprogramming immune polarization has shown efficacy in reversing chemotherapy resistance in vitro and in animal models, providing a promising therapeutic approach for locally advanced, recurrent and metastatic oral cancer (2). Future clinical validation is warranted to translate these preclinical findings into patient benefit. 1Introduction1.1Clinical treatment dilemmas of oral cancer and the current situation of chemotherapy resistanceOral squamous cell carcinoma accounts for more than 90% of oral malignancies (1). Smoking, alcohol consumption, betel nut chewing, HPV infection, obesity and metabolic disorders are the main high-risk factors (2–5). Clinical stage I/II OSCC can be cured by surgery, but more than 60% of patients are initially diagnosed as locally advanced stage III/IV with cervical lymph node metastasis (6). The treatment is mainly surgery combined with neoadjuvant/adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy, and patients with advanced metastasis can only rely on palliative chemotherapy to prolong survival (7). Cisplatin (DDP) or carboplatin combined with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) is the first-line standard regimen, but the objective response rate is only 35% to 48%. More than half of patients develop chemotherapy resistance in the short term, manifested as insignificant tumor shrinkage, recurrence and metastasis, aggravated toxicity, and shortened survival (3, 8).Conventional chemotherapy resistance mechanisms mostly focus on inherent changes in tumor cells: high expression of the DNA repair gene ERCC1 enhances cisplatin damage repair, overexpression of the ABCB1/P-gp drug efflux pump reduces intracellular drug concentration, upregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2/MCL1, and maintenance of stemness of tumor stem cells, etc. However, single-cell sequencing of clinical samples has confirmed that immune remodeling in the tumor microenvironment has a much greater impact on chemosensitivity than mutations in tumor cells themselves. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the infiltration density of M2-type TAMs, MDSCs, and regulatory T cells (Treg) in drug-resistant OSCC tissues increased significantly, and M1 anti-tumor macrophages and functional CD8+ T cells were depleted, creating a dual microenvironment of “immune desert + immunosuppression”. Even if chemotherapy drugs enter the tumor, they fail to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD), ultimately leading to treatment failure.Obesity, as an independent high-risk factor for OSCC, has a 42% lower chemotherapy response rate and a 2.1-fold higher recurrence risk in obese patients with a BMI of ≥28 compared to those with normal weight (5). In obese patients, there is extensive infiltration of adipose tissue around the oral mucosa and submandibular glands into the tumor stroma, differentiation into CAAs, and continuous release of hundreds of adipokines, free fatty acids (FFA), and inflammatory mediators, forming a unique metabolic immune microenvironment (9, 10). Clinical correlation analysis confirmed that the levels of serum leptin, chemerin and resistin in OSCC patients were positively correlated with chemotherapy resistance, lymph node metastasis and poor prognosis; Adiponectin levels were significantly negatively correlated with chemotherapy response rate and overall survival, suggesting that adipokines are the core mediators of metabolic disorders mediating chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer.1.2Research progress on adipokines and tumor immune polarizationAdipose tissue is no longer regarded merely as an energy storage organ but as the largest endocrine organ in the body (11–13) divided into white adipose tissue (WAT), brown adipose tissue (BAT), and tumor stromal CAAs are formed by dedifferentiation of mature adipocytes, with significantly enhanced lipolysis activity and secretion of two types of adipokines: 1 Pro-tumor adipokines: leptin, chemerin, resistin, IL-6, VEGF; 2 Anti-tumor adipokines: adiponectin, GDF15 (bidirectional action), visfatin (bidirectional action) (14). Adipokines act on tumor cells and infiltrating immune cells through autocrine, paracrine, and endocrine pathways, regulating cell proliferation, apoptosis, lipid metabolism, cytokine secretion, and reshaping the polarization phenotype of immune cells.Immune cell polarization is at the core of immune microenvironment plasticity: Macrophages are classified into classically activated M1 type (anti-tumor, secreting TNF-α, IL-12, IFN-γ, strong antigen-presenting ability, killing tumor) and alternatively activated M2 type (pro-tumor, secreting IL-10, TGF-β, CCL22, inhibiting effector T cells, promoting angiogenesis, invasion resistance); CD4+ T cells are classified as Th1 (anti-tumor), Th2, Th17, and Treg (immunosuppressive); CD8+ T cells are divided into functional effector T cells and exhausted PD-1+TIM-3+ T cells; MDSCs and NK cells also have tumor-promoting/tumor-suppressing polarization subtypes.Existing studies in breast cancer, lung cancer and pancreatic cancer have confirmed that leptin induces TAMs M2 polarization and MDSCs proliferation, while adiponectin promotes M1 polarization (15, 16). However, there is still a gap in the study of systemic mechanisms for OSCC: The special anatomical location of maxillofacial adipose tissue, the continuous stimulation of chronic oral inflammation, and the involvement of microbiota in metabolic regulation make the metabolic-immune axis of OSCC tissue-specific. The lack of a complete signaling axis for adipokines-immune polarization-chemotherapy resistance, and the absence of in vivo and in vitro validation systems for targeted adipokines combined with chemotherapy, limits clinical translation. This regulatory network is depicted in Figure 1.Figure 1Adipokine regulation of immune polarization and chemosensitivity in OSCC. Upstream, CAAs and adipocytes release pro-tumor adipokines (leptin, chemerin, resistin, IL-6) and the anti-tumor adipokine adiponectin. These converge on the downstream nodes STAT3, NF-κB, PI3K/AKT, and AMPK: pro-tumor adipokines activate JAK2/STAT3, PI3K/AKT, and NF-κB to drive M2 macrophage polarization, MDSC/Treg expansion, and CD8+ T-cell exhaustion, upregulating ERCC1, ABCB1, and Bcl-2 to promote chemotherapy resistance, whereas adiponectin activates AMPK to reverse this program and sensitize chemotherapy. Pro-tumor adipokines like leptin, chemerin, and resistin activate signaling pathways (JAK2/STAT3, PI3K/AKT, NF-κB), promoting M2 macrophages, MDSCs, Treg, Th17, and CD8+ T cell exhaustion, leading to chemoresistance and increased ERCC1, ABCB1, Bcl-2. In contrast, adiponectin, linked with cancer-associated adipocytes, promotes M1 macrophages, CD8+ effector T and NK cells, improving chemosensitivity by lowering ERCC1, ABCB1, and Bcl-2. full_text_sections.conclusion: 6.2Summary of the study conclusionsThe study systematically explored the effect of adipokines regulating the polarization of immune cells in oral cancer on chemosensitivity and revealed the key role of adipokines in the occurrence, development and chemoresistance of oral cancer (1). Preclinical evidence indicates that adipokines are significantly highly expressed in oral cancer tissues, and their expression levels are positively correlated with the malignancy of the tumor (1). Further studies have shown that adipokines can regulate the polarization state of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) by activating signaling pathways such as PI3K/Akt, promoting their transformation to a pro-tumor phenotype (M2 type), thereby suppressing anti-tumor immune responses and enhancing tumor cell resistance to chemotherapy drugs (16, 26). In addition, adipokines can also affect the immune microenvironment by regulating abnormal lipid metabolism, leading to dysfunction of tumor-infiltrating immune cells and further exacerbating tumor immune escape (2). These findings not only provide a new perspective for understanding the molecular mechanisms of chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer, but also lay a theoretical foundation for developing treatment strategies based on the regulation of adipokines (32).The significance of the study lies in the first organic combination of adipokines, immune cell polarization and oral cancer chemosensitivity, revealing the complex regulatory network among the three (50). This discovery offers a potential new target for overcoming chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer. For example, by targeting adipokines or their downstream signaling pathways, it is possible to effectively reverse the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and enhance the cytotoxic efficiency of chemotherapy drugs against tumor cells. At the same time, the study highlights the importance of multidisciplinary intersections, combining research methods from tumor biology, immunology and metabolomics to provide new ideas for further exploration of the complex pathological mechanisms of oral cancer (2, 18). In conclusion, the study not only expanded the scope of research on adipokines in the field of tumor immunology, but also provided an important theoretical basis for individualized treatment of oral cancer (26). 7.1Full text summaryAdipokines secreted by CAAs are the key bridge connecting metabolic disorders in obesity, OSCC immune polarization and chemotherapy resistance: Pro-tumor adipokines such as leptin, chemerin, and resistin activate STAT3, NF-κB, and PPARγ pathways, induce TAMs M2 polarization, MDSCs and Treg amplification, CD8+ T cell exhaustion, construct an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and upregulate DNA repair, drug efflux, and anti-apoptotic genes, dual mediating cisplatin/5-FU chemotherapy resistance (19, 26, 30, 31). Adiponectin acts as a protective adipokine, reversing immunosuppression through the AMPK pathway, reprogramming M1 macrophages with functional cytotoxic T cells, and significantly enhancing chemosensitivity (15, 32).The combined strategy of targeting the tumor-promoting adipokine pathway, supplementing adiponectin, and reprogramming immune polarization has shown efficacy in reversing chemotherapy resistance in vitro and in animal models, providing a promising therapeutic approach for locally advanced, recurrent and metastatic oral cancer (2). Future clinical validation is warranted to translate these preclinical findings into patient benefit.
full_text_sections.other: 1Introduction1.1Clinical treatment dilemmas of oral cancer and the current situation of chemotherapy resistanceOral squamous cell carcinoma accounts for more than 90% of oral malignancies (1). Smoking, alcohol consumption, betel nut chewing, HPV infection, obesity and metabolic disorders are the main high-risk factors (2–5). Clinical stage I/II OSCC can be cured by surgery, but more than 60% of patients are initially diagnosed as locally advanced stage III/IV with cervical lymph node metastasis (6). The treatment is mainly surgery combined with neoadjuvant/adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy, and patients with advanced metastasis can only rely on palliative chemotherapy to prolong survival (7). Cisplatin (DDP) or carboplatin combined with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) is the first-line standard regimen, but the objective response rate is only 35% to 48%. More than half of patients develop chemotherapy resistance in the short term, manifested as insignificant tumor shrinkage, recurrence and metastasis, aggravated toxicity, and shortened survival (3, 8).Conventional chemotherapy resistance mechanisms mostly focus on inherent changes in tumor cells: high expression of the DNA repair gene ERCC1 enhances cisplatin damage repair, overexpression of the ABCB1/P-gp drug efflux pump reduces intracellular drug concentration, upregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2/MCL1, and maintenance of stemness of tumor stem cells, etc. However, single-cell sequencing of clinical samples has confirmed that immune remodeling in the tumor microenvironment has a much greater impact on chemosensitivity than mutations in tumor cells themselves. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the infiltration density of M2-type TAMs, MDSCs, and regulatory T cells (Treg) in drug-resistant OSCC tissues increased significantly, and M1 anti-tumor macrophages and functional CD8+ T cells were depleted, creating a dual microenvironment of “immune desert + immunosuppression”. Even if chemotherapy drugs enter the tumor, they fail to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD), ultimately leading to treatment failure.Obesity, as an independent high-risk factor for OSCC, has a 42% lower chemotherapy response rate and a 2.1-fold higher recurrence risk in obese patients with a BMI of ≥28 compared to those with normal weight (5). In obese patients, there is extensive infiltration of adipose tissue around the oral mucosa and submandibular glands into the tumor stroma, differentiation into CAAs, and continuous release of hundreds of adipokines, free fatty acids (FFA), and inflammatory mediators, forming a unique metabolic immune microenvironment (9, 10). Clinical correlation analysis confirmed that the levels of serum leptin, chemerin and resistin in OSCC patients were positively correlated with chemotherapy resistance, lymph node metastasis and poor prognosis; Adiponectin levels were significantly negatively correlated with chemotherapy response rate and overall survival, suggesting that adipokines are the core mediators of metabolic disorders mediating chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer.1.2Research progress on adipokines and tumor immune polarizationAdipose tissue is no longer regarded merely as an energy storage organ but as the largest endocrine organ in the body (11–13) divided into white adipose tissue (WAT), brown adipose tissue (BAT), and tumor stromal CAAs are formed by dedifferentiation of mature adipocytes, with significantly enhanced lipolysis activity and secretion of two types of adipokines: 1 Pro-tumor adipokines: leptin, chemerin, resistin, IL-6, VEGF; 2 Anti-tumor adipokines: adiponectin, GDF15 (bidirectional action), visfatin (bidirectional action) (14). Adipokines act on tumor cells and infiltrating immune cells through autocrine, paracrine, and endocrine pathways, regulating cell proliferation, apoptosis, lipid metabolism, cytokine secretion, and reshaping the polarization phenotype of immune cells.Immune cell polarization is at the core of immune microenvironment plasticity: Macrophages are classified into classically activated M1 type (anti-tumor, secreting TNF-α, IL-12, IFN-γ, strong antigen-presenting ability, killing tumor) and alternatively activated M2 type (pro-tumor, secreting IL-10, TGF-β, CCL22, inhibiting effector T cells, promoting angiogenesis, invasion resistance); CD4+ T cells are classified as Th1 (anti-tumor), Th2, Th17, and Treg (immunosuppressive); CD8+ T cells are divided into functional effector T cells and exhausted PD-1+TIM-3+ T cells; MDSCs and NK cells also have tumor-promoting/tumor-suppressing polarization subtypes.Existing studies in breast cancer, lung cancer and pancreatic cancer have confirmed that leptin induces TAMs M2 polarization and MDSCs proliferation, while adiponectin promotes M1 polarization (15, 16). However, there is still a gap in the study of systemic mechanisms for OSCC: The special anatomical location of maxillofacial adipose tissue, the continuous stimulation of chronic oral inflammation, and the involvement of microbiota in metabolic regulation make the metabolic-immune axis of OSCC tissue-specific. The lack of a complete signaling axis for adipokines-immune polarization-chemotherapy resistance, and the absence of in vivo and in vitro validation systems for targeted adipokines combined with chemotherapy, limits clinical translation. This regulatory network is depicted in Figure 1.Figure 1Adipokine regulation of immune polarization and chemosensitivity in OSCC. Upstream, CAAs and adipocytes release pro-tumor adipokines (leptin, chemerin, resistin, IL-6) and the anti-tumor adipokine adiponectin. These converge on the downstream nodes STAT3, NF-κB, PI3K/AKT, and AMPK: pro-tumor adipokines activate JAK2/STAT3, PI3K/AKT, and NF-κB to drive M2 macrophage polarization, MDSC/Treg expansion, and CD8+ T-cell exhaustion, upregulating ERCC1, ABCB1, and Bcl-2 to promote chemotherapy resistance, whereas adiponectin activates AMPK to reverse this program and sensitize chemotherapy. CAA, cancer-associated adipocyte.Infographic showing how adipokines regulate immune polarization and chemosensitivity in oral squamous cell carcinoma. Pro-tumor adipokines like leptin, chemerin, and resistin activate signaling pathways (JAK2/STAT3, PI3K/AKT, NF-κB), promoting M2 macrophages, MDSCs, Treg, Th17, and CD8+ T cell exhaustion, leading to chemoresistance and increased ERCC1, ABCB1, Bcl-2. In contrast, adiponectin, linked with cancer-associated adipocytes, promotes M1 macrophages, CD8+ effector T and NK cells, improving chemosensitivity by lowering ERCC1, ABCB1, and Bcl-2. Arrows indicate regulatory pathways across four main categories.1.3Study significance and innovation pointsBy systematically integrating peer-reviewed basic and clinical evidence to construct a complete regulatory network of “CAAs-adipokines-immune cell polarization-chemosensitivity”, the innovations are as follows:This article is a narrative review rather than a systematic review. To reduce the risk of a biased literature view, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus for English-language articles published up to August 2026 using combinations of the terms oral squamous cell carcinoma, adipokine, leptin, adiponectin, chemerin, resistin, tumor microenvironment, immune polarization, chemotherapy resistance, and immune checkpoint inhibitor. The search terms were combined with Boolean operators and adapted to each database. Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts, discrepancies were resolved by consensus, and the reference lists of eligible articles were hand-searched. Any uncertainty about eligibility was resolved by discussion between the two screeners before a study was included or excluded, so that the review reflects a consensus synthesis of the available evidence rather than a pooled quantitative estimate. Tata Memorial Centre, Homi Bhabha National Institute (HBNI), New-Chandigarh 140901, India Abstract Background: Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among Indian women, with low screening coverage, especially in rural areas. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 16 and 18, is the main cause. This study evaluated socio-demographic factors associated with visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), Pap smear and HPV positivity and compared the diagnostic performance of these screening methods. Methods: This retrospective study included 641 women aged 30 to 55 years screened at two preventive oncology centres in Mullanpur and Sangrur between October 2024 and April 2025. Participants underwent VIA, Pap smear and HPV DNA testing. VIA findings were interpreted according to the World Health Organization guidelines, and Pap smear results were assessed using standard criteria. HPV results were categorised as HPV 16/18 or other high-risk types. Women positive on any screening test underwent colposcopy, with cervical punch biopsy performed when indicated. Results: Among the women screened, VIA positivity was 31.9%, HPV positivity was 18.8% and Pap smear positivity was 1.7%. VIA positivity was higher among rural women and those with lower income, whereas HPV positivity was associated with early age at marriage and higher parity. For detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 2+ (CIN2+) lesions, VIA demonstrated 100% sensitivity and lower specificity, Pap smear showed high specificity (99.5%) but lower sensitivity, while HPV DNA testing demonstrated 93.3% sensitivity and 82.8% specificity, with the highest diagnostic accuracy. Conclusion: HPV DNA testing demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for detecting CIN II+ lesions, while VIA showed high sensitivity but lower specificity, making it a practical screening tool in low-resource settings. Pap smear remained highly specific but detected fewer high-grade lesions. Early marriage, higher parity and lower socioeconomic status were associated with increased HPV positivity. These findings support risk-based cervical cancer screening strategies that integrate HPV DNA testing and VIA to improve early detection and reduce the burden of cervical cancer in resource-limited settings. Keywords: cervical cancer screening, human papillomavirus, visual inspection with acetic acid, Pap smear, socio-economic factors Correspondence to: Vandita Pahwa Email: drvanditapahwa@gmail.com Published: 15/10/2026 Received: 10/02/2026 Publication costs for this article were supported by ecancer (UK Charity number 1176307). Introduction Despite decades of cancer control programmes in India, cervical cancer screening coverage remains very low. Globally, cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer among women, with an estimated 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths reported in 2022 [1]. In India, it is the second most common cancer among women; however, the screening rate for women aged 30 to 49 years in both urban and rural populations remains below 2.5% [2–4]. According to GLOBOCAN 2020, nearly half a million new cervical cancer cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, with 50% mortality [3]. Most patients present at advanced stages, resulting in substantial morbidity and mortality [2,3]. Low literacy levels, limited awareness and socioeconomic challenges, particularly in rural areas, remain major barriers to effective utilisation of screening services [4]. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 16 and 18, is the primary risk factor for cervical cancer [1,5]. Although most HPV infections are transient, persistent infection in the presence of cofactors such as early age at marriage, high parity, smoking, obesity and immuno-suppression can progress to high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN II/III) and invasive cervical cancer [1,5,7]. Additional socio-demographic and behavioural factors, including age at marriage, parity, genital hygiene, medication use and substance use, have also been shown to influence cervical cancer risk [4,7,8]. Screening methods such as visual inspection with acetic acid or Lugol’s iodine (VIA/VILI), Pap smear cytology and HPV DNA testing are widely used for early detection and prevention [1,6,9]. Evidence from India and other low- and middle-income countries suggests that HPV-based screening, combined with cytology or VIA, represents an effective and feasible approach in low-resource settings [5,8,13]. Socio-demographic determinants strongly influence screening outcomes; women from rural areas, those with low literacy or socioeconomic status, and those married at an early age or with high parity are more likely to be HPV positive and less likely to access screening services [4,7,8]. Targeted interventions for these high-risk groups are therefore essential to improve early detection and reduce the burden of cervical cancer. However, variability in the performance of VIA, Pap smear and HPV testing has been reported across different Indian populations, highlighting the need for locally relevant, evidence-based screening strategies [6,9,10]. This study aimed to explore socio-demographic factors associated with HPV, Pap smear and VIA positivity; examine the strengths and limitations of each screening method and evaluate their sensitivity, specificity and diagnostic accuracy. The findings are intended to inform the development of evidence-based cervical cancer screening programmes in India. Materials and methods Study design and setting This retrospective observational study was conducted at the Preventive Oncology Departments of the Mullanpur and Sangrur centres. Medical records of women who underwent cervical cancer screening using Pap smear cytology, HPV DNA testing, VIA/VILI and colposcopy between October 2024 and April 2025 were systematically reviewed. Study population Women aged 30 to 55 years who underwent all three screening modalities (VIA, Pap smear and HPV DNA testing) along with colposcopic examination were included. Records were identified from hospital databases and screening registers. Women with incomplete documentation, a prior hysterectomy, known cervical cancer, or pregnancy were excluded. Only complete records were included in the final analysis. Data collection Data on demographic characteristics, reproductive history, contraceptive use, tobacco exposure, prior screening history, per-speculum clinical findings and screening test results were extracted using a standardised data collection format. Data extraction was performed independently by trained personnel, and discrepancies were resolved through cross-verification with source documents to ensure accuracy and reliability. Screening procedures Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) VIA was performed using 5% acetic acid. VIA positivity was defined as the presence of sharply demarcated, dense aceto-white areas in the transformation zone or columnar epithelium. Pap smear collection and interpretation Cervical cytology samples were collected following appropriate counselling and positioning. Ectocervical and endocervical samples were obtained using cotton swabs, smeared onto labelled glass slides and fixed in 95% ethanol. Cytological interpretation was performed according to the Bethesda system. Results were considered positive if atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) or higher-grade abnormalities (including low-grade squamous lntraepithelial lesion and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL)) were detected, and negative if no intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM) was reported. HPV DNA testing Cervical samples were collected using a Digene conical brush rotated 360° 3 to 4 times at the cervical OS and placed in 1 mL of Digene transport medium. HPV DNA testing was performed using the AnyplexTM II HPV HR Detection Assay, which detects 14 high-risk HPV genotypes, including HPV-16, HPV-18 and 12 additional types (31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66 and 68). Results were categorised as positive for HPV 16/18, positive for other high-risk HPV types or negative if no HPV DNA was detected. Colposcopy and histopathology Women who tested positive by any screening method underwent colposcopic examination. Cervical biopsies were obtained from suspicious areas and submitted for histopathological evaluation to confirm the presence of CIN or invasive malignancy. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarise demographic and clinical characteristics. Age was categorised as <45 years and ≥45 years. Associations between socio-demographic variables and screening outcomes were assessed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate [12]. Univariate logistic regression analysis was performed to estimate odds ratios for associations between demographic and clinical factors and screening test positivity. Variables with an adequate number of events (e.g. VIA positivity = 31.9%) were included in multivariate logistic regression models, with stepwise removal of non-significant predictors [13]. The association between screening test results and histopathological findings was evaluated using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance measures including sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) were calculated using histopathology as the reference standard. Agreement between HPV DNA testing, Pap smear cytology, and VIA/VILI was assessed using κ statistics. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 29 and R version 4.5.1 [14,15]. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Data quality control Records were reviewed for completeness and duplicate entries were removed. Uniform criteria for test positivity were applied consistently across all records. Ethical considerations Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Ethics Committee of Homi Bhabha Cancer Hospital and Research Centre (Project ID: 15000064). As this study involved a retrospective review of medical records, no direct patient contact occurred. All patient data were de-identified, and confidentiality was strictly maintained. Informed consent for cervical cancer screening had been obtained from all participants at the time of their initial evaluation. Results A total of 641 women were included in this retrospective analysis. The majority of participants (79.4%) were <45 years. Most women resided in rural areas (81.3%), while 18.7% were from urban settings. Regarding educational status, 16.7% of participants were illiterate, 48.8% had completed education up to the tenth grade and 34.5% had attained education beyond secondary school. Most participants belonged to the Sikh community (73.6%), with the remaining 26.4% representing other religious groups. The majority of women (82.7%) were housewives. Assessment of per capita income showed that nearly two-thirds of participants (65.2%) had a monthly income below INR 4,411, indicating a predominantly low-income population. Reproductive characteristics revealed that early marriage was common, with 64.0% of women married at or before 21 years of age and 49.5% of participants had their first pregnancy at an early age. Screening results showed that 205 women (31.9%) were VIA positive, 121 women (18.8%) tested positive for HPV DNA, and 11 women (1.7%) had a positive Pap smear. Baseline demographic, socioeconomic, reproductive characteristics and screening outcomes are summarised in Table 1. As shown in Figure 1, among the 284 women who tested positive by at least 1 screening method, 204 (31.8% of the total screened population) had abnormal findings on colposcopy, while the remaining screen-positive women did not show visible cervical lesions. Cervical punch biopsy was performed in 188 women with abnormal colposcopy (92.1%), whereas 16 women (7.8%) declined biopsy despite clinical recommendation. Histopathological examination showed benign results in 173 women (92.0%), CIN II in 6 women (3.2%) and CIN III or higher lesions in 9 women (4.8%). The association of various epidemiological factors including age, socioeconomic status, literacy, gynaecological history0 and other relevant characteristics was evaluated in relation to the outcomes of VIA, Pap smear and HPV testing (Table 2). Some socio-demographic characteristics showed statistically significant associations, particularly with VIA and HPV positivity. VIA positivity Among the 641 women screened, 205 (31.9%) tested positive for VIA. The majority of VIA-positive women were <45 years (85.4%), whereas women >45 years were less likely to test positive (odds ratio (OR) = 0.60; 95% CI: 0.38–0.95; p = 0.03). Rural residence was strongly associated with VIA positivity, with women from rural areas having more than twice the odds of testing positive compared to urban residents (OR = 2.13; 95% CI: 1.45–4.10; p < 0.001). Low per capita income (<4,411 INR) was also significantly associated with higher VIA positivity (OR = 1.78; 95% CI: 1.25–2.53; p < 0.001). No significant associations were observed with education level or other socio-demographic factors. These findings suggest that younger age, rural residence and lower income were the main factors influencing VIA positivity in this population. Table 1. Demographic, reproductive and screening characteristics of study participants (n = 641). Pap smear positivity Pap smear positivity was observed in 11 women (1.7%). Most smears were negative (80.3%), followed by inflammatory changes (13.4%) and bacterial vaginosis (4.5%). Among the positive smears, five cases were ASC-US, three were HSIL and two showed invasive carcinoma. Although no socio-demographic factor reached statistical significance, Pap positivity tended to be slightly higher in women from rural areas, those with low income, early marriage (≤21 years), or having >2 live births. HPV positivity HPV DNA positivity was observed in 121 women (18.8%), with nearly half (48.7%) positive for high-risk HPV types 16 and 18. Early marriage (≤21 years) was significantly associated with HPV positivity (OR = 1.72; 95% CI: 1.11–2.68; p = 0.02), and women with >2 live births had higher odds of being HPV positive (OR = 1.60; 95% CI: 1.05–2.44; p = 0.03). Other socio-demographic factors, including age, residence and per capita income, were not significantly associated with HPV positivity (Table 2). Adjusted odds analysis (AOR) After adjusting for socio-demographic and reproductive factors, VIA positivity was significantly associated with younger age, rural residence, lower income and a history of abortion. Women >45 years had lower odds of VIA positivity compared to those aged ≤45 years (AOR = 0.59; 95% CI: 0.38–0.93; p = 0.02), while rural residents had about twice the odds compared to urban residents (AOR = 2.00; 95% CI: 1.23–3.28; p = 0.01). Lower per capita income showed a borderline increase in odds (AOR = 1.42; 95% CI: 0.98–2.04; p = 0.06) and having at least one abortion was also associated with higher odds of VIA positivity (AOR = 1.41; 95% CI: 1.00–2.01; p = 0.05). In contrast, HPV positivity was not significantly associated with age, residence, income or history of abortion. Early marriage (≤21 years) (AOR = 1.72; 95% CI: 1.11–2.68; p = 0.02) and having >2 live births (AOR = 1.60; 95% CI: 1.05–2.44; p = 0.03) were the main factors associated with HPV positivity. Adjusted odds were not calculated for Pap smear due to the small number of positive cases (Table 3). The performance of VIA, Pap smear and HPV testing for detecting high-grade cervical lesions is summarised in Table 4. Figure 1. Flow diagram of study participants and screening outcomes. Pap smear remained highly specific but detected fewer high-grade lesions. Early marriage, higher parity and lower socioeconomic status were associated with increased HPV positivity. These findings support risk-based cervical cancer screening strategies that integrate HPV DNA testing and VIA to improve early detection and reduce the burden of cervical cancer in resource-limited settings. Introduction Despite decades of cancer control programmes in India, cervical cancer screening coverage remains very low. Globally, cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer among women, with an estimated 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths reported in 2022 [1]. In India, it is the second most common cancer among women; however, the screening rate for women aged 30 to 49 years in both urban and rural populations remains below 2.5% [2–4]. According to GLOBOCAN 2020, nearly half a million new cervical cancer cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, with 50% mortality [3]. Most patients present at advanced stages, resulting in substantial morbidity and mortality [2,3]. Low literacy levels, limited awareness and socioeconomic challenges, particularly in rural areas, remain major barriers to effective utilisation of screening services [4]. Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 16 and 18, is the primary risk factor for cervical cancer [1,5]. Although most HPV infections are transient, persistent infection in the presence of cofactors such as early age at marriage, high parity, smoking, obesity and immuno-suppression can progress to high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN II/III) and invasive cervical cancer [1,5,7]. Additional socio-demographic and behavioural factors, including age at marriage, parity, genital hygiene, medication use and substance use, have also been shown to influence cervical cancer risk [4,7,8]. Screening methods such as visual inspection with acetic acid or Lugol’s iodine (VIA/VILI), Pap smear cytology and HPV DNA testing are widely used for early detection and prevention [1,6,9]. Evidence from India and other low- and middle-income countries suggests that HPV-based screening, combined with cytology or VIA, represents an effective and feasible approach in low-resource settings [5,8,13]. Socio-demographic determinants strongly influence screening outcomes; women from rural areas, those with low literacy or socioeconomic status, and those married at an early age or with high parity are more likely to be HPV positive and less likely to access screening services [4,7,8]. Targeted interventions for these high-risk groups are therefore essential to improve early detection and reduce the burden of cervical cancer. However, variability in the performance of VIA, Pap smear and HPV testing has been reported across different Indian populations, highlighting the need for locally relevant, evidence-based screening strategies [6,9,10]. This study aimed to explore socio-demographic factors associated with HPV, Pap smear and VIA positivity; examine the strengths and limitations of each screening method and evaluate their sensitivity, specificity and diagnostic accuracy. The findings are intended to inform the development of evidence-based cervical cancer screening programmes in India.
